claims.metric: Final training run compute cost

sources.title: Epoch AI: How much does it cost to train frontier AI models?
Forbes/Statista: The Extreme Cost of Training AI Models (AI Index data)
TechRadar: OpenAI spent $80m-$100m training GPT-4

claims.notes: Estimates span methods: Epoch amortized hardware+energy ~$40M; AI Index cloud-rental basis ~$78M; Sam Altman on record 'more than $100 million' (all-in, likely including staff/R&D). Central $70M reflects compute-only; all-in cost with staff exceeds $100M. Anchors the starting scale of frontier fixed costs for T1.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE TRACED. The claim cites Epoch's blog post; the actual primary is Cottier, Rahman, Fattorini, Maslej, Besiroglu & Owen, "The rising costs of training frontier AI models," arXiv:2405.21015v2 (7 Feb 2025), plus its data repo (github.com/epoch-research/training-cost-trends) and the live Epoch database. I pulled all three.

WHAT THE PRIMARY ACTUALLY SAYS (GPT-4, final training run):
- Amortized hardware CapEx + energy: $40.70M (model_costs.csv), quoted as "$40M" in the paper text; the LIVE Epoch database (snapshot current to 2026-07-15, which I downloaded) lists $37.33M (2023 USD).
- Cloud rental price approach: $78.56M (repo) / $81.39M (live db). This IS the Stanford AI Index $78M figure — the paper states the AI Index dataset was produced "in collaboration with Epoch AI... based on cloud rental prices," and Fattorini/Maslej are AI Index staff.
- Hardware acquisition (upfront): $778M (repo) / $806M (live db).
- Amortized hardware over WHOLE development: ~$90M; R&D staff incl. equity = 29% of GPT-4's total → full development cost ≈ $125–140M.

FOUR PROBLEMS WITH THE CLAIM AS WRITTEN:

1) CENTRAL VALUE SKEWED HIGH, AGAINST THE LEAD SOURCE'S OWN RECOMMENDATION. Epoch explicitly writes: "We recommend using the amortized hardware CapEx + energy approach for frontier models wherever it's feasible" and "We expect the cloud-price approach to overestimate frontier model costs, since model developers usually either own or have private rental agreements for their training hardware." OpenAI/GPT-4 is the paradigm case of that caveat — trained on Azure under the Microsoft strategic partnership, not at public list rates. The claim's $70M sits 1.72x above the recommended figure and above the arithmetic mean ($59M) and geometric mean ($56M) of the two published methods. The claim's own cited Forbes/Statista piece renders the Epoch range as "$41M–$78M"; $70M is roughly the 85th percentile of that band.

2) FAKE SOURCE INDEPENDENCE. Three sources are listed as if triangulating. They are one primary source with two methods, plus a tertiary aggregator. AI Index's $78M is not corroboration of Epoch — it IS Epoch's cloud number. TechRadar's "$80m–$100m" is untraceable to any primary disclosure (I fetched it; no sourcing in the body) and appears to splice the AI Index cloud figure to Altman's all-in soundbite — two different quantities.

3) THE CI MISREPRESENTS SOURCE UNCERTAINTY, AND IS TOO NARROW ON THE LOW SIDE. Epoch's Table 5 gives a 90% CI on individual amortized GPU-trained cost estimates of 0.3x to 2x... correction: 0.3x to 4x. Applied to $40.7M that is $12M–$163M at 90%; roughly $16M–$122M at 80%. Separately, Epoch's live database flags GPT-4's underlying training-compute estimate at 2.1e25 FLOP with a 90% CI of 8.2e24 to 4.4e25 (0.39x–2.1x) and notes "this is a rough estimate based on public information, much less information than most other systems in the database" (Confidence: "Likely"). The claim's ci80_low of $35M therefore places Epoch's own headline point estimate ($37.3M live, $40.7M in the paper) essentially AT the 10th percentile of the claim's distribution. An 80% interval that treats your lead source's recommended answer as a tail outcome is not a faithful representation of uncertainty. The high bound of $150M is also too generous for a compute-only metric — it exceeds Epoch's full model development cost including R&D staff and equity (~$125–140M).

4) PROVENANCE IS WEAKER THAN GRADE B IMPLIES. There is NO primary disclosure. The GPT-4 Technical Report (arXiv:2303.08774) deliberately withholds architecture, compute, hardware, and cost. Every published estimate descends from the July 2023 SemiAnalysis leak (25,000 A100s, 90–100 days, 32–36% MFU) — Epoch's own database cites SemiAnalysis for hardware quantity and training time, and labels the training-time note "(Speculative)." SemiAnalysis's own figure was ~$63M at an assumed $1/A100-hour. Altman's ">$100 million" is a verbal, all-in figure for a different quantity and cannot anchor a compute-only estimate.

FRESHNESS CHECK: The Epoch database snapshot I pulled runs through 2026-07-15 and still carries $37.33M for GPT-4 (Mar 2023). Epoch has not revised it upward in two years. For context in the current frontier, GPT-4 now ranks only 6th by amortized training cost behind Grok 4 ($388M), GPT-4.5 ($366M), Grok 3 ($218M), Llama 3.1-405B ($53M) and Llama 4 Behemoth ($45M).

CORRECTION. The compute-only estimates cluster in two methodological families: amortized-owner ($37–41M) and rental-rate (SemiAnalysis $63M, Epoch/AI Index cloud $79–81M). The economically meaningful number for OpenAI in 2022 sits between, tilted toward the amortized end per Epoch's explicit guidance. A log-weighted blend gives ~$50–58M. I set corrected_value = $55M (2023 USD) with an 80% CI of $25M–$120M, which (a) contains every published primary estimate — 37.3, 40.7, 63, 78.6, 81.4 — rather than pushing the recommended one into the tail, (b) honors Epoch's stated 0.3x–4x (90%) method uncertainty compounded with a 0.39x–2.1x compute uncertainty, and (c) caps the upper bound below the documented full-development cost, as a compute-only metric must.

TWO NOTES FOR THE LEDGER, BOTH THESIS-RELEVANT:
(a) Base year. Epoch's figures are 2023 USD. The claim does not state a base year. Any comparison against 2026 frontier run costs must either deflate those or inflate GPT-4's by ~10–12%.
(b) FRAMING RISK FOR T1 (load-bearing). Thompson's argument is that training is "a fixed cost independent of revenue, effectively capex amortized over years." If this claim anchors the scale of that capex, then amortized final-run compute is the WRONG metric — Epoch is explicit that "amortized costs are more relevant for understanding the economics of training and deploying models over an extended period, while acquisition costs give a sense of the capital barriers to entry and financial risks involved." The capital commitment behind GPT-4 was ~$306M (hardware acquisition) to ~$806M (upfront), and the full development cost including experiments and R&D staff was ~$125–140M. Using $70M (or $55M) as the anchor for "the starting scale of frontier fixed costs" understates the actual barrier to entry by roughly an order of magnitude. I recommend the ledger either add a companion claim for full development cost (~$130M, 2023 USD) or relabel this one so downstream arithmetic does not mistake final-run compute for total fixed cost.

Net: the direction of the claim survives (GPT-4-era frontier training was a tens-of-millions fixed cost, and the thesis does not break), but the central is inflated ~27%, the CI's low bound misrepresents the lead source, and the source list overstates independence. Hence adjust, not confirm; grade should drop to B-.

ADJUST. The order of magnitude survives, but the point estimate is biased high and the CI is mis-centered and mis-bounded. Three material problems.

1) THE CLAIM'S CENTRAL SITS ABOVE ITS OWN PRIMARY SOURCE. I downloaded Epoch AI's live Notable AI Models database (2026-07-22). For "GPT-4 (Mar 2023)" (2.1e25 FLOP, 25,000 A100 SXM4-40GB, 2,280 hours, 34% MFU, confidence "Likely") it lists three distinct cost fields:
   - Training compute cost (2023 USD, amortized hardware + energy): $37.3M
   - Training compute cost (cloud rental basis): $81.4M
   - Training compute cost (upfront hardware acquisition): $806M
The Cottier et al. paper (arXiv 2405.21015) states plainly: "the most expensive publicly-announced training runs to date are OpenAI's GPT-4 at $40M and Google's Gemini Ultra at $30M," and notes the cloud-price approach "yields costs that are about twice as large on average." So the only two defensible compute-only methods bracket $37M-$81M. A $70M central is not a blend of these; it is ~75% of the way to the cloud figure. Midpoint is $59M, geometric mean $55M. Notably, the claim's own CI floor of $35M sits *below but adjacent to* Epoch's headline point estimate ($37.3M), i.e. the single most-cited primary estimate lands at roughly the 10th percentile of the claimed distribution. That is a mis-centered interval.

2) SOURCE INDEPENDENCE IS ILLUSORY — ONE SOURCE, NOT THREE. The claim's convergence at "$70-100M" is an artifact of one estimator being laundered through three outlets. The Forbes/Statista piece (source 2), when actually read, says: "ChatGPT-4... had a technical creation cost of $41 million to $78 million, according to the source" — and the source is Epoch AI, with the article explicitly noting Epoch excludes staff salaries, which "can make up 29% to 49% of the final price." That is literally Epoch's amortized-to-cloud band restated. AI Index's widely quoted $78M is Epoch's cloud-basis number. TechRadar (source 3, undated, tertiary trade press, headline framed around a Chinese-lab marketing comparison) reports "$80m-$100m," which appears to splice the cloud estimate with Altman's all-in remark. So the claim has one real estimator (Epoch), one CEO soundbite, and one aggregator — and the cited $41M-$78M band from its own source #2 puts $70M in the top quartile with the CI ceiling of $150M unsupported by *any* compute-only estimate.

3) THE CI CEILING IMPORTS A DIFFERENT METRIC. Sam Altman's "more than $100 million" is all-in development (staff, failed runs, experiments), not final-run compute. Epoch quantifies exactly this separation: amortized *hardware over the whole development* (all experiments, not just the final run) rose "from $4M for GPT-3 to $90M for GPT-4," with R&D staff including equity another 29-49% of total — implying all-in GPT-4 development on the order of $130-190M, entirely consistent with Altman and entirely irrelevant to a "final training run compute" line item. Letting a $150M ceiling stand on a compute-only metric silently smuggles staff and failed runs into a COGS-vs-capex argument where the distinction is the whole point. The genuine upside tail on compute-only comes from compute uncertainty (Epoch's own 90% CI on GPT-4 FLOP is 8.2e24-4.4e25, ~2.1x each way) applied to the cloud basis, which reaches ~$110M at an 80% level, not $150M.

DOWNSTREAM HAZARD FOR THE THESIS (flag this to the parent). The claim is load-bearing as the T1 anchor for frontier fixed costs, which implies comparison against later models. Epoch's amortized 2023-USD series that any such comparison will use gives GPT-4.5 = $366M, Llama 3.1-405B = $53M, Grok-2 = $32M, Gemini 1.0 Ultra = $31M, GPT-3 = $2.1M. On that series GPT-4 is $37M, not $70M. Pairing a cloud-basis GPT-4 with amortized-basis successors understates the 2023-2025 training-cost growth by ~1.9x — a wrong-denominator error of exactly the kind that would make a "fixed costs are exploding" or "fixed costs are modest vs inference COGS" claim quantitatively wrong. Whichever basis the analysis picks, it must be the same basis across models, and the basis must be stated.

WHY NOT REFUTE: nothing here shows the claim is unsupportable. Every credible estimate lands in the tens of millions, the claimed CI does contain the true value, and the qualitative point the thesis needs (a 2022 frontier final run was a one-time cost of order $10^7-10^8, small relative to cumulative inference spend at scale) is unaffected by $40M vs $70M. This is a calibration fix, not a reversal.

CORRECTED: $60M central (midpoint of the two defensible compute-only methods, and near-midpoint of Epoch's own published $41-78M band), 80% CI $30M-$110M — floor lowered so Epoch's $37M amortized point estimate sits comfortably inside rather than at the tail, ceiling lowered to strip out the all-in/staff contamination while still covering the cloud basis plus compute uncertainty. Grade should stay B at best; arguably B- given the single-estimator dependency. If the surrounding analysis uses Epoch's amortized series elsewhere, override this with $37M and note the basis explicitly.

claims.metric: Growth rate of amortized final-run training cost, most compute-intensive models
claims.entity: Frontier models industry-wide (Epoch AI, Cottier et al.)

sources.title: Epoch AI: How much does it cost to train frontier AI models?
arXiv 2405.21015: The rising costs of training frontier AI models

claims.notes: Epoch's published 95% CI is 2.0x-3.1x; cloud-rental method gives ~2.6x/yr. Implies largest runs exceed $1B by 2027. Core quantitative support for T1's claim that training is a large, escalating fixed cost amortized over years.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE LOCATED AND READ IN FULL. I pulled arXiv 2405.21015 (Cottier, Rahman, Fattorini, Maslej, Owen — "The rising costs of training frontier AI models") as PDF and extracted the text, plus the raw HTML of the Epoch blog and Epoch's live Trends page.

WHAT SURVIVES. The point estimate is faithful. Table 1 of the paper (v2) gives, for the preferred "amortized hardware CapEx + energy" method: 2.4x/year, 90% CI [2.0, 2.9], 0.38 OOM/yr [0.29, 0.47], doubling 9 months, R-squared 0.58, N=41. The abstract reads verbatim: "the amortized cost to train the most compute-intensive models has grown precipitously at a rate of 2.4x per year since 2016 (90% CI: 2.0x to 2.9x)." Unit (multiplicative factor/year), entity (top-10 most compute-intensive models at time of release), and the metric wording "amortized final-run training cost" are all faithfully represented. The $1B-by-2027 note is also faithful: Section 3.2 extrapolates from GPT-4's $40M amortized cost (Mar 2023) to "about $1 billion" by start of 2027.

DEFECT 1 — THE CI IS ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE AS LABELED. The claim asserts an 80% CI of 2.0-3.0. An 80% interval must be strictly NARROWER than the source's 90% interval of 2.0-2.9. The claim's is wider at both ends. It is effectively a 90-95% interval wearing an 80% label. Derived properly from the paper's own regression output (0.38 OOM/yr, 90% CI [0.29, 0.47] — symmetric in log space, so sigma = 0.09/1.645 = 0.0547 OOM; 80% offset = 1.2816*sigma = 0.0701), the honest 80% CI is 10^(0.38 +/- 0.0701) = 2.04x to 2.82x. Working instead from the rounded multiplicative bounds gives 2.08-2.77. Rounding: 2.1x to 2.8x. Note the direction of the error is toward false humility, not false confidence, but the lower bound of 2.0 in the claim carries only 5% tail mass, not the 10% an 80% CI implies.

DEFECT 2 — THE NOTES CITE A RETIRED CI. The note says "Epoch's published 95% CI is 2.0x-3.1x." Epoch explicitly retired that. The blog's own changelog states: "Jan. 13, 2025: We removed finetuned models from the data which should not have been included... We also Switched to a 90% CI for everything (instead of sometimes using 95% CI)." arXiv v2 (submitted 7 Feb 2025) carries 90% CI 2.0-2.9. The "95% CI: 2.0x to 3.1x" string does still appear in the blog's summary paragraph — I confirmed this in the raw HTML — but that is an un-updated line Epoch failed to fix, contradicted by its own changelog four paragraphs below and by the paper. The claim inherited a known-stale number. Similarly, the note's "cloud-rental method gives ~2.6x/yr" is the superseded June-2024 figure; v2 Table 1 gives 2.5x [2.1, 3.1].

DEFECT 3 — PERIOD OVERSTATED. The claim says "2016-2024 trend." The dataset contains no 2024 models. The most recent observations are Gemini 1.0 Ultra (Dec 2023), Inflection-2 (Nov 2023), Falcon-180B (Sep 2023); the x-axis is publication date. Correct label is "2016-2023." The "published May 2024" date is also incomplete — the operative version is v2, Feb 2025.

DEFECT 4 — MOST SERIOUS FOR A JULY 2026 THESIS: THE SAME PRIMARY SOURCE NOW PUBLISHES A DIFFERENT NUMBER. Epoch's Trends page, updated Feb 5, 2026, states: "The cost to train frontier language models has increased by 3.5x/year since 2020," 90% CI 2.8x to 4.4x, doubling every 7 months. Epoch's own narrative text reads "Training costs are climbing by 3.5x annually." That figure sits entirely outside the claim's stated interval — even its 90% lower bound (2.8) exceeds the claim's point estimate (2.4). This is not a contradiction of Cottier et al. (different window, 2020-2025 vs 2016-2023; different scope, frontier language models vs top-10 by compute including pre-LLM vision/RL systems), and the paper anticipated it — excluding TPU-based models, whose costs are estimated rather than priced, raises the rate to 3.0x [2.4, 3.7], significantly different at p<0.01. But it means using 2.4x as a description of the current regime understates the escalation by roughly 45%. Directionally this HELPS the thesis (fixed training cost is escalating faster than claimed), so the load-bearing role survives — but a hostile reviewer would rightly object that a 2016-2023 regression is being deployed as a statement about 2026 economics.

OTHER ROBUSTNESS CAVEATS. R-squared is 0.58, i.e. substantial scatter around the fit; the 90% CI is a regression-slope interval adjusted for residual correlation, not a full uncertainty over model selection or cost-estimation method. And a note relevant to how the thesis uses this: the paper is explicit that amortized cost is one to two orders of magnitude below acquisition cost — GPT-4 was $40M amortized vs ~$800M to acquire the hardware — so "training cost" in this claim is NOT the capex figure, and should not be conflated with one in an argument about fixed-cost burden.

RECOMMENDATION. Keep value at 2.4 (correct for the metric as scoped), fix CI to 2.1-2.8, relabel period "2016-2023 (arXiv v2, Feb 2025)", drop the "95% CI 2.0-3.1" and "2.6x cloud" notes as superseded, and either add or substitute Epoch's current 3.5x/yr since 2020 (90% CI 2.8-4.4) if the claim is meant to describe today's regime rather than the historical trend. Grade B is generous given four separate fidelity errors; B-minus/C-plus is fairer until the CI and period are fixed.

The central value 2.4x is quoted accurately from the source, but the claim is pinned to a SUPERSEDED version of the paper and its CI is both stale and mislabeled. Adversarial findings:

(1) LATER CORRECTION (material). Cottier et al. arXiv:2405.21015 has two versions: v1 (31 May 2024) and v2 (7 Feb 2025). v1 abstract: "2.4x per year since 2016 (95% CI: 2.0x to 3.1x)". v2 abstract (current): "2.4x per year since 2016 (90% CI: 2.0x to 2.9x)". The claim's note ("Epoch's published 95% CI is 2.0x-3.1x") cites the withdrawn v1 figure. The cloud-rental figure was likewise revised: blog/v1 says 2.6x/yr; v2 Table 1 says 2.5x [2.1, 3.1]. Epoch's blog page (the claim's primary source, dated 2024-06) still displays the stale v1 numbers and has not been updated to v2 — so the claim is sourced to an un-corrected page.

(2) CI LABEL IS WRONG. The claim reports [2.0, 3.0] as an 80% CI. That range is actually the source's ~90-95% sampling interval. Backing out v2's regression SE from its 90% CI (SE ≈ 0.113 in ln space), the source-implied 80% CI is roughly [2.1, 2.8]. Using a 90-95% interval as an 80% band is a category error, and in this case it also anchors the band too low at the top.

(3) THE HEADLINE 2.4x IS THE LOW END OF THE PAPER'S OWN SPECIFICATIONS. v2 Table 1: excluding models priced off *estimated* Google TPU production costs (the least reliable data points, actual price data used for the rest) raises the rate to 3.0x [2.4, 3.7], N=22, and the paper states this difference is statistically significant (p < 0.01). Other same-paper variants: cloud rental 2.5x [2.1, 3.1]; hardware acquisition cost 2.5x [2.1, 3.0]; power capacity 2.2x [1.9, 2.6]; Appendix B.1 selection-rule variants 2.2x-2.4x (top-20%-of-residuals selection falls to 1.6x); Appendix B.2 top-N variants 2.3x (N=3), 2.3x (N=5), 2.4x (N=10), 2.8x (N=20). So structural/method uncertainty is materially wider than the reported sampling CI, and skews upward once the weakest inputs are removed. R-squared on the headline fit is only 0.58.

(4) INDEPENDENT REFIT ON EPOCH'S OWN LIVE DATA CONTRADICTS 2.4x. I downloaded Epoch's current Notable AI Models CSV (updated 22 Jul 2026) whose "Training compute cost (2023 USD)" field is documented as the identical "amortized hardware capex plus energy" measure (GPT-4 = $37.3M, matching the paper's ~$40M). Replicating the paper's method (log-linear fit on models in the top-N most compute-intensive at time of release, from 2016): with the paper's data cutoff (May 2024) I get 2.53x [2.09, 3.05], N=56; through Dec 2024, 2.70x; through the end of the cost data (Dec 2025), 2.96x [2.54, 3.45], N=64. Across N=3/5/10/20 the paper-window fits are 2.56-2.88x and the full-window fits 2.80-3.21x — every specification lands above 2.4x. (My CIs are somewhat too narrow: unlike the paper I did not adjust for residual correlation.) The 2025 additions driving this are Grok 3 $218M, GPT-4.5 $366M, Grok 4 $388M; point-to-point GPT-4 ($37.3M, Mar 2023) to Grok 4 ($388M, Jul 2025) is 2.74x/yr.

(5) CAVEATS FOR LOAD-BEARING USE, flagged for the parent. (a) Extrapolation past mid-2025 is currently unverifiable: Epoch has published ZERO amortized cost estimates for any 2026 model, and the largest cost estimate on record remains Grok 4 at $388M (Jul 2025). The paper's ">$1B by start of 2027" is on-track-but-unconfirmed (it needs only 1.9x/yr from Grok 4). Epoch's compute data also shows no 2026 model above 3.9e25 FLOP and GPT-5 at only 6.6e25 FLOP vs GPT-4.5's 3.8e26 — likely incomplete coverage of closed labs, but it means the trend line has no public anchor point after July 2025. (b) The metric is final-run amortized hardware+energy ONLY. It excludes R&D staff (29-49% of total development cost with equity, 19-33% without) and experiment compute, and is 1-2 orders of magnitude below hardware acquisition cost ($800M to acquire GPT-4's cluster vs $37-40M amortized). If Thompson's argument is about capex amortized over years, the amortized-final-run series understates the level by roughly 20x even though the growth rate is the right order. For scale: Epoch's Feb 2026 data insight puts Anthropic's 2025 R&D compute at $4.1B vs $2.7B inference compute — i.e., total training-side spend is orders of magnitude above any single final-run figure.

Direction of adjustment does not threaten the thesis — it strengthens the "large and escalating fixed cost" leg. But the claim as written cites a corrected-away CI at a wrong confidence level and a central value that is now the floor rather than the center of the evidence. Corrected: 2.6x/yr central (weighting the paper's v2 2.4x for its own window against the 2.5-2.9x same-window refits and the 2.5x cloud/acquisition cross-checks), 80% CI [2.2, 3.1] (widened beyond pure sampling error to cover the TPU-exclusion and selection-rule sensitivities). Grade B remains appropriate; do not upgrade to A given R-squared 0.58, n≈41-64, and no post-July-2025 anchor point.

claims.metric: Training cost stated by CEO ('a few $10M’s')

sources.title: Dario Amodei: On DeepSeek and Export Controls
The Decoder: Anthropic CEO addresses Claude Sonnet rumors
TechCrunch: Anthropic's latest flagship AI might not have been incredibly costly to train (Claude 3.7 also 'tens of millions')

claims.notes: On-the-record but deliberately vague ('a few $10M's'); excludes research, experiments, and staff. Amodei's same essay says frontier labs run ~$1B-scale training programs and cites the ~4x/yr algorithmic cost-efficiency curve. Key calibration point: a frontier-competitive mid-size model's final run was DeepSeek-order magnitude, supporting T3 (price gap is not a Chinese training-cost miracle).

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE: LOCATED AND VERBATIM-CONFIRMED. darioamodei.com/post/on-deepseek-and-export-controls reads: "Claude 3.5 Sonnet is a mid-sized model that cost a few $10M's to train (I won't give an exact number). Also, 3.5 Sonnet was not trained in any way that involved a larger or more expensive model (contrary to some rumors)." Attribution, unit (USD millions), and on-the-record status are faithful. Corroborated: TechCrunch (2025-02-25) reports Claude 3.7 Sonnet also cost "a few tens of millions of dollars" (<10^26 FLOP), via an Anthropic clarification relayed by Ethan Mollick, with an explicit caveat that the figure excludes safety testing and research. The notes' "~4x/yr algorithmic cost-efficiency curve" is also verbatim-accurate ("I'd guess the number today is maybe ~4x/year").

FOUR DEFECTS, none fatal to the claim's load-bearing function:

(1) CI LOW BOUND IS UNSUPPORTABLE. $15M cannot be reached from "a few $10M's" — that phrase floors at 2x$10M = $20M; $15M would be described as "over $10M." Critically, the direction of Amodei's rhetorical incentive runs toward UNDERSTATING, not overstating: his entire argument is that DeepSeek-V3 (~$6M) sits on the expected cost-reduction curve. A higher Sonnet number would make DeepSeek look MORE impressive relative to his ~4x/yr curve, not less. So there is no mechanism putting 10% of probability mass below $20M.

(2) CI HIGH BOUND IS TOO GENEROUS. $90M requires "a few" to mean 9 and would make the CEO's public statement misleading by ~3x. Independent triangulation caps it: Epoch AI's dataset records Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 2.7e25 FLOP with "Training compute cost (2023 USD) = $25,870,993" — i.e. Epoch's own reading of the identical sentence lands at ~$26M. Bottom-up Fermi on 2.7e25 FLOP: at H100 989 TFLOP/s dense and 40% MFU that is ~18.9M GPU-hours; at $1.5/$2/$3 per GPU-hour that is $28M/$38M/$57M. Widening MFU to 30-50% spans roughly $23M-$75M at the extremes, so a defensible 80% band is ~$20-60M, not $15-90M.

(3) PERIOD IS OFF BY ~A QUARTER. Claim says "trained ~mid-2024." Amodei says training "was conducted 9-12 months ago" as of late Jan 2025 → roughly Feb-Apr 2024. Mid-2024 is the RELEASE date (June 20, 2024), not the training date. Faithful rendering: "trained ~Q1-Q2 2024; released June 2024; stated January 2025." This matters because Amodei's own comparison is framed as DeepSeek matching "US models 7-10 months older."

(4) NOTES CONTAIN A MISATTRIBUTION. The note asserts "Amodei's same essay says frontier labs run ~$1B-scale training programs." It does not. The essay's ~$1B refers to DeepSeek's 50,000-Hopper chip FLEET capex, and Amodei's point is that this is "within a factor ~2-3x of what the major US AI companies have" and that "DeepSeek's total spend as a company... is not vastly different from US AI labs." The only "tens of billions" figures are forward-looking (2026-27 superintelligence-scale buildouts). This should be recorded as cluster capex, not per-program training spend — a distinction that actually sharpens Thompson's fixed-cost-vs-COGS framing rather than weakening it.

MINOR: entity is ambiguous between the June 2024 original and the Oct 22, 2024 upgrade, both named "Claude 3.5 Sonnet." The "9-12 months ago" anchor and Epoch's record (pub date 2024-06-20) both pin it to the ORIGINAL. Should be disambiguated.

CORRECTED VALUES: value 30 ("a few" = 3 read literally; Epoch's independent reading of the same sentence = ~$26M in 2023 USD; Anthropic's own successor-model language is identical). CI [20, 60], right-skewed — the longer right tail absorbs GPU-price/MFU uncertainty plus the possibility of modest CEO understatement, while the floor respects the plain meaning of the words actually said.

THESIS IMPACT: none adverse. Whether $26M, $30M, or $35M, the claim's function — a frontier-competitive mid-size model's final training run was DeepSeek-order magnitude, so the US/China token-price gap is not explained by a Chinese training-cost miracle — survives fully intact and is modestly STRENGTHENED by the tighter interval. Grade A is appropriate for source fidelity; I would keep it, with the period and notes corrected. The one caveat a hostile reviewer should carry forward: this is a final-run figure only, deliberately vague, from a speaker with a live rhetorical stake in the exact comparison the claim is being used to support — it should never be quoted without the "excludes research/experiments/staff" qualifier, which is explicit for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and only inferable for 3.5.

VERBATIM SOURCE VERIFIED. Amodei's essay (darioamodei.com, Jan 2025) says exactly: "DeepSeek does not 'do for $6M what cost US AI companies billions'. I can only speak for Anthropic, but Claude 3.5 Sonnet is a mid-sized model that cost a few $10M's to train (I won't give an exact number). Also, 3.5 Sonnet was not trained in any way that involved a larger or more expensive model." The quote in the claim is accurate. Anthropic reaffirmed the same magnitude for Claude 3.7 Sonnet in Feb 2025 ("a few tens of millions," <1e26 FLOP).

WHAT SURVIVED HOSTILE REVIEW — the point value. I could find no contradicting estimate at any scale. Three cross-checks that do NOT route through Amodei all land at $29-40M for a ~2.7-3.6e25 FLOP mid-2024 model: (1) Epoch's Grok-2 entry (2.96e25 FLOP, confidence "Confident," methodology derived from xAI cluster statements) = $31.6M amortized 2023 USD; scaled to 2.7e25 that is $28.8M. (2) Epoch's Llama 3.1-405B entry (3.8e25 FLOP, "Confident," paper-stated) = $52.9M amortized; scaled to 2.7e25 that is $37.6M. (3) My own Fermi: 2.7e25 FLOP at 40% MFU on H100 BF16 = 18.9M GPU-hours; at the $2/GPU-hr rate DeepSeek itself used for its $5.576M figure, that is $37.9M. Value 35 sits at the center of all three. Confirmed.

WHAT DID NOT SURVIVE — four material defects, none of which move the point value but three of which change how the claim should be recorded and used.

(1) THE CORROBORATION IS CIRCULAR. The claim is graded A on three sources, but all three trace to one statement by one interested party. The Decoder simply reports Amodei; TechCrunch reports Anthropic's own PR on 3.7. Worse, the obvious "independent" check — Epoch AI — is not independent: Epoch's notable-models CSV lists Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 2.7e25 FLOP / $25.87M with confidence "Speculative," and its compute note reads "Blog post by Dario Amodei includes some info on 3.5 Sonnet compute... Using assumptions about GPU pricing, this lets us estimate compute." Epoch back-derived the compute FROM the cost statement. Their separate data-insight page lists 3.6e25 via benchmark imputation with an acknowledged 90% CI of 1.1x-5.0x and precision "Low." Epoch's two published figures for the same model disagree by 33%. This is a one-source, unaudited, self-reported number. Grade should be B, not A.

(2) DIRECTIONAL INCENTIVE TO UNDERSTATE. The essay's rhetorical purpose requires a low Anthropic number: Amodei is rebutting "DeepSeek did for $6M what cost US labs billions," and the smaller Anthropic's figure, the more DeepSeek's $5.576M looks like ordinary movement along the ~4x/yr cost curve rather than a breakthrough. At $35M vs $5.6M the ratio is ~6x over a 7-10 month gap — roughly on-trend, which is precisely his conclusion. A $150M Anthropic figure would have made DeepSeek look ~27x cheaper and undercut his own argument. He also declines to give an exact number. This is the only bias I found, and it points UP, not down.

(3) THE PERIOD FIELD IS WRONG. The claim says "trained ~mid-2024." Amodei says "Sonnet's training was conducted 9-12 months ago" from a late-January-2025 essay, i.e. roughly Feb-Apr 2024. Mid-2024 is the RELEASE date (June 20, 2024), not the training date. This matters because the claim is load-bearing precisely as a timing calibration: Amodei's own framing is "US models 7-10 months older" than DeepSeek-V3 (trained Nov/Dec 2024). Recording the training date as mid-2024 compresses that gap and weakens the very inference the claim is being used for. Separately, there is an unresolved ambiguity the claim does not flag: the cost quote almost certainly refers to the ORIGINAL June 2024 Claude 3.5 Sonnet, while the eval-superiority sentence in the same paragraph leans on the upgraded October 2024 "new" 3.5 Sonnet — a different training run of unstated cost.

(4) WRONG-DENOMINATOR RISK IS REAL AND EXTERNALLY FLAGGED. SemiAnalysis ("DeepSeek Debates," Jan 31, 2025) makes exactly this critique: "Claude 3.5 Sonnet cost $10s of millions to train, and if that was the total cost Anthropic needed, then they would not raise billions from Google and tens of billions from Amazon." The figure is a final-run compute cost only. Epoch's own cost decomposition puts hardware at 47-67% and R&D staff at 29-49% of true development cost, implying fully-loaded cost roughly 2-3x the compute line even before failed runs. The claim's notes do disclose this scope, which is to its credit — but the number must never be used as "what it cost Anthropic to produce Claude 3.5 Sonnet."

CI RECALIBRATION. The stated 80% CI [15, 90] is both too wide and misplaced. The low bound of 15 is indefensible: no one describes $15M as "a few $10M's" (that is "over ten million"), it is below Epoch's own $25.9M amortized figure, and Amodei had every incentive to quote a lower number if one were available. Reaching $15M requires both an implausibly small ~1.5e25 FLOP run AND a $1.5/GPU-hr rate. The upper end is better justified: at Epoch's higher 3.6e25 benchmark estimate and $3/GPU-hr you get $76M, and Epoch's cloud-rate accounting for Llama 3.1-405B (implied $5.01/GPU-hr) scales to $125M for equivalent compute — so real headroom exists above the plain reading of "a few." Given the only identified bias points up, the honest 80% interval is asymmetric to the high side: [20, 75], point estimate unchanged at 35 (geometric center ~39, and the plain-language read of "a few tens" centers on 35).

NET: the number holds; the provenance, the period, and the CI placement do not. Use it as a single-source CEO statement about final-run compute for a Q1-2024-trained mid-size model, not as an audited cost.

sources.title: Epoch AI: What did it take to train Grok 4?

claims.notes: Epoch: 246M H100-hours, median $490M using rental rates of $1.90-2.20/H100-hr (90% CI) and depreciation+power cross-check; energy ~310 GWh. Epoch flags 'significant uncertainty' since inputs derive from vague xAI statements — hence wide CI. Demonstrates frontier final-run costs reached ~half a billion dollars by 2025, on-trend with 2.4x/yr growth.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCES OBTAINED AND REPRODUCED. I did not stop at the cited insight page — I pulled the three upstream artifacts it links (Epoch's calculations spreadsheet, the GPU-hour estimate Google Doc, and the Colab Monte Carlo notebook) plus Epoch's notable-AI-models CSV, and re-ran their simulation.

WHAT CHECKS OUT (every headline number is faithful):
- $490M: the spreadsheet cell reads Cost = 4.87E+08, and the insight states "Median cost estimate: $490 million." Rounding is honest. I reproduced it exactly from the notebook's code: at 245.7M H100-hours, rental method = $502M, depreciation+power = $487M, geometric mean = $495M (~$490M). Not a number taken on faith — it regenerates.
- 246M H100-hours: notebook line `total_h100_hours_grok4 = (172e6)*(5/3.5)` = 245.7M. Spreadsheet: 2.46E+08. Confirmed.
- Rental rate "$1.90–2.20/H100-hr (90% CI)": exact — `lognorm_from_90_ci(1.9, 2.2)`. Confirmed.
- "depreciation+power cross-check": confirmed, though slightly imprecise — the headline is the *geometric mean* of the two methods, not a mere cross-check. Immaterial (they agree within 3%).
- Energy ~310 GWh: I compute 314 GWh from their parameters (700W TDP x 0.75 utilization x 2.03 non-GPU overhead x 1.2 PUE); spreadsheet says 3.14E+08 kWh. Confirmed.
- METRIC LABEL IS FAITHFUL — this is the one I expected to break. The notebook's inherited "About" text describes a total *development* cost including salaries and experiments, which would make "final training run compute cost" a misrepresentation. But the actual code excludes it: `final_rental_based_estimate` and `final_depreciation_based_estimate` are commented "only hardware and power," and the separately-computed salary_costs ($15M) is never added. So $490M is genuinely run compute (hardware + power), not development cost. Also correctly avoids the DB's "Training compute cost (upfront)" = $10.7B, which is whole-cluster capex.
- Period: defensible. Grok 4 released 2025-07-09; Epoch assumes Grok 3's pre-training (2024 Colossus ramp) plus a 2025 RL phase. Insight published 2025-09-12 (claim says "2025").

THE CI — Epoch publishes NO dollar CI, so [220, 900] is the claim author's construction. I tested whether it is honest by running Epoch's own uncertainty spec, including the commented-out line in cell 9 that propagates H100-hour uncertainty (the dominant term, which their published run holds fixed):
- Epoch's own propagated 80% CI: $316M – $751M; 90% CI: $280M – $847M.
- Holding H100-hours fixed (as their published run does), the CI collapses to [$444M, $552M] — i.e. Epoch's stated distributions alone imply only ±12%.
The claim's [220, 900] is therefore WIDER than Epoch's own 90% CI. This is the opposite of the usual failure mode: it does not launder a point estimate into false precision. And the extra width is earned, because I found model-level disagreement Epoch's Monte Carlo does not capture:
1. Epoch's own notable-models database (July 2026 CSV) lists Grok 4 training compute cost = $387.8M in 2023 USD — 21% below the insight's figure.
2. The published Colab notebook, in its current state, computes $208M: a later line `(172e6)*(2.1/3.5)` overwrites the first, implying a revised 2.1e26 FLOP estimate rather than 5e26. Epoch's database still says 5e26, so this is not their published position, but it sits just below the claim's floor of 220.
3. Epoch tags Grok 4's compute Confidence as "Speculative" — their lowest tier.
Three different Epoch numbers for one quantity ($208M / $388M / $490M) is exactly the situation a wide CI exists for. If anything the floor is marginally too high; a slightly better-calibrated 80% CI would be roughly [280, 800], but that is well inside noise and changes nothing load-bearing, so I do not call this an adjust.

TWO CAVEATS THE CLAIM SHOULD CARRY:
(a) Base-year ambiguity. "USD millions" is unlabeled. $490M is nominal 2025 USD; Epoch's cost-trend series (the one yielding 2.4x/yr) is in 2023 USD, where Grok 4 = $388M. The note's "on-trend with 2.4x/yr growth" therefore mixes a nominal figure into a deflated series and overstates by ~26%. The headline value is not wrong, but that specific trend sentence is not deflator-consistent.
(b) Grade B is generous. Epoch's own confidence tag is "Speculative," the inputs derive from an unlabeled y-axis in a livestream slide and a Forbes number Epoch says it is "not entirely confident in," and Epoch publishes three mutually inconsistent figures. C is the honest grade.

THESIS IMPACT: none of this threatens the load-bearing use. Whether the true figure is $388M or $490M, the point Thompson's argument needs — that a frontier final training run is a several-hundred-million-dollar fixed R&D cost, distinct from inference COGS that scales with usage — holds across the entire plausible range. Value, unit, period and metric definition are all faithfully represented, and the CI is honest-to-conservative rather than overconfident.

PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED EXACTLY. Fetched epoch.ai/data-insights/grok-4-training-resources (published 2025-09-12). It states verbatim: 246 million H100-hours ("based on known details about Grok-3's training resources and assumptions about the amount by which training was scaled up for Grok-4"), 310 GWh electricity, and a median cost estimate of $490 million. Rental method uses a log-normal rate with 90% CI $1.90-$2.20/H100-hr; the depreciation+power method uses power costs with 90% CI $0.08-$0.20/kWh. Both methods land on the SAME $490M median. Value, unit, entity, and the substance of the notes field all check out.

CONTRADICTION HUNT — six adversarial angles pursued, none refuting:

(1) UNSOURCED CI [strongest finding]. Epoch publishes NO confidence interval on total cost. Its only published CIs are on INPUT rates: the rental rate CI is ±8%, trivially narrow, and cannot generate a $220-900M spread. The claim's 80% CI is therefore analyst-constructed, not sourced. It is nonetheless well-calibrated: my own sensitivity check shows depreciation-horizon choice alone swings the amortized figure $300-540M (35k/GPU all-in over 2yr = $2.20/GPU-hr → $541M; over 3yr = $1.53/GPU-hr → $377M; over 4-5yr → ~$300M), and Epoch itself flags that compute inputs derive from "public statements from xAI, which are often vague." Combining compute uncertainty (~0.6-1.6x) with cost-per-hour uncertainty (~0.7-1.3x) reproduces roughly 0.45-1.9x of median = $220-930M. So the stated CI survives, but it should be labeled analyst-constructed. This is a sourcing-grade issue, not a value conflict; B grade is fair, arguably B- for the CI specifically.

(2) SINGLE-SOURCE DEPENDENCY. Every secondary citation found (The Verge, RAND Forecasting Initiative citing 5e26 FLOP, apxml, trade press, Epoch's own Substack) merely repeats Epoch. No independent methodology (SemiAnalysis, xAI disclosure, lab counter-estimate) located. Zero triangulation. Not a contradiction, but the claim rests on one analyst shop.

(3) INTERNAL METHODOLOGICAL TENSION. Epoch's own paper "How much does it cost to train frontier AI models?" states cloud-rental estimates run "typically 2x higher" than their PRIMARY amortized hardware+energy method. Yet for Grok 4 both converge on $490M. That convergence is only internally consistent under a short (~2-2.5yr) effective depreciation horizon at very high utilization. Under the 4-5yr horizons hyperscalers use for accounting, the amortized number falls to roughly $300M. This makes the low half of the CI load-bearing and puts $490M at the aggressive end of the amortized interpretation.

(4) ENTITY-SELECTION / GENERALIZATION RISK. The note's inference that "frontier final-run costs reached ~half a billion dollars by 2025" generalizes from the single most compute-intensive run known, produced by the lab most associated with brute-force scaling and poor compute-efficiency per unit capability. Aggregations of 2025-26 frontier estimates put the GPT-5/Gemini-class band at roughly $200-500M — i.e. Grok 4 sits at the TOP of that band, not its center. The metric is correct; the generalization in the note should be softened.

(5) "ON-TREND WITH 2.4x/YR" IS AT THE EDGE, NOT THE LINE. Anchoring on Epoch's GPT-4 amortized ~$40M (Mar 2023), 2.4x/yr over 2.3 years yields ~$285M, not $490M; $490M requires ~3.1x/yr, the very top of Epoch's published 95% CI (2.0x-3.1x). Anchoring instead on Gemini Ultra ($191M, Dec 2023) implies ~1.8x/yr, below trend. So "on-trend" is defensible only within the trend's uncertainty band, not on its central line. Stated more confidently in the note than the arithmetic supports.

(6) SCOPE / DENOMINATOR — CUTS IN FAVOR OF THE THESIS. Epoch explicitly excludes "the costs of human labor, or the compute costs of running experiments or serving Grok 4 to users." Epoch's own development-cost decomposition (hardware 47-67%, R&D staff 29-49%, energy 2-6%) implies a fully-loaded Grok 4 development cost of roughly $700M-$1B+, against reported xAI total spend in the billions. For the load-bearing role here — establishing that training is a large fixed R&D cost distinct from inference COGS — the $490M figure UNDERSTATES the fixed cost. The direction of error is conservative relative to the thesis, so the claim cannot be accused of inflating the fixed-cost side of Thompson's argument.

NEGATIVE RESULTS: no correction or retraction by Epoch found; no xAI/Musk dispute of the figure found; no competing dollar estimate found; the ~750M-liter water figure in the same insight also appears uncorrected (minor 750 vs 754 reporting variance only). An internal consistency note: 246M H100-hrs implies ~3.5e26 FLOP at 40% MFU (BF16) versus the 5e26 FLOP figure Epoch is elsewhere cited for, implying ~57% MFU or FP8 — mild tension, not material to the cost figure since cost is computed from GPU-hours, not FLOP.

VERDICT: CONFIRM. The value ($490M) is exactly the source's median; the CI, though the claim author's construction rather than Epoch's, reproduces almost exactly what a defensible sensitivity analysis of Epoch's own stated uncertainty drivers yields. No materially better value or CI exists in the literature. Recommended non-blocking edits: (a) annotate the CI as analyst-constructed, since Epoch publishes none; (b) soften the note's "frontier costs reached ~half a billion by 2025" to acknowledge Grok 4 is the top of the 2025 band rather than its median; (c) soften "on-trend with 2.4x/yr" to "within Epoch's 2.0x-3.1x growth-rate CI, near its upper end."

LIMITATION: this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was exhausted before I began, so evidence gathering ran through direct WebFetch and DuckDuckGo HTML result pages. Coverage of low-visibility critiques (e.g. LessWrong/HN threads) may be incomplete, though I probed specifically for criticism, disputes, and corrections and found none.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED, EXACT MATCH.

Chain of custody: I pulled the arXiv paper directly (abstract, v1 HTML, v2 HTML) and the official DeepSeek-V3 GitHub README.

1. Number fidelity — exact. arXiv 2412.19437 Table 1 gives, verbatim: Pre-Training 2,664K H800 GPU-hours / $5.328M; Context Extension 119K / $0.238M; Post-Training 5K / $0.01M; Total 2,788K / $5.576M. The body text reads verbatim: "Assuming the rental price of the H800 GPU is $2 per GPU hour, our total training costs amount to only $5.576M." The abstract independently states "DeepSeek-V3 requires only 2.788M H800 GPU hours for its full training," and the official GitHub README repeats it. The claim's value (5.576), unit (USD millions), and the note's arithmetic basis (2.788M GPU-hours x $2/hr) are all faithfully transcribed. Arithmetic checks: 2.788e6 x $2 = $5.576M; stage costs sum to the stated total. I checked v2 as well as v1 — the number is unchanged across revisions, so citing v1 is safe.

2. Period fidelity — correct. Pre-training completed in under two months on 14.8T tokens during 2024; technical report and model released December 2024.

3. Caveat fidelity — correct and load-bearing. The report's exact caveat is: "the aforementioned costs include only the official training of DeepSeek-V3, excluding the costs associated with prior research and ablation experiments on architectures, algorithms, or data." The claim's note reproduces this accurately. The Interconnects secondary source accepts the ~$5.5M as the official final-run figure while estimating the surrounding capability cost far higher (GPU capex "probably over $1B," full org opex "$500M (or even $1B+ easily if operating in the U.S.)," ablations/experimentation 2-4x the reported pre-training compute). So the note's framing — headline number is a marginal line item, not the fixed cost — is exactly what both the primary and the cited secondary support.

4. Internal plausibility check on the GPU-hour count (the one number nobody can audit): 671B total / 37B activated params over 14.8T tokens implies roughly 6 x 3.7e10 x 1.48e13 = 3.3e24 FLOPs. Spread over 2.664M GPU-hours that is ~340 TFLOP/s per H800 sustained, i.e. ~35% MFU at BF16 peak or ~17% at FP8 peak. Both are ordinary, achievable numbers. The disclosure is not internally implausible, which is the main thing a hostile reviewer could attack.

5. CI honesty — the CI is doing the right job and the bounds are defensible. The point value is exact by construction (a disclosed product), so a naive CI would be [5.576, 5.576]. The claim instead correctly prices the only real uncertainty: what a realized H800-hour actually cost DeepSeek. The stated CI [4.5, 9] implies $1.61–$3.23 per H800-hour. Low end: High-Flyer owns its cluster rather than renting, and an owned H800 at ~$25-30K amortized over 4-5 years at high utilization with cheap Chinese industrial power lands near $1.3-1.7/hr all-in — so 4.5 is a fair, if mildly conservative, p10. High end: 2024 China scarcity pricing on H800s (widely reported well above US list), 3-year amortization, sub-100% utilization, plus interconnect/storage/facility/power overhead gets to ~$3+/hr — so 9 is a fair p90. The right-skew (-1.08 / +3.42) is the correct shape, since the residual risk of understated GPU-hours is one-sided upward. I found no basis to move either bound materially.

6. Corroboration that $2/hr is DeepSeek's own standing convention, not a number picked to flatter: their March 2025 open-infra inference-system disclosure uses the identical assumption verbatim — "Assuming the leasing cost of one H800 GPU is $2 per hour" — to compute "$87,072" daily inference cost against "$562,027" theoretical daily revenue. Same accounting rate applied to a case where it makes them look expensive, not cheap. That raises confidence in the $2 anchor.

REMAINING QUIBBLES (not sufficient to downgrade, worth a footnote):
(a) Label/CI mismatch. The metric reads "Disclosed final training run cost," but the CI prices true realized cost. Those are different quantities; the note resolves it, but a hostile reader could call the CI incoherent with its own label. Suggest the metric read "final training run cost (disclosed rental-equivalent)."
(b) "Final training run" is slightly loose: $5.576M spans pre-training + context extension + post-training. Pre-training alone is $5.328M. Both sit inside the CI, so nothing material moves.
(c) DeepSeek never paid $5.576M to anyone. It is a rental-equivalent imputation on an owned cluster, explicitly flagged as an assumption in the paper. The claim already treats it that way.

Grade A and load_bearing=true both hold: this is a first-party disclosure in a peer-reviewable technical report, reproduced identically in three official channels, with the exclusion caveat stated by the source itself rather than inferred.

POINT VALUE SURVIVES HOSTILE REVIEW; THE CI IS MIS-SKEWED. I adjust the interval only.

What I verified in the primary source (arXiv 2412.19437v1, Table 1), verbatim: 2,664K H800 GPU-hours pre-training + 119K context extension + 5K post-training = 2,788K total; "Assuming the rental price of the H800 GPU is $2 per GPU hour, our total training costs amount to only $5.576M"; and the exclusion sentence quoted in the notes is exact ("excluding the costs associated with prior research and ablation experiments on architectures, algorithms, or data"). Arithmetic checks exactly.

CORROBORATION (raises confidence in the point value):
1. Epoch AI independently reconstructed the number from disclosed throughput rather than accepting it: 2,048 H800s, 3.7 days per trillion tokens, 14.8T tokens → ~2.66M H800-hours → "around $5.3M if we price the cost of an H800 hour at $2." An outside party rebuilding the GPU-hour count from first principles and landing on the same figure is the strongest available check.
2. Second official disclosure, nine months later: the DeepSeek-R1 Nature paper (Sept 2025) supplementary put the R1 RL stage at ~$294K on top of a base model costing ~$6M — consistent with, not a correction to, the December 2024 figure.
3. No source I found — including the hostile ones — disputes the 2.788M GPU-hour count for the run itself.

WHAT THE HOSTILE SOURCES ACTUALLY ATTACK: framing, not arithmetic. SemiAnalysis ("DeepSeek Debates") calls the $6M "pointing to a specific part of a bill of materials and attributing it as the entire cost," and estimates ~$1.6B server capex, ~$944M opex, ~50K Hopper GPUs. Interconnects estimates prior research and ablations at "2-4 times the reported number" and total organizational cost at "$500M (or even $1B+) easily" per year, with 139 authors' salaries alone >$10M/yr. Tom's Hardware: "the fabled $6 million was just a portion of the total training cost." The Register's Sept 2025 piece attacks the $294K R1 headline for the same reason. Crucially, this is not contradiction of the claim as written — it is agreement with the claim's own notes, which already state this is NOT the cost to build the model capability. The load-bearing use for T3/T4 (headline Chinese number is a marginal line item, not the fixed cost) survives adversarial pressure intact; every critic is making that exact argument.

WHY I STILL ADJUST — THE CI IS SKEWED THE WRONG WAY. The stated CI80 of 4.5–9 implies $1.61–$3.23/GPU-hour, i.e. it treats $2/hr as near the bottom of the plausible range and allows 60% upside. The evidence pushes the opposite direction:
- $2/hr is an unverified assumption. The Next Platform, the most direct critique of the math: "we have no idea if that is actually the prevailing price in China."
- Chinese H800 rental was advertised as low as 6.99 yuan/card/hour (~$0.96) in 2024, and multiple reports note Nvidia AI GPU rental in China ran cheaper than in the US. Single-card promo rates are not a fair comparator for a reserved 2,048-GPU InfiniBand cluster, but they bound the low side well below $1.61.
- DeepSeek did not rent. It owned the fleet via High-Flyer, so $5.576M is an imputed opportunity cost, not a realized cash outlay. The entire $1.6B rests on one unverified assertion of ~50,000 Hopper-class GPUs, of which SemiAnalysis names only ~20,000 concretely (~10k H800 + ~10k H100); the balance is H20s that the source describes as "orders for many more," i.e. partly committed rather than delivered as of Jan 2025. H20s are materially cheaper per unit than H100/H800. Downside scenario: only the ~20k H100/H800 in hand (~$0.66B at ~$33k/GPU server BOM) plus High-Flyer's disclosed legacy A100 build — Fire-Flyer 1 at 200M RMB and Fire-Flyer 2 budgeted at 1B RMB, ~$170M combined, per DeepSeek's own Fire-Flyer AI-HPC paper and High-Flyer disclosures — lands near $0.8B of actually-spent capex through January 2025. Upside: even the maximalist chip-mix assumption (Alexandr Wang's "50,000 H100s") gives 50k × ~$33k = ~$1.65B; pushing to a rich all-in build (InfiniBand, storage, datacenter fit-out at ~$45k/GPU) gives ~$2.25B. Keep value at 1.6, shift the band to 0.8–2.4 (wider downside for delivery-timing and chip-mix risk, tighter upside because no plausible fleet count reaches 2.8), replace the Techstrong citation, and correct "three orders of magnitude" to ~300x. PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED VERBATIM. SemiAnalysis "DeepSeek Debates" (2025-01-31) states exactly: "Our analysis shows that the total server CapEx for DeepSeek is ~$1.6B, with a considerable cost of $944M associated with operating such clusters," and "We believe they have access to around 50,000 Hopper GPUs, which is not the same as 50,000 H100, as some have claimed." (1) THE CLAIM'S CORROBORATION IS CIRCULAR — the notes are factually wrong. The notes say "Amodei independently put DeepSeek's chip fleet spend 'on the order of ~$1B.'" He did not do so independently. Amodei's essay explicitly sources the count to SemiAnalysis: "This is a mix of H100's, H800's, and H20's, [according to SemiAnalysis](x.com/dylan522p/...), adding up to 50k total," prefaced with "It's been reported — we can't be certain it is true." His ~$1B is the same Dylan Patel fleet count multiplied by his own chip price (chips only, vs. SemiAnalysis's full servers). Strip that, and fx-09 is a SINGLE-SOURCE, single-analyst estimate. The word "independently" must be deleted from the notes, and grade B is not defensible on one unaudited analyst assertion — this is a C.

(2) SEMIANALYSIS'S OWN CONFIDENCE LANGUAGE IS 3x LOWER THAN $1.6B. The same piece says: "We are confident that their GPU investments account for more than $500M US dollars, even after considering export controls." That is what they stake confidence on; $1.6B is what "our analysis shows," asserted with no per-GPU pricing, no itemization, and no derivation published. Epoch AI, the most rigorous independent compute-estimation shop, analyzed DeepSeek's training runs (2,048 H800s for V3 pretraining, ~$5.3M) and produced NO fleet or capex estimate at all — it declined to corroborate rather than confirming. No US government investigation has produced a verified count or dollar value: the Singapore re-export fraud case (three men charged, March 2025) established only that servers "may have contained" Nvidia chips. PRIMARY SOURCE LOCATED AND CHECKED VERBATIM. Epoch AI, "Most of OpenAI's 2024 compute went to experiments," Josh You, published Oct 10 2025 (claim's source date "2025" is right). Retrieved full body + methodology text. The load-bearing sentences:

Upside: Epoch's $2B research figure is a modeling gross-up from a reported $1B amortized expense; "multiple years" could mean 3, which would give $3B research and $6B total. Independent sources of spread: (a) the amortization schedule is Epoch's assumption, not disclosed; (b) the $2B gross-up ignores any 2023 research-compute carryover in the 2024 amortization charge, which would push 2024-incurred research below $2B; (c) Epoch itself warns the figures "rely on projections for the final quarter of 2024" and "should not be considered completely reliable"; (d) it is unknown whether the $3B training line is incurred-basis or expense-basis, so Epoch is arguably mixing bases when it adds it to the incurred-basis $2B. INDEPENDENT SANITY CHECK: OpenAI 2024 revenue ~$3.7B (Bloomberg, via Epoch) against a widely reported ~$5B loss implies ~$8.7B of cost. $6.8B compute + ~$1.5B staffing ≈ $8.3B. I recovered it via Wayback: it reports, from The Information, that "as of March, the company was set to spend nearly $4 billion this year on using Microsoft's servers to run inference workloads for ChatGPT," and that "Training ChatGPT as well as new models could cost as much as $3bn this year." It is a March-2024 forward projection, not an actual. So DCD supports only the $3B training component and the ~$7B total; it is mis-cited as support for the $5B R&D line, and its inference figure is 2.2x Epoch's. Recommend demoting DCD to a corroborator of the training component and total only.

(B) The notes' "fixed R&D compute exceeded inference COGS ~2.7:1 in 2024" is the fragile part, not the $5B. It divides an Epoch-grossed-up numerator by a denominator that Epoch explicitly says is understated: "the $1.8 billion in inference expenses presumably do not include Microsoft spending on inference to run licensed OpenAI models for its own products." Using the expensed research figure instead ($4B R&D) and adding any Microsoft-side inference pushes the ratio toward 2:1 or below; using DCD's $4B inference collapses it to ~1.25:1. The ratio should carry a much wider band than the $5B numerator does. Also, the notes' "~$100M headline run" contrast is stale: Epoch's own GPT-4.5 final-run estimate is 40k–100k H100s for 90–165 days at $1.50–3.00/H100-hour, i.e. roughly $0.13–1.2B, not ~$100M. GRADE: B is right. This is second-hand reporting of investor documents with a projected Q4, filtered through one analyst's amortization assumption. It is not a filing and cannot be graded higher.

The ~$5B central value roughly survives, but three material problems force an adjustment: an unsupportable CI upper bound, a fragile derivation behind $2B of the $5B, and — most seriously for load-bearing use — a denominator in the notes that later evidence contradicts.

WHAT THE SOURCE ACTUALLY SAYS. The Epoch page (published 2025-10-10) reports OpenAI's 2024 cloud compute as ~$7B total: $3B training compute, $1.8B inference compute, and "$1 billion on research compute amortized over 'multiple years'." The $2B research figure is not reported — it is Epoch's own un-amortization: "we estimate that the amortization schedule for research compute was two years, for $2 billion in research compute expenses incurred in 2024." Epoch also states the source is September 2024 investor documents *with projections for Q4*, that the figures "should not be considered completely reliable," and that "how exactly OpenAI distinguishes training and research compute is not known." So half the gap between $3B and $5B rests on an assumed amortization schedule, and the training/research split may overlap. A plain reading of the underlying report ($1B incurred, amortized over multiple years) yields $4B, not $5B.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION IN THE CLAIM'S OWN SOURCES. The second cited source (DCD, July 2024, relaying The Information's March 2024 projections) gives ~$7B for training AND inference combined, with ~$4B on inference and up to $3B on training — no separate $2B research bucket, and inference exceeding training. Used on its own terms, that source implies R&D compute ~$3B and inference > R&D compute, the opposite of the thesis point. The two cited sources are not mutually consistent about the 2024 split; the claim silently takes the more favorable one.

NEW EVIDENCE (post-dating both cited sources) — OpenAI's leaked FY2024 income statement, reported June 2026 by Fortune, Quartz, Ars Technica and Zitron: revenue $3.7B, cost of revenue $2.65B, R&D expense $7.81B, total costs and expenses $12.4B, net loss attributable $5.09B. This is the best check available. Reconciliation: 2024 stock-based comp was $4.4B (The Information, 119% of revenue); allocating 60-80% of that to R&D plus ~$0.7B of R&D cash salaries leaves roughly $3.6-4.5B of the $7.81B R&D line for compute and data. That is consistent with Epoch's *expensed* compute ($3B training + $1B amortized research = $4.0B) and with a cash-incurred figure of ~$5B — so the claim is not refuted. But it also caps the number: $7B of R&D compute is arithmetically impossible ($7B R&D compute + $1.8-2.65B inference + $4.4B SBC = $13.2-14.1B against $12.4B of total 2024 costs). The CI80 high of 7 must come down; ~$6B is the realistic ceiling. Note also that $7B was Epoch's figure for TOTAL 2024 compute including inference, so a $7B R&D-only upper bound looks like it was anchored on the wrong number.

THE LOAD-BEARING RATIO IS WRONG. The notes assert R&D compute exceeded inference COGS ~2.7:1 in 2024 ($5B / $1.8B). OpenAI's actual 2024 cost of revenue was $2.65B, giving 1.9:1. Separately, leaked Microsoft documents (Zitron, Nov 2025; corroborated by The Register, TechCrunch, the-decoder) put OpenAI's 2024 Azure inference spend at $3.767B, giving 1.3:1. And comparing like with like on an accrual basis ($4.0B R&D compute expense vs $2.65B cost of revenue) gives 1.5:1. The 2.7:1 figure mixes a cash-incurred numerator with the lowest available accrual denominator — classic wrong-denominator inflation. The directional point (2024 fixed R&D compute > inference COGS) survives comfortably; the stated magnitude is inflated by roughly 40-100%.

FURTHER CAVEAT FOR THE THESIS. The Register and others note that much of OpenAI's 2024 training compute was paid in Azure credits from Microsoft's investment, making it "primarily non-cash," and that Microsoft-side figures may be grossed up relative to what OpenAI actually paid. So "$5B of R&D compute spend" is an economic-cost figure of uncertain cash content, and the Microsoft-side and OpenAI-side books do not cleanly reconcile.

VERDICT. Keep the metric but shade the center down slightly (the $2B research component is an assumption; the plain reading gives $4B; the source is a partial projection) and tighten the top end hard (7 is arithmetically excluded). Corrected: $4.5B, CI80 [3.3, 6.0]. Grade should stay B at best, and the accompanying ratio claim in the notes should be restated as roughly 1.3-1.9x, not 2.7x.

But the claim is load-bearing for a thesis being tested in July 2026, and its own notes extend the inference to "as of mid-2026" - and four months of newer public data materially change the picture.

(1) THE TREND FORECAST WAS FALSIFIED. The same SemiAnalysis piece headlined "Pricing is Only Going One Way For Now" and anticipated "another 15-20% month-on-month" increases through end-March. Compounded from $2.35 that implies ~$3.6-4.0/hr by June 2026. It did not happen. Silicon Data's neocloud H100 index (SDH100RT): 2026-04-01 $2.63; 2026-04-08 trough $2.47 (-6% in one week); 2026-04-30 $2.59; 2026-05-30 peak $2.76; net +3.8% end-to-end across April-May, 11.7% trough-to-peak swing, 18.4% annualized volatility. The current index reading on Silicon Data's product page is $2.53/GPU-hour (July 2026). Q2 was elevated-and-choppy, not accelerating. The claim's "+38% and rising" framing does not survive Q2 data.

(2) TWO-REGIME PROBLEM - WRONG DENOMINATOR FOR THE INFERENCE. Silicon Data, "H100 Index, May 2026: Same Chip, Two Tiers, Two Regimes" (2026-06-16), shows the H100 market split. Neocloud tier: $2.47-2.76, volatile, +7.1% in May. Hyperscaler tier: $7.44 (Apr 1) -> $7.51 (Apr 30) -> $7.46 (May 31), +0.27% net, 3.8% annualized vol. The companion April piece ("A Benchmark in Flat Mode", 2026-04-27) reports the hyperscaler index open $7.50 (Mar 1) / close $7.48 (Apr 20), high $7.52, low $7.40, unchanged on 39 of 50 daily transitions, 0.47% CV. Silicon Data explicitly describes the hyperscaler tier as "an administered price ceiling" that "reprices occasionally rather than daily," with demand "constrained by switching costs rather than price sensitivity." So the entire rising-price signal lives in the thin, short-tenor neocloud market priced at roughly one-third the hyperscaler rate - NOT in the contracted, at-scale channel where OpenAI/Anthropic actually procure. This does not kill the claim (neocloud is arguably the better marginal-scarcity signal), but "direct evidence of the supply constraint" is materially overstated as an unqualified statement when the at-scale tier shows literally zero movement.

(3) THE CITED CORROBORATION IS APPLES-TO-ORANGES. The notes say Silicon Data "corroborates $2.00 to $2.20 between 2025-12-09 and 2026-01-06." But SemiAnalysis says the 1-year contract series only broke above $2/hr in LATE JANUARY 2026 - three weeks AFTER Silicon Data was already at $2.20. These are different instruments: SDH100RT is a standardized index normalized across "rental term length, cluster scale, and interconnect," not a 1-year contract tenor. The level agreement is coincidental, not confirmatory. Two independent-looking sources are being used to cross-validate a number neither one measures the same way.

(4) TROUGH-BASELINE ARTIFACT. The "+38-40%" is measured off an October 2025 cyclical low that followed a two-year collapse in H100 rates (2023 on-demand ran $4-8/hr). $2.35 - and $2.53 today - remains well below 2023-24 levels. The directional point (2-3-year-old silicon appreciating at all is notable) survives; the magnitude is a baseline artifact.

(5) MINOR - THIN GB200 CORROBORATION. GetDeploying (updated 2026-07-23) does report GB200 median on-demand up ~42% from $13.25 to $18.77/GPU-hr since July 2025. But only two providers publish rates: CoreWeave $10.50 and Azure $27.04 per GPU-hr. A "median" over a two-point sample with a 2.6x spread is a weak statistic. Separately, GetDeploying's H100 SXM on-demand listings in July 2026 (Novita $3.39, Crusoe $3.90, Together $3.99, Lambda $4.29; RunPod $2.69 community / $2.99 secure) are consistent with a 1-year contract rate in the mid-$2s, so the claim's level is not implausible.

CORRECTION. If the metric is to characterize the state as of the thesis date (mid-2026) rather than a March snapshot, the better central estimate is ~$2.55/GPU-hour: the current SDH100RT reading is $2.53, the April-May neocloud range was $2.47-2.76, and the term structure is in contango on the shortage narrative (Silicon Data's forward-curve product exists precisely because near-term tightness is being priced). CI80 [2.35, 2.80] - lower bound anchored on the confirmed March 1-year print, upper on the May 30 peak. Note the corrected point value sits at the top of the original CI80 (2.15-2.60) and the corrected upper bound exceeds it, so the original interval is biased low for a mid-2026 read.

NET EFFECT ON THE THESIS. The load-bearing direction SURVIVES: H100 rental prices in July 2026 are materially above October 2025, hardware input costs are not collapsing, and the T5 umbrella-collapse has not begun. But two supporting framings should be dropped: "38% and accelerating" (Q2 was +3.8% over two months with a -6% drawdown) and the implication that this is a market-wide repricing (the hyperscaler tier is administratively flat to four decimal places of boredom). Recommend downgrading grade from B to B-: the point value is directly sourced but four months stale, the trend forecast attached to it was falsified, and the two cited corroborating sources measure different instruments than the headline metric.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND AND THE HEADLINE NUMBER IS EXACT. The InferenceX compare page states verbatim: "Around the middle of the 67–266 tok/s/user interactivity band — at 166 tok/s/user — B200 runs $0.04 per million tokens on gpt-oss 120B while H100 runs $0.26." Entity, hardware, model, interactivity target and period all check out (InferenceX v2 newsletter is dated 2026-02-16). The published H100 grid at 1k/1k · FP4 is $0.14 @117, $0.26 @166, $0.49 @216 tok/s/user, priced off "SemiAnalysis Market August 2025 Pricing Surveys & AI Cloud TCO Model" with H100 at $1.30/GPU/hr and B200 at $1.95/GPU/hr. So the value survives a hostile read. Four defects justify "adjust" rather than "confirm."

(1) UNIT IS MISSTATED. The source says "Owning-hyperscaler TCO normalized by OUTPUT tokens." The claim's unit reads "USD per million tokens." At the default 1k/1k ISL/OSL these differ by 2x — per-total-token would be $0.13. Any downstream comparison against blended API pricing silently doubles the number. The unit must read "per million OUTPUT tokens."

(2) THE CI'S STATED RATIONALE CONTRADICTS THE METRIC. The notes justify [0.10, 0.55] as "config sensitivity (tok/s/user target, FP8 vs FP4, batch size)" — but the metric explicitly PINS ~166 tok/s/user. Reintroducing interactivity variance imports uncertainty from a dimension the metric holds fixed. The $0.10 floor is not a plausible 166 tok/s/user value under any pricing basis; it corresponds to roughly 100 tok/s/user in the source's own grid ($0.14 is the 117 tok/s/user point). With interactivity pinned, the dominant real uncertainty is the COST BASIS, and it is one-sided upward: SemiAnalysis's own site offers "hyperscaler, neocloud, and rental pricing," and $1.30/GPU/hr is an owner-TCO floor from an August 2025 survey. Repricing at neocloud rental (~$1.9–2.5/hr) scales the figure ~1.5–1.9x to roughly $0.40–0.50. Hence a corrected, honestly-shaped CI of [0.18, 0.60] — tighter on the bottom (the source's measurement is precise) and slightly wider on top (basis risk).

(3) TWO OF THREE FACTUAL ASSERTIONS IN THE NOTES ARE WRONG. "NVIDIA cites $0.14/M on H100 for this workload" — $0.14 is SemiAnalysis's OWN H100 measurement at 117 tok/s/user, sitting in the same table as the $0.26. It is presented in the claim as independent vendor corroboration when it is an adjacent cell of the identical source. That falsely inflates the evidentiary weight of a load-bearing claim. Separately, "B200 measures $0.02–0.31/M" is unsupported: the source shows B200 at $0.03/$0.04/$0.06 across the published band. The $0.31 upper figure also contradicts the note's own "3–7x cheaper than H100" line (against a $0.55 H100 ceiling, $0.31 would be 1.8x).

(4) THE "PRODUCTION-STYLE BATCHING" LABEL IS MISLEADING AT THIS OPERATING POINT. The same page reports concurrency: at 166 tok/s/user the H100 serves only ~17 concurrent users, versus ~64 users at 117 tok/s/user. 17 concurrent users is the high-interactivity, low-concurrency corner — the expensive end — not what production serving of a 120B model typically looks like. The $0.26 is a defensible measured point but should be labeled as a high-interactivity target, not as representative production batching.

THESIS RELEVANCE (a hostile reviewer will raise this). The claim is used to anchor a floor supporting "marginal costs are back in a big way," but the same primary source cuts the other way on two counts. First, the identical workload on B200 measures $0.04/M — a ~6.5x collapse in marginal cost from one hardware generation, which is the strongest available evidence AGAINST durable inference-cost pressure. Citing the H100 number as the anchor while the source's own headline is the Blackwell improvement is selective. Second, gpt-oss-120B is a mid-size open model, not frontier; Thompson's argument concerns frontier-quality intelligence, and a 120B open-weights model's serving economics do not transfer to frontier models with far larger parameter counts and reasoning-token overhead. The number is real; the inferential load it is being asked to carry exceeds what it supports.

NET: value 0.26 confirmed exactly against primary source. Adjusting the CI to [0.18, 0.60], correcting the unit to output tokens, and flagging that the "NVIDIA cites $0.14" and "B200 $0.02–0.31" supporting notes should be struck as unsupported. Grade B is about right — arguably B+ for the point value given it is an exact, reproducible, independently-measured figure with public CI logs, but the notes' errors and the single-source dependency keep it from higher.

VALUE VERIFIED, FRAMING BROKEN. I pulled the raw HTML of the primary source and decoded its embedded SSR JSON, so this is not a WebFetch paraphrase. Verbatim: "at 166 tok/s/user - B200 runs $0.04 per million tokens on gpt-oss 120B while H100 runs $0.26." Underlying record for H100 at target 166: total throughput 1379.34 tok/s/GPU, outputTput 672.61, inputTput 706.73, cost 0.26185, costOutput 0.53781, costInput 0.50971, concurrency ~17; nearest MEASURED run is interactivity 169.32, tp=4, concurrency 16, costh 0.27219. So $0.26 is real, reproducible, and interpolation-adjacent to a measured point. Five material problems, though:

(1) WRONG DENOMINATOR — and in the opposite direction to what the page's prose implies. The page says "Owning-hyperscaler TCO normalized by output tokens," but the arithmetic says otherwise: 0.26185 x 1379.34 tok/s x 3600/1e6 = $1.3003/GPU-hr, exactly the stated H100 TCO, while the same computation on output tokens alone gives $0.63. The site's own costOutput field for this point is $0.538. So "$0.26 per million tokens" = per million TOTAL (input+output) tokens at a 1k/1k mix; the per-output-token figure is $0.54. Any downstream comparison against an output-token API price is off by 2x. (An earlier note in the scratchpad, mc-05-verification.txt line 20-21, has this backwards — it asserts per-total-token would be $0.13. It is not; $0.26 IS the total-token number.)

(2) "PRODUCTION-STYLE BATCHING" IS FALSE. Concurrency at this operating point is ~17 interpolated; the nearest measured run is 16 concurrent requests on a tp=4 H100 deployment, i.e. ~4 in-flight requests per GPU, for a model whose MXFP4 weights fit on one H100. That is the latency-optimized corner, not production batching. The same curve at 117 tok/s/user (~64 concurrent) is $0.139, and InferenceX's own "Best Throughput per GPU" for H100 on this model (10,284 tok/s) implies $0.035/M. The chosen point is 1.9x the mid-band point and ~7x the throughput-optimal point — a thesis-favorable selection, since it inflates apparent inference COGS.

(3) COST IS MODELED, NOT MEASURED. Throughput is measured; dollars come from SemiAnalysis's proprietary AI Cloud TCO model (Aug 2025 pricing survey) at the cheapest of three published bases — owning hyperscaler, $1.30/GPU-hr, implicitly 100% utilization. The dataset's own neocloud basis (costn) is 1.30x higher: $0.354/M total at the measured 169 tok/s/user point ($0.711/M output). A lab renting H100 capacity at ~$2/GPU-hr sees ~$0.40/M. Labs rent; they do not own. Calling this a "measured serving cost" overstates its empirical status.

(4) WRONG HARDWARE FOR "MARGINAL COST TODAY." Same benchmark, same workload, same 166 tok/s/user: B200 = $0.036/M (7.3x cheaper), and the H200-vs-H100 page shows H200 = $0.25 (Hopper is Hopper). Marginal new serving capacity in 2026 is Blackwell, so the H100 line is a legacy upper bound, not the marginal cost of new capacity. This cuts against the thesis it is being used to support: one hardware generation collapses the number by ~7x.

(5) EXTERNAL MARKET CONTRADICTION. OpenRouter lists gpt-oss-120b at $0.03/M input and $0.18/M output = ~$0.105/M blended at a 1:1 mix — the market clears at ~40% of the claimed H100 "cost," reconcilable only via newer silicon and far larger batches, which is exactly what the B200 line shows.

Also, two of the claim's three supporting notes are wrong: "NVIDIA cites $0.14/M on H100" — $0.14 is InferenceX's OWN H100 number at 117 tok/s/user on the same page, not independent NVIDIA corroboration; and "B200 measures $0.02-0.31/M" — the published B200 band is $0.027-$0.061 across 117-216 tok/s/user, with $0.31 unsupported.

CI: [0.10, 0.55] is the wrong shape. At the pinned config the number is near-deterministic (0.262 interpolated vs 0.272 measured), and residual uncertainty is one-sided UP (neocloud basis $0.35, rental ~$0.40, sub-100% utilization higher still, output-token convention $0.54). A $0.10 floor is unreachable at 166 tok/s/user on Hopper in this dataset — $0.10 corresponds to roughly 100 tok/s/user. I set the corrected floor at 0.14 (the same source's genuinely production-batched point, 117 tok/s/user at ~64 concurrent), because the metric's own words say "production-style batching," and keep the 0.55 ceiling to cover the rental/neocloud basis and the output-token convention. If the operating point is allowed to float to true throughput-optimized serving, the floor drops to ~$0.035 and the claim's usefulness as a COGS anchor collapses.

Verdict adjust rather than confirm: the scalar survives, the metric string does not. Required relabel: "gpt-oss-120B on H100, 1k/1k, MXFP4, ~166 tok/s/user (~17 concurrent, latency-optimized), $ per million TOTAL tokens, owning-hyperscaler TCO $1.30/GPU-hr (modeled)." Load-bearing caveat for the thesis: use it as a legacy-hardware ceiling, never as the 2026 marginal cost of serving — the same benchmark's B200 figure ($0.036) and the ~$0.105/M market price are the numbers a hostile reader will reach for.
