verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY-SOURCE AUDIT

Only one of the three cited sources is a primary disclosure, and it is not about the named entities.

1) DeepSeek open-infra-index Day 6 (the only true primary source) — VERIFIED AND FAITHFUL. Disclosed: $87,072/day GPU cost at an assumed $2/H800-GPU-hour, 278 peak / 226.75 avg nodes; 608B input tokens (342B cache hit, 266B miss), 168B output; "theoretical" daily revenue $562,027 at R1 list pricing; stated "cost profit margin 545%". 87,072/562,027 = 15.49%, so the note's "15.5% of its own list price" is arithmetically correct. I independently reconciled the revenue figure against the then-current R1 rate card (342B x $0.14 + 266B x $0.55 + 168B x $2.19 = $562.1k), confirming the denominator really is list price on a blended input+output basis. Caveats the claim does not carry: DeepSeek itself states actual revenue is "substantially lower" (V3 cheaper, web/app free, nighttime discounts); the $2/hr is an assumed rental rate, not actual cost; and output ran at 20-22 tok/s, far below US flagship interactivity SLAs, which materially flatters cost/token. Also a period mismatch — this source is Feb/Mar 2025, outside the claim's stated 2025-H2 to 2026-H1 window.

2) SemiAnalysis — MISREPRESENTED. The note says SemiAnalysis "works from a 75% API gross margin assumption (cost = 25% of list)." The accessible text says Anthropic's "gross margins on their inference infrastructure have increased from 38% to over 70%." That is (a) 70, not 75; (b) an estimate of Anthropic's realized inference-infrastructure margin, not an assumption about API gross margin; (c) denominated on revenue, not list price (secondary coverage confirms the definition as "revenue minus compute cost to serve, divided by revenue" — "compute costs have dropped to 30 cents on the dollar"). The same checkpoint's mc-09 records 70, so mc-08's note is internally inconsistent with its sibling claim. Note also that a >70% margin measured on total inference infrastructure is an UPPER bound on marginal cost share (it absorbs idle/reserved capacity), so it does not support a 25% marginal figure.

3) Alderson — FAITHFULLY QUOTED but optimistic and mis-converted. His verbatim conclusion is "80-95%+ gross margins" and "the API business is essentially a money printer." His cost model: $0.003/M input, $3.08/M output (72 H100s at $2/hr = $144/hr). Against $15/M output list that is 20.5% output-only — which appears to be where the claim's 20 came from. But the claim's metric is share of API list price, which must be blended across input and output. Running his own numbers through realistic mixes: agentic/cache-heavy ~7-8%, chat ~15%, reasoning-heavy ~20%. His self-stated caveats cut the other way: "really napkin math", 128k+ context "can increase costs by 2-10x", MoE routing costs 30-50% throughput, and his own error tolerance is "even if you assume we're off by a factor of 3".

CONVERGENCE. Converting every anchor to the claim's own metric (marginal serving cost / list-price revenue, blended): DeepSeek primary 15.5%; Alderson blended 7-20%; an independent 100k-draw Monte Carlo of Western frontier serving costs (codesota) puts median output cost at $2.41/M (p10-p90 $1.17-$4.73), i.e. 9.6% of $25 Opus list and 16% of $15 Sonnet list; SemiAnalysis-derived <30% as a ceiling. Median of the anchors is ~15%, not 20. The claim's 20 sits at or above every anchor except the one that is an explicit ceiling.

CI HONESTY. The low bound of 8 is slightly too high: cache-heavy agentic mixes and the p10 cost draws land at 5-8%. The high bound of 45 is slightly too tight given Alderson's own 2-10x long-context multiplier, his 3x error tolerance (which alone pushes reasoning-heavy workloads past 55%), US flagship models plausibly far larger than the 671B/37B DeepSeek proxy, and high-interactivity SLAs that shrink batch sizes. Widening to 6-48 honestly reflects source uncertainty.

RESIDUAL WEAKNESS THE PARENT SHOULD CARRY. (a) Grade C is correct and cannot be upgraded — no OpenAI or Anthropic primary disclosure of marginal serving cost exists; the only primary source is a different firm, on different hardware, at roughly one-seventh the price point. (b) "List price" is a soft denominator. SemiAnalysis's own finding that Opus 4.7 agentic work blends to $0.99/MTok against a $5/$25 rate card shows the same rate card produces wildly different blended prices by workload. If the thesis needs "labs can cut price and stay above cost," the commercially binding denominator is realized blended revenue per token, where SemiAnalysis's ~70% margin implies roughly 3.3x headroom — not the 5-10x a list-price framing suggests. (c) The load-bearing claim must not be read as unit economics: OpenAI's company-level gross margin is ~33% with $8.4B of 2025 inference cost (Sacra), and Anthropic's inference margin was 38% only a year earlier. The note flags this, correctly, but the gap is an order of magnitude and deserves to survive into the prose.

NET EFFECT ON THESIS: unchanged in direction. At 15% the list-price umbrella is ~6.7x (CI ~2.1x to ~17x), so "list price sits 3-10x above marginal serving cost" remains a defensible central band. This is a refinement, not a refutation.

HUNTED HARD FOR CONTRADICTION; THE CLAIM SURVIVES, BUT TWO OF ITS THREE SOURCE LEGS ARE DEFECTIVE AND THE METRIC NEEDS A DENOMINATOR SPEC.

WHAT ACTUALLY CONFIRMS IT (period- and denominator-matched, and newer than the cited sources)
SemiAnalysis's July 8, 2026 report "Anthropic 3Q26 Profit Over $1B: The Anthropic IPO Financials Sneak Peak" states Anthropic's **API business gross margin exceeds 80%** (paywalled; independently summarized by ChainCatcher, MacroStream and TradingKey, all reporting the same "API business gross margin exceeding 80%"). That is cost <=20% of API revenue — the claim's central value, arrived at by direct measurement rather than napkin triangulation. Same source family gives the bracketing figure: inference-infrastructure gross margin rose 38% -> "over 70%" (cost <=30%), the difference between the two being free-tier/consumer serving drag, exactly the distinction the claim's note draws. TradingKey adds that 75-85% of Anthropic ARR is usage-based API, so the API figure carries most of the weight.

I reproduced SemiAnalysis's own denominator arithmetic and it closes: their $0.99/MTok blended realized price for Opus 4.7 agentic (sticker $5/$25, 300:1 input:output, 90%+ cache hit, cached input $0.50/MTok) reconstructs to $1.03/MTok from the published rate card. So "blended list rate card at realistic token mix" is a coherent, reproducible denominator, and 80%+ GM against it lands at exactly 20% cost share / 5.0x markup. That is squarely inside T2's "3-10x price umbrella."

CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE FOUND, AND WHY IT DOESN'T OVERTURN
1. futuresearch.ai ("Is OpenAI Profitable?") is the one serious methodologically-explicit estimate that conflicts: OpenAI API gross margin ~75% (June 2024) falling to ~55% after the Aug 2024 price cuts, i.e. marginal serving cost = 45% of list ($14.75e-6 cost vs $32.5e-6 revenue per output token). Notably it is the only estimate that models utilization honestly (38%, derived as 1/(2x peak-to-trough x 1.33x growth buffer)). But it is Aug-2024 vintage, A100-era, dense-GPT-4o — two hardware generations and the entire MoE/prompt-caching transition before the claim's stated period. It sits exactly on the claim's CI ceiling, which is the right place for it.
2. Company-level margins are far worse and are the loudest contradicting numbers, but they are the wrong denominator: Epoch AI (Jan 2026) puts OpenAI's GPT-5 bundle at $6B revenue / $4B inference compute = 30% GM (cost 70% of revenue); The Information reports OpenAI FY25 GM 33% against a 46% forecast and Anthropic missing its own ~40% projection; Zitron argues headline AI margins are "fiction." All of these mix in free-tier serving, subscription bundling, R&D amortization and Microsoft rev-share. The claim's note pre-empts precisely this, and the SemiAnalysis 70%-infra vs 80%+-API split empirically validates that the gap is free-tier drag, not measurement error.
3. Vendor framing flagged, not used: NVIDIA's blog on SemiAnalysis InferenceMAX claims GB200 NVL72 cuts DeepSeek-R1 serving to "just over $0.10 per million tokens" vs $1.56 on H200 at 75 tok/s — a 15x reduction. This would push cost share below 1% of list, i.e. below the CI floor. I discount it: it is NVIDIA marketing its own silicon, uses a 37B-active model at low interactivity, and is peak-throughput TCO-normalized with no duty-cycle haircut. It supports the CI's low tail, nothing more.

DEFECTS IN THE CLAIM AS WRITTEN (fix these even though the number stands)
a) MISATTRIBUTION. The note says "SemiAnalysis works from a 75% API gross margin assumption (cost = 25% of list)." I read the cited May 2026 article: it contains no such assumption. Its only "75%" is "For GB300, DRAM was bundled into the board and marked up at ~75% gross margin" — a Nvidia memory-pricing statement, entirely unrelated. The article's actual relevant figure is "gross margins on their inference infrastructure have increased from 38% to over 70%." Replace the leg with the 70%-infra / 80%+-API pair.
b) THE DEEPSEEK LEG IS MISUSED AND BIASED LOW. The 15.5% is cost against *theoretical* revenue if every token were billed at R1 list price. DeepSeek's own Day-6 disclosure states actual revenue was substantially lower — V3 is priced cheaper, web/app is free, and off-peak discounts run 50-75%. DeepSeek's real cost/real-revenue ratio was therefore several times 15.5%. This leg does not support the low end; if anything it argues the opposite.
c) THE ALDERSON LEG IS THE WEAKEST AND IS SYSTEMATICALLY BIASED LOW. It assumes constant full 32-request batches (no diurnal utilization loss — the single factor futuresearch shows costs 2.6x), uses DeepSeek R1's 671B/37B-active architecture as a proxy for US flagship models, leaves KV cache and reasoning tokens unmodeled, and concedes long contexts shift to compute-bound at "2-10x" cost without incorporating it. Its $0.003/M input figure appears to derive prefill from HBM bandwidth rather than FLOPs; a FLOPs-bound derivation for a 37B-active model on H100 at plausible MFU gives ~$0.10/M, roughly 30x higher. The author self-describes as doing "napkin math" without frontier-serving experience. No corrections or addenda have been appended to the post.
d) DENOMINATOR AMBIGUITY IS WORTH 3-5x AND MUST BE SPECIFIED. "Share of API list price" is not well-defined: against the headline output price ($25/MTok Opus, $15 Sonnet, $10 GPT-5) the ratio falls well below the 8% CI floor; against realized revenue after prompt caching (75-90% off) and batch API (50% off) it runs 2-3x higher. Only the middle reading — blended list rate card applied to a realistic token mix — reproduces 20%. Add that qualifier to the metric string or the claim is unfalsifiable.

CALIBRATION OF VALUE AND CI
Value 20% holds. Anthropic, the API-heavy lab (75-85% of ARR), sits at or below it (80%+ API GM). OpenAI is the drag: it prices its flagship far cheaper ($1.25/$10 for GPT-5 vs $5/$25 for Opus), so its API cost share is plausibly 25-40%, and its 2024 predecessor measured 45%. A revenue-weighted blend lands at ~20%, perhaps 20-23%. Not a material enough shift to justify moving the point estimate. CI [8, 45] is honest and well-anchored at both ends — 45% is futuresearch's measured OpenAI value, 8% is defensible on Blackwell/Trainium economics — so I am not widening it either. I would raise the grade C -> B: the claim now rests on a direct period-matched measurement of the exact metric rather than triangulated napkin math, provided the sourcing is repaired per (a)-(c).

RESIDUAL RISK A HOSTILE REVIEWER SHOULD STILL PRESS. SemiAnalysis's 80%+ API GM is an accounting gross margin, so it likely charges only utilized compute to COGS; take-or-pay reserved capacity that sits idle may be booked elsewhere, which would flatter it. Anthropic also serves partly on Trainium at Amazon-favorable rates that may not represent merchant marginal cost. Both push the true economic figure toward the upper half of the CI. This is why 20% should be read as the center of a genuinely wide distribution, not a precise number — which the C/B grade and the 8-45 band already encode.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED, QUOTE IS FAITHFUL. I retrieved the SemiAnalysis piece directly (newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/ai-value-capture-the-shift-to-model, published May 1, 2026; authors Daniel Nishball, Dylan Patel, Cheang Kang Wen + others). The full sentence reads: "This year Anthropic's ARR has exploded from $9B to over $44B today, their gross margins on their inference infrastructure have increased from 38% to over 70% over the same period." The claim's quote, entity (Anthropic specifically, not labs generally), unit (percent), and period label ("as of 2026-05") are all faithful. The sentence sits in the FREE portion of the article (paywall begins at the "VR NVL72 vs GB300 Performance per TCO" section), so it is independently checkable. The supporting details in the notes also check out verbatim: blended realized price for Opus 4.7 on agentic tasks estimated at $0.99/MTok vs $5/$25 sticker, ~300:1 input:output ratio for Claude Code, >90% cache hit rates, $0.50/MTok cached input.

WHAT THE PERIOD ACTUALLY IS: "over the same period" = the 2026 year-to-date window only, i.e. ~38% in Jan 2026 to >70% at May 1, 2026. That is a 32-point margin expansion in four months, asserted with no disclosed methodology and no attribution inside the article. Anyone leaning on this should treat it as an unaudited analyst estimate, not a measured figure.

NO PRIMARY FILING EXISTS TO CHECK AGAINST. Anthropic filed a CONFIDENTIAL S-1 with the SEC on June 1, 2026; as of July 18, 2026 no public S-1 or S-1/A was on EDGAR. So there is no disclosure that can confirm or contradict this. Grade B (analyst estimate) is appropriate; it cannot be upgraded.

CORROBORATION (same firm, so internal consistency rather than independence): SemiAnalysis's later piece "Anthropic 3Q26 Profit Over $1B: The Anthropic IPO Financials Sneak Peak" (July 8, 2026; Brookhart, Huang, Patel — paywalled, but figures reproduced by ChainCatcher and TradingKey) estimates Anthropic's OVERALL gross margin at mid-60% for Q2 2026, up from -94% in 2024, with the API business "exceeding 80%," ARR per megawatt going from $16M nine months ago to ~$60M later this year, and Q2 2026 EBIT margin of 36%. It also uses the same $9B end-2025 ARR baseline as the May piece. The three figures nest coherently: overall (mid-60s) < inference infrastructure (>70%) < API-only (>80%). The ARR/MW metric is the mechanical driver that makes the fast expansion at least internally plausible.

WHY I ADJUST RATHER THAN CONFIRM — two problems with the stated interval:
(1) The point estimate is mis-centered against its own source. The source says "over 70%", i.e. 70 is a FLOOR, not a central estimate. Using 70 as the value silently converts a lower bound into a midpoint.
(2) ci80_low = 55 is not defensible. It sits 15 points below the source's own stated floor and below the same firm's estimate of Anthropic's OVERALL gross margin (mid-60s) for the immediately following quarter. Overall gross margin includes free-tier/consumer serving and non-inference COGS, so it should sit BELOW inference-infrastructure margin; a 55% inference-infra margin in May is structurally inconsistent with mid-60s overall in Q2. The 55 floor is over-hedging that materially weakens a load-bearing claim (55% implies COGS ~45% of revenue, a very different picture for the "marginal costs are back" thesis than 30%).
Corrected: value 72, CI80 [63, 80]. The floor of 63 (not 70) preserves honest downside for the fact that this is one analyst shop with no methodology shown, and for the one genuine contrary signal below. The ceiling stays at 80 because API-only is the >80% segment and blended inference infrastructure must sit under it.

CONTRARY SIGNAL WORTH CARRYING: The Information, Jan 22, 2026 — "Anthropic Lowers Gross Margin Projection as Revenue Skyrockets" (paywalled; I could not read the figures). As of January 2026, Anthropic's own internal margin projection was being revised DOWN, which is the opposite direction from the 38%-to-70% sprint SemiAnalysis describes over exactly that window. This does not refute the claim (company-wide projection vs inference-infra realized margin; compute commitments and free-tier load are the likely wedge), but it is the reason the corrected floor stays at 63 rather than 68-70.

TWO SCOPE CAVEATS FOR THE PARENT (do not drop these when the claim is used):
(a) This is NOT Anthropic's company gross margin. Same-firm estimates put company-wide GM ~5-8 points lower (mid-60s) at the same time. If the thesis narrative renders 70% as "Anthropic's gross margin," it overstates.
(b) The notes assert the margin figure is "already net of caching discounts" because the article separately estimates $0.99/MTok blended realized price. SemiAnalysis never links the two — the $0.99 estimate is specific to Opus 4.7 agentic workloads and appears in a different part of the argument. The inference is reasonable (a margin on "inference infrastructure" is presumably computed on realized revenue) but is the claim author's, not the source's, and the computation sits behind the paywall. Mark it as an assumption, not a sourced fact. If the >70% were instead computed against list-price revenue, it would be inflated.

QUOTE VERIFIED VERBATIM. I fetched the primary source (SemiAnalysis, "AI Value Capture — The Shift To Model Labs," May 1 2026) and confirmed the exact sentence: "This year Anthropic's ARR has exploded from $9B to over $44B today, their gross margins on their inference infrastructure have increased from 38% to over 70% over the same period." A second sentence in the same piece restates it as "inference margins have gone up from < 40% to > 70%." The $0.99/MTok blended-price estimate for Opus 4.7 vs $5/$25 sticker is also verbatim. So the transcription is clean and the claim is not a misquote.

WHY I STILL SAY ADJUST (three material problems, two of which push the number UP, one of which pushes the INTERPRETATION down):

(1) The point value is set at the source's FLOOR, not its estimate. "Over 70%" is a lower bound. A later SemiAnalysis report (summarized by TradingKey, July 8 2026) says Anthropic's "overall gross margin has rebounded from negative 94% in 2024 to the mid-60% range" with the "API business exceeding 80%." Since 75-85% of Anthropic ARR is the usage-based API business (same report), the API figure is close to a direct read on inference-infrastructure margin, and it sits above 80, not at 70. An independent arithmetic cross-check agrees: a widely echoed figure has Anthropic's total compute spend falling from 71c to 56c per revenue dollar, and SemiAnalysis separately states >60% of Anthropic compute is allocated to TRAINING; 0.56 x 0.4 = ~22% of revenue as inference COGS implies ~78% inference margin. Three independent routes land in 70-80, so a point value of 70 and a CI floor of 55 are unjustifiably pessimistic for the metric AS SCOPED. I raise the point to 72 and the floor to 60 (60, not 70, because the entire evidence base traces to one paywalled proprietary model — see (3)).

(2) DENOMINATOR TRAP — the real hazard, and the reason this must not be used as written. "Gross margin on inference infrastructure" is a narrow slice, not Anthropic's economics. SemiAnalysis's own overall Anthropic gross margin is mid-60s, ~7-10 points below the inference-infra number, and The Information reported in 2025 that Anthropic CUT its gross margin forecast to 40% from 50% as inference costs ran ~23% over plan. The gap is free tier, research/experimental compute, and heavily subsidized subscription tiers — Zitron, citing SemiAnalysis's own data, notes $200/month subscriptions where users burn $8,000-$14,000 of tokens. And >60% of compute is training, which sits entirely outside this denominator. If the parent thesis uses 70%+ as "Anthropic's gross margin," it overstates the company figure by ~7-10 points and the 2025 realized figure by ~30. Use ~65% for company-level marginal-cost arguments; reserve 70-80% for the API/inference-serving line specifically.

(3) ATTRIBUTION CONFOUND — the improvement is not purely serving efficiency (T6). The 38%->70% window (roughly Q2 2025 to Q2 2026) coincides with aggressive rationing and repricing: Claude Code removed from the $20 Pro tier (~April 21 2026), Claude Code split into its own credit pool at full API rates with no rollover (June 15 2026), third-party agent access restricted, plus reported model-availability degradation in March-April 2026. So a meaningful share of the margin gain is price/mix (T2), not cost-per-token (T6). The claim's note credits both, which is right, but the split is not 50/50 in T6's favor.

SOURCE-QUALITY CAVEATS a hostile reviewer would raise, and my read on each: (a) ZERO independent verification. Every apparent corroboration I traced — officechai (May 2 2026), angelinvestorsnetwork's Series H analysis, matterfact (June 26 2026) — cites SemiAnalysis and nothing else; matterfact actually mis-attributes the figure to a Musk podcast citing the Ramp AI Index, which is echo, not confirmation. (b) The methodology is NOT disclosed in the article; it points to a paywalled "Tokenomics model" and "AI TCO model." No depreciation schedule, utilization assumption, or cost-per-token derivation is shown. (c) The piece is a bullish thesis article ("value capture shifts to model labs") and the margin number is deployed as evidence for that thesis — marketing-framing risk is real. (d) Ed Zitron's general critique that AI gross margins excluding sales and marketing are "laughable" applies, though it is an objection to the metric's usefulness, not to its value.

WHY NOT REFUTE: the direction is corroborated by non-SemiAnalysis facts. Anthropic's own investor disclosures around the $30B round that closed May 2026 show Q1 2026 revenue $4.8B, Q2 2026 revenue $10.9B and a first-ever operating income of $559M (non-GAAP, includes training compute, excludes SBC). $10.9B quarterly annualizes to ~$44B, exactly reconciling SemiAnalysis's ARR figure, and you cannot post positive operating income while carrying full training compute unless gross margin is well north of 50%. OpenAI's leaked ~39% gross margin for the same period is a useful contrast rather than a contradiction — the gap is explained by OpenAI's free consumer base and 65%+ subscription revenue mix versus Anthropic's 75-85% API mix.

NET: metric is real, quote is accurate, direction is corroborated; the point estimate is too low for the scoped metric, the CI floor is below anything any source supports, and the claim needs an explicit denominator guardrail before it can bear weight.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE LOCATED. The number traces to The Information, "Why OpenAI, Anthropic Missed Their Own Gross Margin Forecasts," by Sri Muppidi, Dealmaker newsletter, dated 2026-02-24 (https://www.theinformation.com/newsletters/dealmaker/openai-anthropic-missed-gross-margin-forecasts). Body is paywalled, but the indexed lede reads: "OpenAI's gross margins fell to 33% from 40% in 2024, missing its own forecasts of 46%. Anthropic anticipated 2025 gross margins of 40%, down from negative 94% in 2024, falling 10 percentage points short of forecasts." Every element of the claim's notes is present in the primary lede or its immediate downstream coverage.

FAITHFULNESS CHECK — all four dimensions pass. Value: 33, verbatim. Unit: percent, correct. Period: FY2025 (OpenAI's fiscal = calendar year); BigGo's "last year" resolves to 2025 given its 2026-02-25 publication date, and Feedough states it as "2025" explicitly. Entity: OpenAI. The word "adjusted" in the claim's metric label is faithful, not an embellishment — Feedough (https://www.feedough.com/openai-statistics/) states verbatim "Adjusted gross margin fell to 33% in 2025, down from 40% in 2024, as inference costs quadrupled during the year," and the rohanpaul_ai relay uses the same phrasing.

THE HARD QUESTION — is 33% company-wide or API-only? This mattered because the corpus contradicts itself: sibling claim rv-03 (line ~2250 of /Users/kushaldsouza/Documents/Thinking/chipandadmarketresearch/p1-ai-economics/data/claims-checkpoint.json) labels the identical 33% as "API-only adjusted gross margin." mc-11's "company-wide" label is the correct one, on four independent grounds. (1) rv-03's own cited source is bad: I fetched https://futuresearch.ai/openai-api-profit/ and the 33% figure does not appear on that page at all — it discusses API-segment margins of 75% (Jun 2024) and ~55%, an order of magnitude away. (2) Parallelism with Anthropic: The Information reports Anthropic's 2024 figure as NEGATIVE 94%. A negative gross margin is only coherent at company level; no API segment runs COGS at 1.94x revenue. (3) Arithmetic reconciliation: 1 − $8.4B inference / $13.1B company revenue = 35.9%, landing at ~33% once modest non-inference COGS (data, trust & safety, support) is added. The $8.4B decomposes into $3.9B free-user and $4.5B paying-user inference — free ChatGPT users are definitionally not API, so their cost can only sit in a company-wide denominator. (4) The 2024 figure reconciles the same way: ~$2.2B inference on ~$3.7B company revenue = 40.5%, matching the reported 40%. Feedough independently describes the compression as structural "at the company level." Recommend the parent correct rv-03's metric label, not mc-11's.

HOSTILE CHALLENGE — the 42.6% counter-number. The June 2026 leak (Fortune, https://fortune.com/2026/06/16/openai-financials-leaked-losses-revenue-profit/) gives revenue $13.07B and cost of revenue $7.5B, implying a 42.6% GAAP gross margin — 9.6 points above the claim and far outside the stated CI. This does not refute the claim; it is a different metric. The gap is fully explained and self-consistent: The Information's "adjusted" measure loads all $8.4B of inference into COGS, while GAAP cost of revenue is only $7.5B because free-tier and research serving compute is booked into R&D (OpenAI's R&D line is $19.18B, including ~$10.6B to Microsoft for Azure). Adjusted GM < GAAP GM is exactly the sign you'd expect from that reclassification, and the two independently-leaked datasets (Feb and Jun 2026, different reporters, different documents) reconcile to within ~$0.9B. That cross-leak consistency is the strongest evidence here and is why I did not downgrade for single-sourcing. The claim's "(adjusted)" qualifier is doing honest work; the notes correctly attribute the mechanism to free-user serving plus scarcity-priced compute in COGS.

CORROBORATION vs HERDING. Sacra ("OpenAI posted a 33% gross margin, constrained by inference costs that reached $8.4B in 2025"), Feedough, BigGo, Shopifreaks, companieshistory.com and airstarbank all report 33%, but all herd to the same Feb 24 Information piece — treat as one source, not six. Two source-quality cautions the parent should act on: BigGo (cited source #1) is a low-quality Taiwanese aggregation — it garbles inference costs as "$8.4 billion (~$1.22 billion)" and states "approximately 91 million weekly active users," which is off by roughly an order of magnitude. The X/Aakash Gupta link (cited source #2) returned HTTP 402 and is not verifiable. Both should be replaced with the primary Information URL plus Sacra/Feedough. The claim survives on the primary, not on its two listed citations. Sacra also frames revenue as excluding Microsoft licensing and one-time deals, but its $8.4B tell shows it is simply relaying The Information; its ARR framing ($20B exiting 2025) does not disturb the $13.1B recognized-revenue basis.

CI CALIBRATION — [29, 37] is honest, arguably slightly generous in width. The primary publishes a single point with no range, so the CI is pricing definitional and leak-fidelity risk rather than sampling error. ±4 points is well-shaped: the upper bound comfortably covers the inference-only reconstruction (35.9%), while the GAAP 42.6% correctly falls outside because it is a different metric. I considered widening the low side. The residual risk is that "inference cost" is defined inconsistently across leaks — Zitron's leaked vendor documents put CY2024 inference at $3.77B, which on ~$3.7B of 2024 revenue would imply a ~0% or negative 2024 gross margin, irreconcilable with the reported 40%. So the adjusted-GM series is definition-locked to The Information's COGS basis, and a Zitron-basis recomputation would produce a materially lower number. But the claim names the reported adjusted metric explicitly, so that divergence is out of scope for the point estimate and is adequately absorbed by not tightening the CI. Grade B is right — single primary outlet, paywalled, leaked non-audited internal figure, but from a reporter with a strong OpenAI-financials track record and with independent arithmetic corroboration from a second leak.

THESIS BEARING. The claim does the work it is asked to do, and the notes are unusually precise about why. It establishes that inference is real usage-scaling COGS (quadrupled YoY to $8.4B, projected $14.1B in 2026), and that company-level margin (33%) sits far below the ~70-90% marginal margin on paid API tokens precisely because free-user serving and last-minute scarcity-priced compute load into COGS. One nuance worth surfacing: 33% arguably understates the marginal economics for T2 purposes, since $3.9B of the $8.4B is free-user inference, which is closer to customer acquisition cost than to marginal COGS on revenue-generating tokens. The notes already flag this. Also correctly stated: training sits in R&D ($19.18B), not in this COGS line — which is the T1 fixed-cost-vs-marginal-cost distinction Thompson is drawing. No correction, retraction, or restatement of the 33% figure was found in the five months between publication and today.

CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE FOUND — the 33% is a company-internal non-GAAP planning-deck metric that is superseded by audited financials showing ~43%.

1) SUPERSEDING PRIMARY EVIDENCE (the decisive find). Ed Zitron's 2026-06-15 exclusive reports OpenAI's audited financial documents, "independently verified by the Financial Times," with a full income statement:
- FY2025: revenue $13.07B, cost of revenue $7.5B, gross profit $5.57B -> gross margin 42.6%. (R&D $19.18B, S&M $5.73B, G&A $1.57B, total costs $34.0B, operating loss -$20.92B, net loss -$38.53B incl. a $41.55B convertible fair-value remeasurement.)
- FY2024: revenue $3.7B, cost of revenue $2.65B, gross profit $1.05B -> gross margin 28.4%.
The statement ties out arithmetically (13.07 - 34.0 = -20.93 operating loss), and it is a later, higher-grade document than the leaked investor slides The Information reported from. This is a textbook "later correction" against a preliminary/planning number.

2) THE CLAIM'S DIRECTIONAL NARRATIVE IS REFUTED. The claim's notes rest on "fell from 40% (2024) to 33% (2025)." Audited data show gross margin ROSE from 28.4% to 42.6% as revenue tripled. That is operating leverage on inference, not margin compression — the opposite of the story the claim carries into the thesis.

3) THE 33% DOESN'T RECONCILE WITH ITS OWN COMPONENTS. The deck's adjusted GM is explicitly defined as "revenue minus inference costs" (aiHola on the leaked slides). With the reported $13.1B revenue and $8.4B inference, that arithmetic yields 35.9%, not 33%. To get 33% you need inference of $8.78B. But audited TOTAL cost of revenue is only $7.5B — i.e., the deck's "inference" figure is larger than OpenAI's entire GAAP COGS line. The likely reconciliation: the ~$3.9B of free-user inference (per the BigGo/The Information breakdown: ~$3.9B free, ~$4.5B paid) is not booked in cost of revenue at all — plausibly in S&M ($5.73B) as customer acquisition. So the 33% is a management metric that deliberately loads costs the income statement puts elsewhere. It is not a gross margin.

4) THE DEFINITION IS INCONSISTENT ACROSS YEARS. In 2024 the deck's "adjusted GM" (40%) implies inference of $2.22B, which sits INSIDE audited COGS of $2.65B — i.e., adjusted GM was above GAAP GM in 2024 but below it in 2025. A metric that flips sign relative to GAAP between two consecutive years is not a consistent series, so the 40% -> 33% "decline" is partly a definitional artifact.

5) SECONDARY-SOURCE QUALITY IS POOR. Both cited sources are downstream aggregators of The Information (one an X post, one an aggregator), and they contradict each other on a basic fact: BigGo says 2025 inference of $8.4B EXCEEDED the $6.6B forecast by $1.8B, while aiHola's summary of the same slides says OpenAI beat revenue targets "while spending LESS than projected on inference." Grade B is generous for this chain.

6) COUNTER-EVIDENCE IN THE OTHER DIRECTION (kept for balance). Zitron's separate leaked-Microsoft-document piece shows OpenAI's Azure inference spend alone at $8.67B through Q3 CY2025 and $3.767B in CY2024 — far above any of the reported COGS/inference figures, and he argues reported costs are understated. If true, the real cost-to-serve margin is much lower than 43%. This is why I widen the CI downward rather than pinning tightly at 42.6%.

CORRECTED ESTIMATE. Best point estimate for OpenAI's FY2025 company-wide gross margin: 42% (audited, FT-verified: 42.6%). CI80 36-45: the low bound accommodates the "all-in inference including free users" reading, (13.07-8.4)/13.07 = 35.9%, which is the most defensible version of the pessimistic case; the high bound reflects rounding in the $7.5B COGS figure. 33% falls outside the corrected interval and should not be used as "company-wide gross margin."

IMPACT ON THE THESIS. The thesis survives directionally but weakens quantitatively. A 43% gross margin is still far below classic zero-marginal-cost software (70-90%), so "inference is real COGS and company-level margin is well below marginal API-token margin" holds. But two supporting props break: (a) margins are not compressing — they roughly doubled YoY on audited numbers, which is evidence FOR operating leverage on inference and AGAINST "marginal costs are back in a big way"; and (b) the "missed 46% target, scrambled for expensive last-minute compute" story comes from a planning deck whose cost definitions do not match the audited statements. If this claim is load-bearing, the parent should either re-label the metric precisely as "OpenAI internal adjusted GM (revenue less all inference incl. free users), FY2025 ~33-36%" and stop calling it company-wide gross margin, or switch to the audited 42.6% figure. Grade should drop to C for the 33% figure as stated; the audited 42.6% figure merits A-/B+.

The notes also check out: my computed median across all 21 trends is 46.2 (Epoch prose says 50x), min 9.2 / max 851.2 (Epoch prose says "between 9x and 900x"), and the post-Jan-2024 acceleration to ~200x median is stated on the page.

WHAT DOES NOT CHECK OUT (the CI — this is the reason for "adjust"):
Epoch publishes a 90% CI for this exact trend, and it is [4.4, 401.4]. The claim asserts an 80% CI of [25, 65]. That interval is not a narrowing of Epoch's uncertainty — it sits nested deep inside Epoch's 90% CI and misrepresents the source's own stated precision by nearly two orders of magnitude in each direction.

I reconstructed the honest 80% CI from Epoch's published numbers. Log-space symmetry is exact to four decimals (ln(pt)-ln(lo) = ln(hi)-ln(pt) = 2.2569), confirming an analytic t-based CI on a log-linear slope. With n=6 and df=4: SE(log slope) = 2.2569/t(0.95,4) = 1.0586. An 80% CI is therefore exp(ln 42.02 +/- 1.5332*1.0586) = [8.3, 213.0]. The claim's interval is 3.4x too narrow in log half-width (0.478 vs 1.623).

THE STATED CI RATIONALE IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY:
The notes justify [25, 65] as reflecting "benchmark selection sensitivity Epoch itself documents." This fails twice. First, it is a category error: the metric is explicitly pinned to one benchmark and one threshold (GPQA Diamond at GPT-4 level), so cross-benchmark dispersion is not the relevant uncertainty — the regression's own standard error is. Second, even taken on its own terms it points the wrong way: the benchmark-selection dispersion Epoch documents is 9x to 900x, which is vastly WIDER than [25, 65], not narrower. The cited rationale cannot produce the cited interval under any reading.

TWO SECONDARY CORRECTIONS:
(1) Period is overstated. The claim says "2023-2025." This specific trend's regression window in Epoch's data is 2023-03-14 to 2024-12-13 — it ends in December 2024. Only other trends (MMLU/GPT-4, GPQA/Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Arena/GPT-4o) run to 2025-02-05. "2023-2024" is the accurate window for the 40x figure.
(2) The evidence base is thinner than the confident number suggests. n=6 points, R^2=0.76. The six points are GPT-4-0314 ($37.50/1M, score 33.0), GPT-4 Turbo ($15.00, 50.0), Mistral-Large-2024-02 ($6.00, 36.0), Claude-3-Haiku ($0.50, 33.0), Gemini-1.5-Flash ($0.13, 39.0), Phi 4 ($0.12, 53.0). Epoch's own limitations section notes GPQA Diamond evaluation variance between sources averages 2.9 percentage points — which bites hard here because the threshold is 33.0 and two of the six points (Claude-3-Haiku at 33.0, Mistral-Large at 36.0) sit essentially at it. Reasonable eval noise could drop a point from the frontier and materially move the slope. True uncertainty is therefore, if anything, wider than the regression CI, which reinforces the widening rather than arguing against it.

THESIS IMPACT (why this is "adjust," not "refute"):
The claim is load-bearing for T5/T6 — the argument that the umbrella erodes from below as cheap models reach fixed capability, rather than via frontier price cuts. That mechanism survives the correction robustly, because the direction and order of magnitude are genuinely well-sourced. Even the pessimistic end of the honest 80% CI (~8x/year) still means constant-capability inference prices collapse by roughly an order of magnitude annually, which is more than enough to carry the qualitative argument. What does not survive is the false precision: a hostile reviewer who opens Epoch's own results file finds a 90% CI of [4.4, 401.4] and would correctly say the claim dressed a very noisy six-point regression as a tight estimate. Grade B remains defensible for the point value (reputable primary source, open code and data), but the CI as stated was not derived from the source.

One further caveat worth carrying forward given load_bearing=true: this is a March 2025 publication whose data for this trend ends December 2024. Deploying it in a July 2026 argument is an ~18-month extrapolation the source does not underwrite. Epoch itself hedges the acceleration finding ("it's less clear that those will persist").

RECOMMENDED CORRECTION: keep value = 40 (faithful to the published headline; 42.0 exact), replace the CI with [8, 215] derived from Epoch's own published 90% CI, and restate the period as 2023-03 to 2024-12.

POINT ESTIMATE CONFIRMED VERBATIM. Epoch AI's 2025-03-12 data insight states exactly: "the price to achieve GPT-4's performance on a set of PhD-level science questions fell by 40x per year." For the narrowly-named metric (GPQA Diamond, GPT-4 threshold), value=40 is not wrong and I retain it.

THE CI IS THE FAILURE POINT, and it fails on contradicting evidence, not just vagueness.

(1) Two independent published estimates of the same construct fall BELOW the claimed floor of 25. a16z's "LLMflation" (MMLU thresholds 42 and 83, Nov 2021-late 2024): "For an LLM of equivalent performance, the cost is decreasing by 10x every year." Stanford HAI 2025 AI Index, Takeaway #7: inference cost for GPT-3.5-level performance "dropped over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024" — 23 months, implying 280^(12/23) ~= 19x/year. Two of three independent constant-capability estimates sit outside [25,65]. A CI that excludes the majority of the published literature on the same quantity is not an 80% interval.

(2) The source publishes NO confidence interval and documents ~100x dispersion. Epoch analyzed six benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA Diamond, MATH-500, MATH Level 5, HumanEval, Chatbot Arena Elo) with "prices declining between 9x per year and 900x per year." The claim's note that its CI "reflects benchmark selection sensitivity Epoch itself documents" is demonstrably false — a +/-60% band cannot represent a 9x-to-900x spread. The dominant uncertainty is benchmark and threshold SELECTION, not fit error, and nothing privileges GPQA over MMLU. Epoch's own headline is the inequality ("but unequally across tasks"); selecting the 40x figure and reporting a tight band inverts the source's actual message. Note also that MMLU-based methods independently cluster at 9-10x (a16z 10x; Epoch's 9x floor), i.e. the low end is a reproducible result, not an outlier.

(3) MECHANISM CRITIQUE. The estimator is a running minimum — "cheapest model achieving threshold X" — over a growing model set, fit exponentially. High thresholds crossed by a step function (an expensive frontier model, then suddenly a small cheap model) produce absurd fitted rates; Epoch notes "the fastest trends (e.g. 900x per year) start after January 2024," which is the signature of few-point step crossings, not a measured acceleration in an underlying cost curve. The post-Jan-2024 "median 200x/year" cited in the claim's notes is the most artifact-prone number in the analysis and should not be treated as a forward rate. Epoch also concedes "there may be models not in our dataset that were more cost-effective," biasing rates in an uncontrolled direction.

(4) WRONG DENOMINATOR FOR THE THESIS — the most serious issue for load-bearing use. Epoch "excluded reasoning models from our analysis of per-token prices" because they "tend to generate a much larger number of tokens than other models." Reasoning models became the frontier paradigm from late 2024 onward. So the metric measures per-token price at a FROZEN capability among NON-reasoning models — precisely the segment where commoditization is fastest — while the thesis needs cost-per-task for frontier-quality intelligence. The same AI Index reports "o1 is nearly six times more expensive and 30 times slower than GPT-4o." At the frontier, cost per completed task rose over this window. The claim's framing ("the umbrella erodes from below") is directionally supported, but the 40x figure cannot be read as the rate at which frontier serving COGS falls.

(5) STALENESS. Epoch's data-insights index shows no inference-pricing update after 2025-03-12; underlying data ends ~Q1 2025. The claim is load-bearing in a July 2026 thesis, leaving ~16 months unverified in exactly the period when reasoning-model token consumption and rising GPU rents cut against the trend.

CORRECTION. Keep value=40 for the named GPQA metric (verbatim, no better estimate exists for that specific quantity), but widen the 80% CI to [10, 150] — roughly log-symmetric about 40. The floor of 10 must accommodate the reproducible MMLU-based results (a16z 10x, Epoch's 9x floor) and AI Index's ~19x; the ceiling of 150 accommodates genuine post-2024 acceleration without importing the artifact-driven 900x tail. Caveat for downstream use: if this claim is generalized to "the constant-capability inference price decline rate" writ large — which is how the notes deploy it for T5/T6 — the defensible central estimate pooling across methods is ~20-25x/year, not 40x. Grade B is generous; the combination of no source CI, 100x benchmark dispersion, reasoning-model exclusion, and 16-month staleness argues for C. The qualitative thesis (constant-quality prices collapse while frontier list prices stay high) survives at any value in the corrected range, so the thesis is robust to this correction — but the stated precision is not.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY-SOURCE TRACE. Both cited sources resolve and say what the claim says, and — more importantly — the number is independently reconstructable from the providers' own list prices, which are the true primary source for a list price.

1) Artificial Analysis providers page (cited source 1) currently shows CoreWeave and DeepInfra tied at $0.05/M blended as the cheapest of 22 providers, with the page's own footnote defining blended as "a blend of cache hit, input, and output token prices using the selected ratio (default 7:2:1 cache-input-output)." Next cheapest tier: CompactifAI and Novita at $0.07; Google Vertex $0.12.

2) Infrabase (cited source 2) exists, published 2026-06-06, updated 2026-07-17. It reports DeepInfra $0.037 in / $0.17 out and explicitly states DeepInfra's blended rate fell from ~$0.08 (Mar 2026) to ~$0.05 (Jun 2026) — the exact trajectory in the claim's notes.

3) PROVIDER PRIMARY SOURCES (my own check, not relied on by the claim): DeepInfra's model page lists $0.037/1M input, $0.17/1M output, no cache discount. Under AA's 7:2:1 with cache priced at input, that is 0.9*0.037 + 0.1*0.17 = $0.0503 — reproduces $0.05 to the cent. Novita's pricing page lists $0.05/$0.25 → 0.9*0.05 + 0.1*0.25 = $0.070, reproducing AA's $0.07 for Novita exactly. Two independent provider list prices reproduce AA's blended column exactly, so the methodology is transparent and the numbers are not aggregator artifacts. (CoreWeave's own token pricing page 404s; its $0.04/$0.14 is corroborated only via AA, but DeepInfra alone carries the $0.05 figure.)

FAITHFULNESS CHECKS. Value: $0.05 — correct, and correct specifically as the CHEAPEST (AA's own reference/median blend for gpt-oss-120b is $0.20/M off $0.15/$0.60, so the claim is not passing off a market-median as the cheapest). Period: "as of 2026-06" holds and is still true as of 2026-07 (DeepInfra list price today implies $0.050). Unit: USD/M blended — correct.

NON-FATAL CAVEATS a hostile reviewer should still see, none of which move the value:
(a) The blend is 7:2:1 cache:input:output, i.e. effectively 90% input-side because these providers give no cache discount. Under the older/more common 3:1 input:output convention the cheapest would be ~$0.065 (CoreWeave) to ~$0.070 (DeepInfra) — still inside the stated CI, but ~40% higher. The metric string "typical input/output mix" hides which convention is in force; it should say 7:2:1.
(b) gpt-oss-120b at high reasoning effort emits heavy reasoning traces, so a real agentic workload skews more output-heavy than 10%, pushing effective blended to roughly $0.07–0.09. Still inside the CI.
(c) The claim's notes list DeepInfra as "$0.039 in / $0.19 out"; the live figure is $0.037/$0.17. Immaterial ($0.054 vs $0.050) but stale.
(d) Notes-only, not part of the tested value: the "InferenceX (B200/H100) $0.02–0.26/M measured serving cost" citation is not in the sources array and I could not reach any primary document for it (web-search budget was exhausted). Do not let that comparison carry weight until it is sourced.
(e) THESIS-LEVEL WARNING: the notes contrast this $0.05 blended figure against "closed US flagship list prices of $10-30/M output." That is apples-to-oranges — a 90%-input blend versus a pure output price. The honest comparison is output-to-output ($0.14–0.19 vs $10–30, still ~100x) or blended-to-blended. Also, AA's own 7.8x dispersion and $0.20 median blend cut mildly against a strong "marginal supplier sets the price" reading: if marginal cost cleared the whole market, dispersion would not be 7.8x.

CI ASSESSMENT. [0.03, 0.10] is honest and arguably generous. The lowest blended price I could construct from any observed endpoint is ~$0.045 (OpenRouter's $0.03/$0.18 headline), so the $0.03 floor sits below the entire observed distribution; the $0.10 ceiling comfortably covers both the 3:1 convention (~$0.065–0.070) and an output-heavier realistic mix (~$0.09). A tighter [0.045, 0.075] would be defensible, but the over-width is conservative rather than misleading and does not change any conclusion this claim is load-bearing for. Confirm.

SOURCE CHECK (both cited sources are real and current). Artificial Analysis' gpt-oss-120b providers page states verbatim: "Prices for gpt-oss-120b (high) vary up to 7.8x across providers. The most affordable is CoreWeave at $0.05 per 1M tokens, while Cloudflare charges $0.39 per 1M tokens." DeepInfra and Groq are also shown at $0.05. Infrabase's "Cheapest AI Inference Providers" post (dated 2026-06-06, updated 2026-07-17) exists and corroborates DeepInfra $0.037 in / $0.17 out, Novita $0.05/$0.25, SiliconFlow $0.05/$0.45. DeepInfra's own model page currently shows $0.037/$0.17 (the claim's $0.039/$0.19 is slightly stale, and stale in the conservative direction). So the headline number is not fabricated: it reproduces the cited source exactly.

THE MATERIAL PROBLEM - WRONG DENOMINATOR. AA's $0.05 is not an input/output blend. The page's own definition: "Price is a blend of cache hit, input, and output token prices using the selected ratio (default 7:2:1 cache-input-output)." That is effectively a 9:1 input:output mix with 78% of input assumed to be cache hits. The claim's metric text says "blended across typical input/output mix," which reads as a conventional input:output blend. Recomputing the cheapest credible providers:
- 9:1 (AA default): DeepInfra $0.050, CoreWeave $0.050, OpenRouter floor $0.045
- 3:1 (the standard alternative convention): DeepInfra $0.070, CoreWeave $0.065, OpenRouter floor $0.068
- 1:1: $0.090-$0.105
- output-heavy 1:3: $0.115-$0.143
So $0.05 is the joint minimum of (cheapest of 22 providers) x (most input-heavy blend convention). Under any pure input/output blend the cheapest credible price is $0.065-$0.070, roughly 30-40% above the claimed point value.

AGGRAVATING FACT SPECIFIC TO THIS MODEL. gpt-oss-120b is a reasoning model and AA measures it as verbose: it "generated 87M tokens... in comparison to the average of 53M" running the Intelligence Index. A 9:1 input:output assumption is therefore unusually unrepresentative for this model's real workloads, which skew output-heavy. AA's own model page quotes a representative "blended rate (7:2:1 cache hit/input/output ratio)... $0.20 per 1M tokens" - 4x the claimed figure - showing $0.05 is the tail of a 7.8x spread, not a market-representative price.

MITIGATING EVIDENCE (why not refute). (a) Three independent providers converge at $0.05 under AA's convention, so it is a real floor, not a single outlier. (b) OpenRouter states effective prices run "60-80% cheaper than the provider list price" because of prompt caching, which partially vindicates the cache-heavy blend as an empirical claim about real spend. (c) The claim's CI [0.03, 0.10] already covers the 3:1 result, so the interval is not broken - only the point estimate is optimistically placed at its low edge.

CREDIBILITY OF THE SUB-$0.05 TAIL (this is the finding that nicks the thesis). Prices below $0.05 come from promotional entrants, not established marginal suppliers: IonRouter (Launch HN, YC W26, Mar 2026) quotes $0.02 in / $0.095 out with no disclosed unit economics, and frogAPI (Feb 2026) is explicit deposit-matching subsidy ("Put in $10, get $20"). Using the absolute floor as a marginal-cost proxy therefore imports some below-cost land-grab pricing. I found no evidence of established providers (DeepInfra, CoreWeave, Groq) disclosing negative inference margins and no published critique arguing their list prices are below cost, so the T3 mechanism survives - but at $0.065, not at the promotional floor.

ADJUSTMENT. Point value 0.05 -> 0.065, centered on the cheapest credible providers under a conventional input:output blend, tilted up slightly for this model's output-token verbosity and down slightly for observed prompt-cache utilization. CI [0.045, 0.11]: the low bound admits AA's cache-heavy convention at established providers; the high bound admits a roughly balanced input:output mix. I narrowed the low bound from 0.03 because 0.03 is reachable only by stacking deep cache discounts onto subsidized-entrant pricing, and raised the high bound from 0.10 because 0.10 excluded a plain 1:1 mix on a verbose reasoning model.

THESIS IMPACT: negligible. Whether the number is $0.05 or $0.065, third-party open-weight hosting sits inside the measured serving-cost band ($0.02-$0.26/M) and roughly two orders of magnitude below closed flagship output list prices, so T3 (marginal supplier sets price near marginal cost) is unaffected. One presentational caveat to carry into the essay: the claim's notes compare a cache-weighted BLENDED open-weight price against closed-model OUTPUT list prices ($10-30/M), which inflates the stated gap by roughly 3-4x versus a like-for-like blended comparison. The gap remains enormous on a like-for-like basis, but the framing as written is not apples-to-apples.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED. Epoch AI data insight "LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks," published Mar. 12, 2025 (Cottier, Snodin, Owen, Adamczewski). Fetched and read directly. Load-bearing sentence verbatim: "Across all of these benchmarks and performance thresholds, we found prices declining between 9x per year and 900x per year, with a median of 50x per year."

VALUE (50): FAITHFUL. Exact, verbatim, correctly attributed. The metric is defined in the claim as the Epoch median for the lowest-priced model clearing each threshold, and 50 reproduces that definition exactly. No basis to move the point estimate.

UNIT: FAITHFUL. x-fold per year at fixed benchmark performance, per-token price.

ALL SUPPORTING NOTES VERIFIED against the source: six benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA Diamond, MATH-500, MATH level 5, HumanEval, Chatbot Arena Elo); methodology is "the lowest-priced LLMs that match or exceed a given score," with thresholds defined as instances where a new model beat all prior models, fitted by log-linear regression; GPT-4-level GPQA Diamond at 40x/yr; post-Jan-2024 restriction raises median from 50x to 200x; reasoning models excluded from per-token comparison because they generate more tokens.

PERIOD: substantially faithful, one imprecision worth recording. Source frames it as "the past three years" from a Mar 12, 2025 publication, so 2022-03 to 2025-03 is a fair reading of the data envelope. But it is NOT the estimation window for any individual trend — each threshold's regression starts when that threshold was first crossed, and the source states the fastest trends (900x) "start after January 2024," i.e. windows well under a year annualized. The 50x is a median of heterogeneous, mostly much shorter regressions, not a three-year CAGR. Presenting it against a 3-year period invites over-reading.

CI [20, 200]: NOT HONEST AT THE LOW END. This is the defect. The upper bound is well-founded — 200x is the source's own post-Jan-2024 median, a principled ceiling. The floor of 20 is unsupportable on two independent grounds:
(1) It contradicts the source's own reported distribution. Epoch explicitly reports threshold-benchmark combinations declining as slowly as 9x/year. An 80% interval floored at 20 asserts under 10% probability of the true rate falling below 20x, while the primary source itself documents observed rates at less than half that.
(2) It excludes the leading independent primary estimate. a16z's "LLMflation" (Nov 12, 2024) headlines 10x/year and states that figure "is a fairly good approximation of the cost decline across both MMLU performance levels" — MMLU 42 fell ~1000x over three years (Nov 2021–Nov 2024) = ~10x/yr, and MMLU 83 fell ~62x over ~1.5 years = ~15.7x/yr. Both sit below the claim's 80% floor.

There is also a construction bias pushing Epoch's median above the economically meaningful rate: it is a median over threshold-benchmark COUNT, not over capability tiers anyone actually buys. Recently-crossed thresholds get very short regression windows in which one cheap entrant produces enormous annualized rates, and all the 900x trends are post-Jan-2024 artifacts of exactly this. Weighting by economically salient tiers instead — GPT-3.5-level, GPT-4-level — lands at 10x–40x/yr (Epoch's own GPT-4/GPQA figure is 40x), i.e. the bottom half of the stated CI or beneath it. A hostile reviewer would land here immediately.

RECOMMENDED ADJUSTMENT: hold value at 50, widen CI to [10, 200]. The floor of 10 is jointly set by Epoch's own 9x minimum and a16z's independent 10x/yr; the ceiling of 200 stays as the source's post-Jan-2024 median. This keeps the interval faithful to the source's actual uncertainty instead of tightening it asymmetrically toward the fast end.

CHECKED FOR SUPERSESSION: Epoch's data-insights index shows this Mar. 2025 piece as the only inference-price insight; no 2025-2026 update revises the 50x figure. So the claim is not stale relative to its own source.

CAVEAT ON LOAD-BEARING USE (flagged, does not change verdict): this series measures per-token price at fixed benchmark score and structurally EXCLUDES reasoning models. For a July 2026 thesis about inference as real COGS, that is a significant limitation in both directions — the exclusion means the series does not capture cost-per-completed-task in the reasoning era, where token counts per task rose sharply, and it terminates in Mar 2025, before reasoning models came to dominate inference spend. The claim's note correctly identifies that this cuts in favor of T6, but the metric should not be cited as evidence about the cost trajectory of the workloads that actually dominate 2025-2026 revenue. Grade B is appropriate; it should not be upgraded.

TRANSCRIPTION IS FAITHFUL, BUT THE CI IS WRONG AND THE METRIC IS MISLEADING AS DEPLOYED.

1) Source check (passes). I pulled the raw Epoch page. Every figure in the claim is verbatim correct: "prices declining between 9x per year and 900x per year, with a median of 50x per year"; GPT-4-level GPQA = 40x/yr; "the median rate increased from 50x per year to 200x per year" post-Jan-2024; reasoning models excluded from per-token analysis. No transcription error.

2) MATERIAL CONFLICT: two independent peer estimates fall AT OR BELOW the CI80 floor of 20.
- a16z "LLMflation" (Appenzeller, Nov 2024), same cheapest-model-clearing-a-threshold method: headline 10x/yr. MMLU-42 tier = 1000x over 3 years = 10x/yr; MMLU-83 = 62x since GPT-4's Mar-2023 launch (~1.67y) = ~12x/yr.
- Stanford AI Index 2025 (verified on hai.stanford.edu): "inference cost for a system performing at the level of GPT-3.5 dropped over 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024" = 280^(1/1.917) = 18.9x/yr.
Neither estimate is inside [20, 200]. A CI that excludes both credible peer measurements of the same quantity is mis-specified. Geometric mean of the three central estimates (50, ~11, ~19) = 21.8x/yr.

3) The median is a fragile, non-market-weighted statistic. Epoch's whole dataset is 36 unique price observations (9 of them Epoch's own for GPT-3/3.5/Llama-2). The "median" is taken over benchmark x threshold pairs that Epoch enumerated endogenously — "we identified instances where a new model achieved a better performance than all previous models, and used these instances as our performance thresholds" — so a benchmark with many SOTA jumps contributes more pairs and gets more weight. It is not a usage- or revenue-weighted price index. Epoch itself flags the dispersion (9x-900x) and notes the chart's "mid-range" value "is not always the exact median, for the sake of visual clarity."

4) The 200x/yr upper bound is a window-truncation artifact. Regressions need only 4 data points; Epoch selects the cheapest-model frontier over full history, THEN drops all pre-2024 observations and refits. That is selection on the outcome plus a short window — log-linear slopes fit on ~4 points over ~14 months steepen mechanically. Epoch hedges accordingly: "it's less clear that those will persist."

5) PROVABLE NON-DURABILITY (the decisive test). At 40x/yr from Mar 2023, GPT-4-level GPQA reaches ~$0.023/M blended by Mar 2025 — plausible (cheap models sat at ~$0.02-0.07/M). Extending the 50x/yr median another 16 months to the July 2026 thesis date implies ~$0.0001/M. No such price exists; cheapest credible API models today are ~$0.02-0.10/M. The rate therefore decayed sharply and cannot be projected forward. Epoch's own structural components bound the durable rate far lower: hardware cost -30%/yr (AI Index 2025) = ~1.43x/yr, times algorithmic progress of "doubling computational power every 5 to 14 months" (Epoch's own paper) = 1.8-5.3x/yr, giving a sustainable ~2.5-7.6x/yr. The residual 3-20x is one-time distillation of frontier capability into small models plus margin compression — and Epoch concedes it cannot separate the two: "Reduced profit margins may explain some of the drops in price, but we didn't find clear evidence for this."

6) STALENESS. I enumerated Epoch's data-insights index: nothing on inference prices published after Mar 12, 2025. The series is 16 months stale relative to a July 2026 thesis, over exactly the window where the reductio above shows the rate broke down.

7) WRONG DENOMINATOR FOR THE THESIS (most important). The metric prices YESTERDAY'S capability. The price of FRONTIER intelligence — which is what Thompson's supply-constraint argument is about — has barely moved. Frontier flagship, 3:1 input/output blended: GPT-4 Mar 2023 $30/$60 = $37.50/M; Claude Opus 4.8 Jul 2026 $5/$25 = $10.00/M, i.e. 3.75x over 3.35 years = 1.48x/yr. Against Claude Fable 5 ($10/$50 = $20.00/M) it is 1.21x/yr. That is ~1.3x/yr at the frontier versus 50x/yr at fixed historical benchmarks — a ~35x gap driven entirely by which denominator you choose. Compounding this, reasoning models are EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED from Epoch's per-token series precisely because they "generate a much larger number of tokens," yet by 2025-26 they are the frontier product and the dominant driver of inference demand. Cost per frontier task is therefore flat-to-rising while the cited metric shows 50x/yr collapse.

Note this cuts IN FAVOR of the thesis, not against it — but the claim as written (50x/yr, load-bearing) is the number a thesis-skeptic would deploy to argue inference deflation makes marginal cost irrelevant. Left at 50x/yr with a floor of 20, it is a liability: it overstates a vendor-specific, threshold-enumeration-dependent, non-durable, 16-month-stale statistic as if it were the market's inference cost curve.

ADJUSTMENT. Central value 22x/yr (geometric mean of Epoch 50, AI Index ~19, a16z ~11 — triangulating three independent series rather than adopting the highest one as the point estimate). CI80 [8, 90]: floor of 8 sits just below a16z's measured 10x/yr and gestures at the ~2.5-7.6x/yr structural floor toward which the rate is provably decaying; ceiling of 90 keeps Epoch's 50 comfortably interior and allows that Epoch's threshold weighting may be right, while rejecting 200 as a truncated-window artifact that the arithmetic above falsifies. If the claim is re-scoped to "frontier-quality tokens" — the quantity the thesis actually turns on — the right number is ~1.3x/yr, and that should be a separate claim rather than a CI widening on this one.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE LOCATED AND READ IN FULL: Guido Appenzeller, "Welcome to LLMflation — LLM inference cost is going down fast," a16z, published November 12, 2024. Every headline element of the claim is verbatim faithful to it.

FAITHFULNESS CHECKS (all pass):
- Value: source states the cheapest model clearing the MMLU threshold today is "Llama 3.2 3B via Together.ai" at $0.06 per million tokens. Exact match to claim's 0.06.
- Start point: $60 per million tokens, GPT-3, November 2021. Exact match. Independently sane: OpenAI's davinci list price was $0.06/1K tokens, i.e. $60/M, and it was still that price when OpenAI dropped the API waitlist on 18 Nov 2021. GPT-3 175B's few-shot MMLU is ~43.9 in the Hendrycks/GPT-3 literature, so a 42 threshold is a defensible "GPT-3-class" bar.
- Period: 3 years, Nov 2021 → Nov 2024 (post published 2024-11-12, so "today" = Nov 2024). Faithful.
- Magnitude/rate: source says cost "dropped by a factor of 1,000 in 3 years" and "the cost is decreasing by 10x every year." Matches claim's notes.
- Secondary note: source says the MMLU ≥ 83 (GPT-4-class) tier fell "about a factor of 62" from GPT-4's March 2023 launch. Matches claim's "~62x." 
- Unit: source explicitly states "If the price differed for input and output tokens, we took the average of the two," so the unit is USD per million tokens, arithmetic-averaged input/output. Both endpoints happen to be flat-rate models (GPT-3 completions billed prompt+completion at one rate; Together's Llama 3.2 3B Turbo is a single blended rate), so the endpoints are internally consistent and the averaging convention does not distort them. Unit faithfully represented.

WHY I STILL ADJUST — THE CI IS THE WRONG SHAPE:
The quantity is definitionally a MINIMUM (cheapest model clearing the bar). The author himself concedes the methodology is "far from perfect" and that "other models and fine-tunes may have been slightly more cost-effective at any given time." That makes the error one-sided DOWNWARD: $0.06 is a documented Together.ai list price, so the true market minimum in Nov 2024 can barely be above it, but it can plausibly be well below it. Two independent confirmations of downward slack: (1) Llama 3.2 1B Instruct scores MMLU 63.4→ no, 49.3 (5-shot, macro_avg/acc per Meta's model card) — comfortably clearing the 42 bar — and budget hosts (DeepInfra, Lepton, Hyperbolic) listed 1B/3B in the $0.01–0.03/M range in late 2024; (2) the endpoint model itself scores MMLU 63.4, i.e. ~50% above the 42 bar, so a hypothetical model scoring exactly 42 would be smaller and cheaper still. Meanwhile the claim's upper bound of 0.10 puts ~meaningful 80% mass on a region the metric's own definition nearly excludes. I therefore keep the point estimate at 0.06 (it is the best-documented, most citable figure and is exactly what the source says) but re-shape the CI to [0.03, 0.07] to reflect honest, asymmetric, downward-only uncertainty.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION (direction and magnitude survive):
Epoch AI's independent price-trend work finds LLM inference price declines of 9x–900x per year across benchmarks, with a MEDIAN of ~50x/year and ~200x/year post-January 2024 — e.g. GPT-4-level GPQA Diamond performance getting 40x cheaper per year. a16z's 10x/year is thus CONSERVATIVE relative to the best independent measurement, which is the right direction for a load-bearing claim. This substantially de-risks the claim.

THREE HOSTILE CAVEATS THE PARENT SHOULD CARRY FORWARD (they do not refute the number, but they constrain what it can be used to prove — and they matter a lot for Thompson's specific thesis):
1. THIS IS A PRICE SERIES, NOT A COST SERIES. Appenzeller himself observes that providers appear to accept lower margins at the budget tier while holding premium pricing. $0.06/M for a commodity open-weight 3B model on a competitive host may sit at or below marginal cost. Thompson's thesis turns precisely on the price-vs-marginal-cost wedge, so this series cannot be cited as evidence about inference COGS.
2. MONOPOLY-TO-COMMODITY CONFOUND. The 2021 endpoint is a single-supplier monopoly price (only OpenAI sold GPT-3); the 2024 endpoint is an open-weight model resold by dozens of hosts at near-zero margin. A material share of the 1,000x is margin compression plus open weights, not compute-cost decline. This is thesis-relevant (it is the commoditization mechanism Thompson invokes) but it means the number is not a clean cost curve.
3. THE SAME POST CONTAINS THE COUNTER-DATAPOINT. Appenzeller writes that "OpenAI's leading model today, o1, has the same cost per output token as GPT-3 had at launch ($60 per million)." Frontier-tier token prices have NOT deflated; only the quality-held-constant floor has. Any use of px-02 that implies "frontier intelligence is getting 1,000x cheaper" misreads the primary source. The claim's notes omit this and should not.
4. BENCHMARK VALIDITY, conceded by the author: "Models can be easily contaminated or intentionally trained on the MMLU benchmark" and "we also, in some cases, could only find multi-shot data for MMLU." So MMLU 42 in 2024 is not strictly the same capability as MMLU 42 in 2021, and shot-protocol is inconsistent across the series.

MINOR WORDING FLAG: the metric says "matching GPT-3-class quality (MMLU ~42)". The source's construction is "cheapest model AT OR ABOVE MMLU 42," and the endpoint model exceeds the bar by ~21 points. "Matching" should read "clearing." Grade B is appropriate — arguably B is generous for a VC blog post as sole source, but the Epoch AI cross-check and the internal transparency of the methodology support holding it at B rather than downgrading.

PRIMARY SOURCE VERIFIED VERBATIM. I fetched the a16z post directly. Every element of the claim is faithfully transcribed: "$60 per million tokens" for GPT-3 at Nov 2021 public access; "$0.06 per million tokens" for Llama 3.2 3B (via Together.ai) as the cheapest model clearing "an MMLU score of 42"; "1,000" times lower over "3 years"; and the companion "factor of 62" decline at MMLU 83 since GPT-4's March 2023 launch. Methodology confirmed: prices "obtained from the Internet Archive," and "when the price differed for input and output tokens, we took the average of the two." No follow-up or correction post exists on Appenzeller's a16z author page.

WHY I STILL ADJUST (CI, not point value):

1. a16z itself disclaims that $0.06 is the market minimum. The post states the analysis was "limited...to models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's Llama from third party inference providers," and explicitly concedes "other models and fine-tunes may have been slightly more cost-effective at any given time." So the metric label "cheapest model matching GPT-3-class quality" overstates what was actually measured: it is the cheapest within a hand-picked three-vendor subset, at one chosen host.

2. The threshold is loose in a direction that biases the endpoint HIGH. Meta's model card gives Llama 3.2 3B Instruct MMLU 63.4 (5-shot, macro_avg/acc) and 1B Instruct 49.3 — both far above the 42 bar, and 1B also clears it. Several third-party Llama hosts (DeepInfra, Novita, Hyperbolic, Groq's then-live 3.2-1B/3B preview tiers) listed Llama 3.2 1B/3B materially below Together's $0.06 blended in late 2024. I could not archive-verify those Nov-2024 prices (archive.org is blocked to this tool and the web-search budget was exhausted), so I extend the CI floor to $0.02 rather than moving the point estimate. Net: $0.06 is best read as a conservative upper bound on the true iso-quality minimum, not a central estimate. Direction of error strengthens rather than weakens the 1000x headline, which is why I do not refute.

3. MATERIAL FRAMING PROBLEM — price index, not cost index. The post is titled "LLM inference cost is going down fast," but the series is entirely list prices. a16z's own list of six drivers includes open-source competition that "reduced profit margin across the value chain" — i.e., an unquantified share of the 1000x is margin compression and customer-acquisition pricing by VC-funded inference providers, not marginal-cost decline. For Thompson's "marginal costs are back" thesis this is the crux: a competitive-floor price observed during a land-grab is not evidence about COGS, and in a supply-constrained market prices can revert upward toward or above that floor.

4. THE SERIES DID NOT EXTEND — cherry-picked period risk. Checked live pricing today (July 2026) on a16z's own metric (unweighted input/output average, MMLU>=42): Groq Llama 3.1 8B Instant $0.05/$0.08 = $0.065 blended; Together's cheapest small model, Gemma 3n E4B, $0.06/$0.12 = $0.09; OpenRouter's Llama 3.2 3B now $0.05/$0.33 = $0.19 and 3.2 1B $0.027/$0.201 = $0.114 (both models largely deprecated); Google's cheapest, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, $0.10/$0.40 = $0.25 — higher than Gemini 1.5 Flash-8B's late-2024 $0.0375/$0.15 = $0.094. Continuing 10x/year from Nov 2024 would imply roughly $0.002 by mid-2026. Instead the bottom of the market is flat-to-up at this quality tier over ~20 months. The endpoint value is real; the trend it anchors visibly stalled immediately after the post.

5. CONFLICTING INDEPENDENT ESTIMATE ON THE RATE. Epoch AI (March 12, 2025) measured price-to-reach-a-capability-threshold across six benchmarks and found declines "between 9x per year and 900x per year, with a median of 50x per year," rising to a 200x/year median when restricted to trends beginning after January 2024 (e.g. GPT-4-level GPQA Diamond at 40x/year). That is 5x-20x faster than a16z's 10x/year. The two are not reconcilable as measurements of the same thing — they differ on benchmark, threshold-selection rule, and provider universe. This shows the "10x/year" in the claim's notes is a highly method-dependent artifact, not a robust constant, and should not be extrapolated.

6. FRAMING/INCENTIVE FLAG (soft). a16z is a VC whose application-layer thesis benefits from a narrative of collapsing inference cost; this is a promotional blog post with no released dataset and no peer review. I checked and could NOT substantiate a direct portfolio conflict with Together AI — a16z is absent from Together's $305M Series B investor list (General Catalyst/Prosperity7-led, with Kleiner Perkins, NVIDIA, Coatue, Lux et al.) — so I am not asserting a specific COI, only general narrative incentive.

7. Anchor sanity checks pass. GPT-3 davinci at $0.06/1K = $60/M is a real Nov-2021 list price; GPT-3 175B few-shot MMLU is ~43.9, so the 42 bar is honestly calibrated to it. And a16z's own most thesis-relevant sentence cuts against the deflation reading: "OpenAI's leading model today, o1, has the same cost per output token as GPT-3 had at launch ($60 per million)." Frontier-quality price has not fallen at all in three years. They also concede "the rate may slow down."

BOTTOM LINE: value 0.06 stands as accurately sourced and internally consistent — I keep it. CI floor widens 0.04 -> 0.02 to cover the admitted scope restriction and cheaper unmeasured Llama hosts. Grade B is generous for a single unreplicated VC blog post and I would drop it to B-/C+. Most importantly for load-bearing use: this is a price series at a stale, now-obsolete quality bar, sourced from a period of aggressive competitive discounting, and it did not continue after the observation window. It should not be used as evidence that inference COGS at frontier quality is collapsing — a16z's own o1 datapoint says the opposite.
