verification.reasoning:
POINT VALUE: exact and confirmed. Both endpoints verified against contemporaneous primary-adjacent sources. GPT-4 (Mar 14, 2023) launched at $0.03/1K prompt = $30/M input, $0.06/1K completion = $60/M output (TechCrunch launch-day coverage quoting OpenAI). GPT-5 (Aug 7, 2025) launched at $1.25/M input, $10/M output (Simon Willison's launch-day post quoting OpenAI). 30/1.25 = 24.000 exactly. The notes' supporting arithmetic also checks: output 60/10 = 6.0x exactly; CAGR over 2.40 years = 3.76x/yr, matching "~3.5-4x/yr." Note: openai.com and platform.openai.com return HTTP 403 to fetch, so I could not read OpenAI's own 2023 pricing page directly, but the endpoints are uncontested across independent contemporaneous sources and both cited compilations.

WHY "ADJUST" NOT "CONFIRM" — the CI is fabricated uncertainty. Both endpoints are exact published list prices, not measurements or estimates. The ratio is deterministic: exactly 24.0. A symmetric [20, 28] band implies +/-17% measurement/sampling error that does not exist. The genuine uncertainty here is DEFINITIONAL (which SKU counts as "flagship"), and it is asymmetric and much wider than the stated band: 24x on the gpt-4-8k convention (modal, and what the claim uses); 48x if you anchor GPT-4-32K at $60/M (the notes concede this); ~1.5x if "flagship" means the best API model actually available in Aug 2025 (o3-pro at $20/M input, launched Jun 2025). The stated CI simultaneously invents error around the one exact reading and excludes every genuine alternative reading. It fails the "CI honestly reflects source uncertainty" test even though the point estimate is exact. Correct treatment: report 24 as a point value under a stated tier convention with 48x as a named sensitivity, not a smeared band. I have set the corrected CI to [24, 24] to signal the quantity is arithmetic on two exact list prices, not an estimate.

SECOND, MORE SERIOUS ISSUE — the window is 11 months stale and the trend has reversed, which is decisive for the thesis. Today is 2026-07-22. Per OpenAI's own current pricing docs (developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), flagship input price has risen steadily since GPT-5: $1.25 (GPT-5, Aug 2025) -> $1.25 (GPT-5.1, Nov 2025) -> $1.75 (GPT-5.2, Dec 2025) -> $1.75 (GPT-5.3, Feb 2026) -> $2.50 (GPT-5.4, Mar 2026) -> $5.00 (GPT-5.5, Apr 2026) -> $5.00 (GPT-5.6 Sol, Jul 2026, listed as the current flagship). That is a 4x INCREASE in flagship input price over 11 months. Measured GPT-4 launch -> today, the decline is 30/5.00 = 6x, not 24x (1.70x/yr, not 3.76x/yr). Output is only 2x ($60 -> $30). Pro tier is $30/$180.

THE CLAIM'S OWN CITED SOURCE CONTRADICTS IT. TokenCost's AI Price Index (cited source #2, published Mar 20, 2026) states "the frontier model went from $30 to $2.50 - about 12x" using GPT-5.4 as the endpoint. That is half the claim's headline figure at that source's own vintage. Neither cited source is primary: both are secondary compilations, and both show sloppiness (mungomash dates text-davinci-003 to Jun 2020, which is wrong, and lists GPT-4o output at $10 when launch pricing was $15). The actual primary sources are OpenAI's launch announcements and pricing page.

THESIS IMPACT. Thompson's argument is that marginal costs are back and supply-constrained labs hold pricing power. The post-Aug-2025 data strongly SUPPORTS that thesis: flagship token prices stopped falling and quadrupled. A load-bearing claim frozen at Aug 2025 reporting "24x decline" reads as evidence for relentless deflation, i.e. the opposite framing, unless the reversal is stated alongside it. Recommendation to the parent: keep 24 only as an explicitly closed historical window (Mar 2023 - Aug 2025), and add or substitute the live metric — GPT-4 launch to current flagship = 6x input / 2x output, with flagship input up 4x since GPT-5 launch — which is both current and far more probative of the thesis. Grade A is defensible for the endpoints; the "load_bearing: true" flag is not safe on the 24x figure as currently framed.

ARITHMETIC HOLDS, FRAMING DOES NOT. Both endpoints verify exactly: mungomash's pricing history lists GPT-4 at $30.00/$60.00 on Mar 14 2023 and GPT-5 at $1.25/$10.00 on Aug 7 2025. 30/1.25 = 24.0 precisely, and 24^(1/2.40yr) = 3.76x/yr, matching the note's "3.5-4x/yr." So the literal computation is not wrong. But three stacked selection choices each push the number to its maximum, and the third is fatal for a claim load-bearing in a July 2026 essay.

(1) ENDPOINT IS THE ALL-TIME TROUGH, AND THE TREND HAS SINCE REVERSED. Aug 2025's $1.25 is the historical minimum for OpenAI flagship input pricing. Every subsequent flagship is MORE expensive: GPT-5.2 $1.75/$14 (Dec 11 2025), GPT-5.3 $1.75/$14 (Feb 5 2026), GPT-5.4 $2.50/$15, GPT-5.5 $5.00/$30 (Apr 23 2026), GPT-5.6 Sol $5.00/$30 (Jul 9 2026). I confirmed the current state directly on OpenAI's own pricing page (developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing): gpt-5.6-sol $5.00 input / $30.00 output. So flagship input price is 4x HIGHER today than at the claim's endpoint, and GPT-4 to the flagship actually in market when Thompson published (Jul 20 2026) is only 6.0x ($30 to $5.00), or ~1.7x/yr. Cutting the series at Aug 2025 — 11 months before publication — is a cherry-picked period that reverses sign if extended to the essay's own date.

(2) THE CLAIM'S OWN SOURCE PUBLISHES A DIFFERENT NUMBER. TokenCost's AI Price Index, cited in the claim, headlines: "the frontier model (the best thing OpenAI sells at any given moment) went from $30 to $2.50 — about 12x." One of the two cited sources therefore contradicts the 24x headline by a factor of two.

(3) TIER CHOICE FLIPS THE SIGN ENTIRELY. "Constant flagship tier" is doing enormous work. OpenAI's actual top-of-line tier today, gpt-5.4-pro and gpt-5.5-pro, is priced at $30.00 input / $180.00 output. Input is IDENTICAL to GPT-4's March 2023 launch price (1.0x, zero decline in 3.3 years) and output is 3x HIGHER than GPT-4's $60. o3-pro was $20/$80 in Jun 2025, two months before the GPT-5 endpoint.

(4) INPUT-ONLY IS THE MOST FAVORABLE DENOMINATOR. Output fell only 6x ($60 to $10) over the same window, as the note concedes. Blended at a 3:1 input:output mix, $37.50 to $3.44 = 10.9x; at 1:1, $45 to $5.63 = 8.0x. And mungomash explicitly flags that "reasoning tokens count as output" — GPT-5 is a reasoning model emitting billed reasoning tokens, so cost-per-completed-task fell far less than any per-token figure implies.

CORRECTION. I set the point at 12x, which is triply anchored: it is TokenCost's own published frontier figure, it approximates the blended-token decline over the claim's own stated period (10.9x), and it sits mid-range. CI low of 6 is doubly anchored — output fell exactly 6x over the stated period, and input fell exactly 6x from GPT-4 to the flagship on sale at the essay's publication date. CI high of 24 retains the claim's own input-only trough reading as the optimistic edge. A maximally hostile reviewer would go to 1.0x on the pro tier; I did not put that in the interval because pro is arguably not the constant tier, but it belongs in any footnote.

GRADE. Should drop from A to B. The endpoint prices are official and undisputed (A-quality inputs), but the ratio is a compound of three discretionary framing choices, and the metric is not robust: it moves between 1x and 24x on tier and denominator alone.

IMPLICATION FOR THE THESIS — this cuts FOR Thompson, not against. The corrected picture is that flagship per-token prices bottomed in Aug 2025 and have risen 4x since, with the top tier back at GPT-4's exact 2023 input price and above it on output. That is direct evidence that inference is real COGS under supply constraint and that labs are pricing above a hard floor. If the essay deploys px-03 as "prices fall relentlessly at 24x," it is both overstated and pointed the wrong way; if it deploys it as "flagship prices fall far slower than constant-capability prices," the correction strengthens it substantially. Recommend rewriting the claim as: flagship input price fell ~12x from GPT-4 launch to the Aug 2025 trough on a blended basis, then rose ~4x into mid-2026, netting ~6x over the full 3.3 years (~1.7x/yr) — versus ~1.0x at the top-of-line tier.

Source #3's URL (openrouter.ai/announcements/gpt55-cost-analysis) is a redirect stub returning no data; the real content is at openrouter.ai/blog/insights/gpt55-cost-analysis. The claim keeps its A grade only because OpenAI's own page independently confirms it.

CAVEATS THAT DON'T CHANGE THE NUMBER BUT WEAKEN THE INFERENCE (flagged because load_bearing = true). (1) The metric is top-of-line price, and OpenAI simultaneously widened the ladder downward: gpt-5.6-luna at $1.00/$6 is BELOW the Aug-2025 flagship's $1.25/$10. "OpenAI's best token got 4x more expensive" and "OpenAI's cheapest general token got 20% cheaper" are both true; part of the 4x is tier segmentation, not a price hike on a fixed good. (2) Cost-per-outcome rose far less than 4x — OpenRouter's own analysis of the 5.4→5.5 step found realized cost up 49-92%, not 100%, because GPT-5.5 emits 19-34% fewer completion tokens on long prompts. That is Thompson's own "tokens are not the commodity, intelligence is" point cutting against using a nominal token-price ratio as the evidence. (3) Output price rose only 3x ($10→$30) over the same window versus 4x on input; the claim cites the larger of the two. (4) A nominal price ratio alone cannot establish the note's assertion that prices "moved AWAY from marginal cost" — that needs a marginal-cost series, and capability per token rose over the same window.

CORRECTION: keep value = 4.0; tighten CI to [3.9, 4.4]. The 3.9 floor is a token allowance for definitional slack (if "flagship" were read as the default/mid tier, terra at $2.50 gives 2.0x — but that is a definition change, properly a caveat, not an interval). The 4.4 ceiling is the data-residency-uplift maximum. Anything wider misrepresents a quantity that is directly readable off the vendor's price list.

ENDPOINTS VERIFIED, CI CEILING IS IMPOSSIBLE, TIMELINE IN THE NOTES IS WRONG.

1) The 4.0x itself survives hostile checking. OpenAI's official pricing page (fetched today) shows gpt-5.6-sol at $5.00 input / $0.50 cached / $30.00 output and gpt-5.5 at $5.00/$30.00. OpenRouter's OpenAI model registry gives the dated ladder: GPT-5 $1.25/$10 (Aug 7, 2025), GPT-5.1 $1.25/$10 (Nov 13, 2025), GPT-5.2 $1.75/$14 (Dec 10, 2025), GPT-5.3 Codex/Chat $1.75/$14 (Feb 24 / Mar 3, 2026), GPT-5.4 $2.50/$15 (Mar 5, 2026), GPT-5.5 $5/$30 (Apr 24, 2026), GPT-5.6 Sol $5/$30 (Jul 9, 2026). $1.25 is the genuine trough for an OpenAI mainline flagship (GPT-4.1 was $2 before it), so $1.25 -> $5.00 = exactly 4.00x nominal input.

2) CI high of 4.5 is arithmetically unreachable and must come down to 4.0. I checked every billing tier for a way to exceed 4x and none exists: cached input is 10% of base in both eras ($0.125 -> $0.50 = 4x); batch is -50% in both eras; flex for gpt-5.6-sol is $2.50/$15 (50%); priority for gpt-5.6-sol is $10/$60, i.e. 2x standard, the same multiplier GPT-5 priority carried ($2.50/$20) — so priority-to-priority input is also 4x. There is no reading of nominal list input price that yields more than 4.0x. A grade-A claim whose 80% interval contains impossible values is a defect worth fixing.

3) The uncertainty is entirely one-sided (downward), so keeping the low bound at 2 is right but the reason should be restated. The claim's stated reason ("short-context tier ambiguity") is not what the evidence shows; legacy GPT-5/5.1/5.2 are delisted from the pricing page entirely, so nobody is still billed $1.25. The real downside readings are: (a) output rose only 3x ($10 -> $30), so input-only 4x is the highest slice of the nominal pair; (b) the pro tier rose only 2x on input ($15/$120 for GPT-5 Pro, Oct 6 2025 -> $30/$180 for 5.4-pro/5.5-pro); (c) OpenAI shipped the 5.6 generation as three same-day tiers — Sol $5/$30, Terra $2.50/$15, Luna $1.00/$6 — so a current-generation buyer can sit at 2x (Terra) and the generation's entry tier at $1.00 is 20% BELOW the 2025 trough; (d) realized cost per comparable request rose far less than per-token price (px-05's own source: +49% to +92% for a nominal 2x step, because 5.5 emits 19-34% fewer completion tokens on 10K+ prompts). Chaining that verbosity effect through both steps puts cost-per-task nearer 2-2.5x than 4x.

4) Two factual errors in the period/notes that should be corrected even though they don't move the value. First, there were THREE increases, not two, and the first was GPT-5.2 on Dec 10, 2025 ($1.25 -> $1.75/$14, with 5.2-pro at $21/$168); GPT-5.3 held $1.75; then Mar 5 and Apr 24, 2026. The claim's "(increases Mar 5 and late Apr 2026)" understates how early the reversal began — which actually strengthens the thesis, since the turn predates the Mar/Apr window. Second, "first sustained flagship price INCREASE in OpenAI history" is contestable: GPT-4.5 (Feb 2025) shipped as OpenAI's largest model at $75/$150 and o1 ($15/$60) / o1-pro ($150/$600) were priced far above the concurrent GPT-4o ($2.50/$10). What is genuinely new in 2026 is a higher-priced mainline successor with the cheaper predecessor retired; the wording should be narrowed to that or it invites an easy rebuttal.

5) Source hygiene: the nxcode.io citation is unreliable and should be dropped or demoted. It gives the release date as both "early March 2026" and "March 13, 2026" (registry says Mar 5), its headline says $2.50/$15 while its own table says $10/$30, and it prices GPT-5.3 Codex at $2/$8 against the registry's $1.75/$14. The OpenRouter announcement URL in the claim is a redirect stub; the live article is at /blog/insights/gpt55-cost-analysis/.

6) Framing caution for the thesis (T2/T5). The 4x is real and it is the correct headline for top-of-line list input price, but it is the maximum of the defensible nominal set, and the same official page that proves it also shows frontier-generation capability available at $1.00/M (Luna) — below the 2025 trough. Presenting 4x as "the cost of using OpenAI rose 4x" would be the misleading version; presenting it as "the top-of-line list price moved up 4x while cheaper tiers persisted" is the defensible one.

sources.title: GPT-5.5 Price Increase: What It Actually Costs - OpenRouter

claims.notes: Per-token prices doubled but GPT-5.5 emits 19-34% fewer completion tokens on 10K+ prompts (52% MORE on 2-10K prompts); observed net cost +49% (50-128K prompts) to +92% (<2K prompts). Textbook T6 evidence: per-token price changes do not map 1:1 to cost-per-outcome. Central estimate is midpoint of observed range.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND AND VERIFIED. https://openrouter.ai/blog/insights/gpt55-cost-analysis exists, is first-party (OpenRouter's own billing data), published 2026-05-04. Every number the claim quotes is faithfully transcribed:

- Cost per million tokens by prompt bucket: <2K +92%, 2–10K +69%, 10–25K +51%, 25–50K +62%, 50–128K +49%, 128K+ +85%. Claim's "+49% (50–128K) to +92% (<2K)" is exact.
- Completion tokens: <2K +7%, 2–10K +52%, 10–25K −32%, 25–50K −19%, 50–128K −28%, 128K+ −34%. Claim's "19–34% fewer on 10K+, 52% more on 2–10K" is exact (it omits the <2K +7% case).
- Price doubling independently confirmed on OpenRouter model pages: GPT-5.4 $2.50/$15 per 1M (released Mar 5, 2026), GPT-5.5 $5/$30 per 1M (released Apr 24, 2026). Exactly 2x on both input and output.
- Period: source windows are GPT-5.4 Apr 21–23 and GPT-5.5 Apr 25–28 (launch day excluded). The claim's "2026-04-21 to 2026-04-28" spans this but hides that the windows are unequal (3 vs 4 days) and differently composed by day-of-week: Apr 21–23 = Tue–Thu, Apr 25–28 = Sat–Tue. A weekend-inclusive post window against a weekday-only pre window is a real compositional confound in a workload-mix-sensitive measurement.

THREE PROBLEMS, ONE OF WHICH IS ARITHMETIC.

(1) The CI's lower bound is unattainable from the source. The source reports NO blended figure, NO request/token/spend shares per bucket, and NO sample size (methodology says only "text-only, non-cancelled requests"). Any weighted average of six values in [49, 92] must itself lie in [49, 92]. So ci80_low = 40 sits below the floor the primary source can produce under any weighting. Plausible weightings I constructed span roughly 63–74 (request-weighted, skewing small prompts: ~74; spend-weighted, skewing long-context agentic traffic: ~63). Unweighted mean of the six buckets is 68.0; the claim's 70 is the midpoint of the extremes (70.5), which is a coincidentally decent proxy. So the point estimate is fine; the interval is miscalibrated, too wide on the low side and slightly loose on the high side.

(2) Metric/unit fidelity is overstated. The source measures "average cost per million OpenRouter tokens" within prompt-size buckets. The claim relabels this "realized cost-per-task increase" and "cost per comparable request." Within a bucket, cost-per-request ≈ cost-per-M-token × tokens-per-request, and tokens-per-request moved only −0.05% to +0.7% (completions are a rounding error against 10K–128K prompts), so the per-request translation is fine to ~1pp. But "per task" is not measured at all: the source never observes turns-per-task or task completion, so if GPT-5.5 resolves agentic tasks in fewer turns the true cost-per-task increase could be well below 49%. That unmeasured downside is the only honest justification for a sub-49 lower bound, and it is not the justification the claim gives.

(3) The stated mechanism does not survive arithmetic. Prices doubled EXACTLY on both input and output, so for a fixed request mix cost per million tokens must rise exactly +100% regardless of the input/output split. Reduced verbosity cannot pull it down materially: in the 128K+ bucket completions are ~215 → 143 tokens against ~150K prompt tokens, i.e. ~1% of cost, so a 34% verbosity cut saves ~0.3% — yet that bucket shows +85%, and 50–128K shows +49%. The 51-point gap from +100% to +49% is arithmetically impossible to attribute to completion-length reduction. It must come from composition/caching effects (cache-read tokens price at 0.1x–0.5x of fresh input per OpenRouter's own Jul 21, 2026 caching post; cache-hit rates plausibly differ between a Tue–Thu window and a Sat–Tue window of freshly-migrated agentic workloads), from unreported reasoning-token changes (the post never mentions reasoning tokens), or from switcher-cohort selection. Note the perverse direction too: cost-per-M-token normalizes BY tokens, so it partly divides out exactly the verbosity saving the claim says it is "net of." The claim's note calls this "textbook T6 evidence that per-token price changes do not map 1:1 to cost-per-outcome" — the conclusion happens to be right, but the source's own decomposition does not support the verbosity mechanism, and neither the source nor the claim identifies what actually produced the offset.

WHY NOT REFUTE: the number, direction, and magnitude are real, first-party, and faithfully quoted; the price doubling is independently confirmed; the load-bearing conclusion (realized cost rose materially but sub-2x despite a 2x per-token reprice) survives.

WHY NOT CONFIRM: a hostile reviewer breaks the 40 lower bound immediately (impossible under the source), and would object that the metric label ("cost per task") claims more than the source measures and that the mechanism attribution is unsupported.

CORRECTION: value 68 (unweighted mean across the six buckets; also the center of the 63–74 band spanned by request- vs spend-weighted aggregations), CI80 [50, 90] — floor set just at the source's attainable minimum, ceiling near the observed maximum and below the +100% pure-repricing theoretical cap. Grade should drop from B to C+/B-: single first-party vendor source with no sample size, no bucket shares, no blended figure, unequal and day-of-week-mismatched observation windows, self-selected switcher cohort, and an unexplained gap between measured and theoretically-implied cost change. Also recommend relabeling the metric to "cost per comparable REQUEST (cost per million tokens, prompt-size-bucketed)" and dropping "net of reduced verbosity" from the metric name, since verbosity demonstrably explains almost none of the offset.

SOURCE VERIFIED, BUT THE HEADLINE NUMBER IS A CONSTRUCT, NOT AN OBSERVATION.

The OpenRouter post is real and the underlying figures check out. Correct metadata: published May 4, 2026 (not "2026-04"), author Justin Summerville. Method: cohort of users whose top model by request count was GPT-5.4 and who switched to GPT-5.5; GPT-5.4 window Apr 21-23, GPT-5.5 window Apr 25-28 (launch day excluded); media, cancelled and zero-token requests dropped. Published buckets (cost per million OpenRouter prompt tokens): <2K $4.89→$9.37 (+92%); 2-10K $2.25→$3.81 (+69%); 10-25K $1.42→$2.15 (+51%); 25-50K $1.02→$1.65 (+62%); 50-128K $0.74→$1.10 (+49%); 128K+ $0.71→$1.31 (+85%). List prices doubled ($2.50/$15 → $5/$30, still $5/$30 on OpenRouter as of Jul 2026, so no later repricing invalidates the window).

FOUR MATERIAL PROBLEMS.

(1) 70 is the midpoint of the min and max bucket — an arbitrary statistic with no traffic behind it, despite the entity field claiming "OpenRouter observed traffic." I recomputed a spend-weighted blend from the published buckets under several traffic mixes. Agentic-heavy mix (OpenRouter's own data: agentic tokens passed human usage ~Feb 1 2026 and agentic requests burn ~15x more tokens): +65%. Balanced mix: +66%. Only a short-prompt/chat-heavy mix reaches ~+79%. The blended per-request answer is robustly ~62-68%, not 70, and — importantly — never approaches +100%. The claimed CI80 upper bound of 100 (full pass-through of the list-price doubling) is not reachable under any mix of the published data.

(2) WRONG DENOMINATOR relative to the metric label. The metric says "cost-per-task"; the unit says "cost per comparable request"; the source measures neither — it measures cost per million prompt tokens. Cost per completed task additionally depends on turns/retries per task, which OpenRouter did not measure. OpenAI's launch claim (repeated by LLM Stats, Build Fast with AI, CometAPI, Medium coverage) is that GPT-5.5 reaches equivalent quality with ~40% fewer tokens on complex agentic problems (Terminal-Bench 82.7%). That is vendor marketing and OpenRouter's observed per-request completion counts partly contradict it (only -19% to -34% at 10K+, and +52% at 2-10K), but the turns-per-task channel is genuinely unmeasured and can only push realized cost-per-task below the per-request figure. This is exactly the "wrong denominator" failure the claim itself is meant to illustrate — the claim commits it while diagnosing it.

(3) THE STATED MECHANISM IS ARITHMETICALLY WRONG for the buckets that produce the low end. At 50-128K prompts, ~150 completion tokens against ~80K prompt tokens contribute roughly $0.05 of the $1.10 cost per million prompt tokens. Verbosity cannot explain why that bucket rose 49% instead of 100%. Reverse-engineering the numbers, GPT-5.4 at 50-128K implies an effective input rate of ~$0.70/M against a $2.50/M list rate — i.e. ~80% prompt caching. OpenRouter's own model page states effective pricing after caching runs 60-80% below list, and they shipped caching/sticky-routing work through this period (Jul 21 post). The sub-doubling in every 10K+ bucket is driven by cache-hit economics and routing, not by reduced verbosity, and the article explicitly discusses neither caching nor reasoning tokens. The claim's note ("net of reduced verbosity") attributes the effect to the wrong channel; a rising cache-hit rate between the Apr 21-23 and Apr 25-28 windows is an uncontrolled time confound that flatters GPT-5.5.

(4) SELECTION AND WINDOW. Three days vs four days immediately post-launch, restricted to users who voluntarily switched their top model within a week. Price-sensitive workloads that refused to switch are excluded by construction, so this is the cost increase experienced by the least price-sensitive adopters, before integrators retuned reasoning-effort or caching settings. Also, the note's "longer prompts, smaller increase" gradient is broken by the 128K+ bucket at +85% (OpenAI applies 2x input / 1.5x output multipliers above 272K), so the cited 49-92 range is not a clean ordering.

NO CONTRADICTING QUANTITATIVE ESTIMATE EXISTS. The Register, MegaOneAI, WinBuzzer and PromptCost all restate the 49-92% range rather than replicate it independently; I found no correction, retraction, or rival measurement. The direction of the finding (100% list increase → clearly less than 100% realized increase) is solid and the T6 point survives.

ADJUSTMENT. Recenter from midpoint-of-extremes to the spend-weighted blend (~65% per request), then apply a modest downward allowance for the unmeasured turns-per-task channel that the "cost-per-task" label promises: corrected_value 60. Widen the low end to 38 to cover an agentic-heavy mix combined with even a partial realization of the fewer-turns effect; cap the high end at 85, since no published bucket and no plausible mix reaches full pass-through and effective post-cache prices cushion the list-price doubling. Grade should stay B at best, and the note should be rewritten: the offset is mostly caching, not verbosity.

sources.title: OpenAI Developers on X: o3 80% price cut announcement
OpenAI announces 80% price drop for o3 - VentureBeat

claims.notes: OpenAI on the record: 'We optimized our inference stack... Same exact model — just cheaper.' ARC Prize independently confirmed unchanged performance. Timing coincided with competitive open-weight releases.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE RETRIEVED VERBATIM. X's oEmbed API (publish.twitter.com/oembed) returned the full text of @OpenAIDevs post 1932532777565446348, dated June 10, 2025: "We're cutting the price of o3 by 80% and introducing o3-pro in the API, which uses even more compute. / o3: Input: $2 / 1M tokens / Output: $8 / 1M tokens / Now in effect. / We optimized our inference stack that serves o3. Same exact model—just cheaper." Every element of the claim maps one-to-one onto this text: value (80), unit ($/M tokens in/out), new prices ($2/$8), period (2025-06-10, "now in effect"), entity (OpenAI o3, API only), and attribution (inference-stack optimization, model unchanged). The metric line's word "attributed" is the honest framing — it reports OpenAI's stated cause rather than asserting it as verified fact.

PRE-CUT BASELINE INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED. The claim's $10/$40 is not merely back-derived from the 80% figure. A Wayback snapshot of OpenRouter's o3 page from 2025-04-18 (web.archive.org/web/20250418055707) reads "Created Apr 16, 2025 / 200,000 context / $10 /M input tokens / $40 /M output tokens." $10→$2 and $40→$8 are each exactly 80%, so the figure is arithmetic on both axes, not a rounded marketing headline where only one axis moved.

CORROBORATION FROM THREE MORE CHANNELS. (1) Sam Altman, same day, tweet 1932434606558462459: "we dropped the price of o3 by 80%!!" (2) OpenAI's customer announcement email, quoted verbatim by HN user ctoth on 2025-06-10: "Today, we dropped the price of OpenAI o3 by 80%, bringing the cost down to $2 / 1M input tokens and $8 / 1M output tokens. We optimized our inference stack that serves o3—this is the same exact model, just cheaper." (3) Simon Willison's 2025-06-10 post confirms $10/$40 → $2/$8, 80%, and quotes OpenAI's Adam Groth on "the engineers optimizing inferencing."

PRICE PERSISTED, NO REVERSAL. Live OpenRouter models API pulled today (July 2026) shows openai/o3 at exactly $2.00/M input and $8.00/M output, thirteen months later. No correction, walk-back, or re-pricing found.

CI [80, 80] IS HONEST. This is an administered list price posted by the seller, not a measurement or an estimate. There is no sampling error, no methodology to disagree with, and no reasonable alternative reading. A degenerate interval is the correct representation of zero uncertainty; widening it would misrepresent the epistemics.

THREE HOSTILE FINDINGS THAT DO NOT MOVE THE VALUE OR CI, BUT SHOULD BE FIXED IN THE NOTES FIELD:

(1) The notes assertion "ARC Prize independently confirmed unchanged performance" is UNSUPPORTED and should be struck. I retrieved the actual ARC Prize June 10 thread. Tweet 1932535378080395332 reports o3-PRO semi-private eval results (ARC-AGI-1: 44/57/59% at $1.64-$4.16/task; ARC-AGI-2 <5%) with takeaways "o3-pro in line with o3 performance" and "o3's new price sets the ARC-AGI-1 Frontier" — the latter is a recomputation of the cost axis using the new $2/$8 price, not a re-run of o3 confirming unchanged accuracy. The next tweet in the thread (1932535380865347585) says only that o3-pro is not the same model as the Dec '24 o3-preview. ARC Prize's blog index contains no June 2025 post on the price cut or any o3 retest. Worse for the notes: ARC's one o3-specific analysis (arcprize.org/blog/analyzing-o3-with-arc-agi) predates the cut and documents the released o3 scoring LOWER than the December o3-preview, i.e. a precedent for the "o3" label covering differing performance. So the independent-verification leg is absent.

(2) "Same exact model" rests entirely on OpenAI's unaudited self-report. Contemporaneous HN discussion on the announcement day includes a user reporting a "sharp drop in o3 performance" over the preceding week and another explicitly speculating quantization. These are anecdotes, not evidence, and I found no rigorous pre/post A/B — but equally, no independent party demonstrated the weights were unchanged. The claim's own metric text says "with identical model," which slightly overstates what is verified; "OpenAI states identical model" is what the record supports.

(3) The load-bearing inference in the notes — "an 80% cut on an unchanged model implies gross margin headroom of at least that order" — is not entailed by the primary source. An 80% price cut bounds pre-cut margin only if the post-cut price still sits at or above marginal serving cost. Competitive timing makes a thin- or negative-margin strategic cut a live alternative: the cut shipped the same day as o3-pro at $20/$80, roughly two weeks after DeepSeek R1-0528, and amid Gemini 2.5 Pro pressure. The defensible disjunction is: EITHER pre-cut price sat far above marginal serving cost, OR OpenAI realized roughly 5x serving-cost improvement on fixed weights, OR it cut into margin under competitive pressure — most likely a mix. For the Thompson thesis this datapoint is evidence that a large price-cost gap existed at some point, not evidence about where price sits relative to cost today.

Net: the number, the unit, the period, the entity, and the interval are all faithful to a directly retrieved primary source and survive hostile checking. Confirm at 80 with CI [80, 80]. Grade A is warranted for the metric itself. Recommend editing the notes to drop the ARC Prize confirmation sentence, hedge "identical model" to "OpenAI-stated identical model," and replace the margin-headroom assertion with the three-way disjunction above.

Method note: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted, so verification ran entirely on direct retrieval — X oEmbed API for verbatim tweet text, Wayback CDX and snapshot fetches for pre-cut pricing, the live OpenRouter models API for persistence, HN Algolia API for the announcement email text and contemporaneous skepticism, and direct fetches of arcprize.org and simonwillison.net.

THE NUMBER SURVIVES; THE INFERENCE DOES NOT. Splitting the claim into (a) the price fact and (b) the load-bearing economic reading.

(a) PRICE FACT — fully confirmed, no contradicting source found. On 2025-06-10 OpenAI cut o3 list API pricing from $10/$40 to $2/$8 per M tokens in/out — exactly 80% on both dimensions (cached input $2.50 -> $0.50 is also 80%). Verbatim OpenAI wording is confirmed by a third party, not just the X post: "We optimized our inference stack that serves o3. Same exact model—just cheaper" (BleepingComputer). Model string o3-2025-04-16 unchanged. ARC Prize independently retested and reported "We compared the retest results with the original results and observed no difference in performance." I actively searched for degradation/quantization/distillation claims: rumors did circulate at the time, and both OpenAI staff and ARC Prize publicly rebutted them; I found no substantiated report of degraded o3 after 6/10. No later correction, no price reversal (o3 stayed at $2/$8 through deprecation; it is no longer on OpenAI's pricing page as of 2026).

(b) THREE MATERIAL PROBLEMS that justify adjust rather than confirm:

1. WRONG DENOMINATOR (basis for the widened CI floor). OpenAI had already been selling o3 at $5/$20 since 2025-04-17 via Flex processing (50% off, latency-tolerant), and Batch API had long carried a 50% discount. Against the cheapest tier already available to a price-sensitive buyer, the June 10 move was a 60% cut, not 80%. The 80% figure is list-to-list, which is the announced and conventional framing, but it overstates the change in realized effective price for exactly the volume-heavy segment the thesis cares about. I could not retrieve documentation of post-cut o3 Flex/Batch rates, and there is contemporaneous developer speculation on the OpenAI forum that the flex discount was folded into the "inference efficiencies" rather than stacked — so I cannot confirm the 80% carried through every tier. Hence CI80 [60, 80] on effective price; the list-price cut itself remains exactly 80.

2. THE ATTRIBUTION IS SELF-REPORTED AND UNFALSIFIABLE. "Inference-stack optimization" is OpenAI's own causal story. ARC Prize verified output quality, not the cause of the price change. Strong circumstantial evidence for a competitive-pressure driver sits right on the date: Gemini 2.5 Pro's 06-05 update at $1.25/$10, DeepSeek R1-0528 (5/28) at roughly $0.55/$2.19, Claude 4 (5/22), and Mistral Magistral shipping the same day (6/10). Latent Space had already called the reasoning price war in February 2025 ("Reasoning is less of a moat than anyone thought"). The metric string should read "OpenAI-attributed to inference-stack optimization," not "attributed to."

3. THE LOAD-BEARING INFERENCE IS INTERNALLY INCOHERENT AND SHOULD BE DOWNGRADED. The note uses OpenAI's statement to establish "identical model," then infers "pre-cut prices sat far above marginal serving cost." But the same statement asserts the opposite causal mechanism: that serving cost fell. You cannot take the first half at face value and discard the second. Read on OpenAI's own terms, this datapoint is evidence that marginal serving cost for a FIXED model fell ~5x in under two months — which is arguably evidence FOR Thompson (inference is real COGS that engineering attacks hard, and cost curves move fast) rather than evidence of 80% pre-cut gross margin. A ~5x serving-cost improvement in that window is independently plausible (continuous/prefix batching, KV-cache and speculative-decoding gains, NVL72-class hardware transitions, scale amortization) and matches documented industry cost-decline rates. Worse, an 80% cut on an unchanged model is equally consistent with pricing AT or BELOW cost to defend share; with zero public o3 COGS data the datapoint cannot discriminate among margin-compression, cost-decline, and below-cost-defense. It therefore does not establish gross-margin headroom in either direction and should not be carried as "the strongest single datapoint" for the T2 umbrella. Recommend load_bearing be flipped to false for the margin claim; it remains an A-grade fact about price levels and about the speed of serving-cost/price movement.

Minor conflation risk to flag: coverage of the same announcement also reports an ~87% cut (o3-pro at $20/$80 vs o1-pro's $150/$600). Do not let the 87% number migrate into this claim.

Grade A on the guidance statement itself is justified.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION FROM THE FILING. Q3 cash "Additions to property and equipment" = $30,876M ($30.9B); nine-month FY26 YTD = $80,146M. On the call Hood gave "Capital expenditures were $31.9 billion" plus "total finance leases were $4.7 billion" (~$36.6B all-in) and guided Q4 to "increase to over $40 billion." An H1 CY2026 of roughly $78-80B against a $190B full-year plan implies ~$55B/quarter in H2 — a steep but internally coherent ramp. The notes' "~$118B calendar-2025" base is not a Microsoft disclosure but a derived figure; it reconciles with reported quarters on an including-finance-leases basis (FQ3 FY25 $21.4B + FQ4 FY25 $24.2B + FQ1 FY26 ~$34.9B + FQ2 FY26 ~$37-38B), and 190/118 = 1.61 reproduces the stated "up ~61%."

TWO CAVEATS THE CLAIM OVERSTATES. (1) Basis ambiguity: the notes assert "incl. finance leases" with more confidence than the transcript plainly supports. Hood mentions finance leases as a source of variability ("the full value is recorded in the period of lease commencement") but does not, in the retrievable text, explicitly label the $190B as an including-leases figure. Two separate automated reads of the same transcript reached opposite conclusions on this. The including-leases reading is the more plausible one — it matches Microsoft's long-standing guidance convention and is the only reading under which the required H2 ramp is credible (a cash-only $190B would demand ~$59B/qtr cash, nearly doubling off $31B in two quarters) — but this should be flagged as an inference, not a quotation. (2) The "$154.6B analyst consensus" and the "~$35B above consensus" framing rest solely on Global Data Center Hub, a secondary newsletter; I could not verify them independently. The CNBC URL returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it at all — its headline and date are consistent with the confirmed Apr 29 announcement, but it is unverified by me and is in any case the weaker citation. Recommend replacing CNBC with the two Microsoft IR links as the citations of record.

WHY I ADJUST THE CI RATHER THAN CONFIRM. The interval is skewed the wrong way. The claim runs -25/+15 around 190, i.e. a bearish tilt, justified in the notes as "widened for execution slippage and lease-definition variance." Both risks are real, but the interval widens only the downside and imports a bearish prior that the evidence contradicts: (a) as of today, 2026-07-22, roughly 40% of the plan year is already reported or tightly guided (Q1 CY26 actual ~$36.6B; Q2 CY26 guided "over $40 billion," reporting within days), so genuine uncertainty attaches to only ~$111B of H2 spend, not the full $190B; (b) the base rate in this cycle is unambiguous — hyperscaler calendar-capex guides, Microsoft's included, have been revised up nearly every quarter, essentially never down; (c) the $25B price component is a weak source of downside specifically because Microsoft is capacity-constrained — under supply constraint, component price relief converts into additional units rather than into reduced dollars, so the dollar total is stickier than the price sensitivity suggests; and (d) H2 component pricing is largely contracted by mid-year. The one legitimate large-variance channel is the finance-lease timing lumpiness Hood herself flagged, where a single large lease commencing on either side of Dec 31 moves several billions — that argues for a genuinely wide band but a roughly symmetric one, and it cuts both directions.

I therefore keep the value at 190 (verbatim primary source, no basis to move it) and correct the interval to [178, 206]: floor raised because ~40% of the year is locked and the downside mechanisms are weaker than the notes assume, ceiling held slightly above 190 to respect the strong base rate of upward revision plus Hood's own "roughly." Note the direction of the residual error matters for the thesis: if this number is wrong it is more likely wrong high than low, which if anything strengthens rather than weakens the fixed-cost/capex-amortization leg of Thompson's argument. The claim remains load-bearing-safe either way — nothing in the marginal-cost thesis turns on 178 vs 190 vs 206.

VALUE CONFIRMED EXACTLY; CI AND NOTES NEED MATERIAL CORRECTION.

WHAT SURVIVES HOSTILE REVIEW. The $190B figure is verified to the dollar. Near-verbatim CFO quote recovered: "For calendar year 2026, we expect to invest roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures, which includes approximately $25 billion from higher component pricing" (Amy Hood, FQ3 FY2026 call, Apr 29 2026), corroborated by 5+ independent outlets (CNBC, 247wallst live blog, equity-insider, mirrorreview, thebuildout.ai, semiconalpha, Global Data Center Hub). Every checkable number in the notes passes: $154.6B Visible Alpha consensus (190 - 154.6 = 35.4, matching "~$35B above") and $25B component pricing.

THE BASIS CLAIM IS PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED. I reconstructed CY2025 from quarterly capex-including-finance-leases: $21.4B (CQ1'25) + $24.2B (CQ2'25) + $34.9B (CQ3'25) + $37.5B (CQ4'25, verified: CNBC "$37.5 billion, up 66%", Motley Fool "finance leases accounted for $6.7 billion") = $118.0B. 190/118.0 = 1.610, exactly Hood's stated "up 61% from 2025." On a PP&E-only basis the 61% does not compute. So the note's "incl. finance leases" is confirmed by arithmetic, and the "~$118B" base is confirmed to one decimal. No revision, correction, or walk-back found between Apr 29 and Jul 22 2026 (a Jul 6 article still cites $190B); FQ4 FY2026 earnings land Jul 29 2026.

CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE FOUND (why this is "adjust", not "confirm").

(1) THE SAME CALL DISCLOSED A CAPEX MISS AND A SEQUENTIAL DECLINE. FQ3 FY2026 (= calendar Q1 2026) capex including finance leases was $31.9B - BELOW the $34.9B Visible Alpha consensus and DOWN sequentially from $37.5B. Primary-source confirmation from Microsoft's own FQ3 FY2026 press release cash-flow statement: additions to property and equipment $30.876B for the quarter, $80.146B for the nine months. That implies finance leases added only ~$1.0B in FQ3'26, versus $6.7B in FQ2'26 and ~$15.5B in FQ1'26 (derived: FQ1+FQ2 PP&E = 80.146 - 30.876 = $49.27B). The finance-lease component - the lumpiest, most discretionary, least verifiable part of the number - has declined three quarters running, precisely as guidance calls for it to explode.

(2) $190B IS SEVERELY BACK-LOADED - A PLAN, NOT A RUN-RATE. CQ1 actual $31.9B + CQ2 (FQ4'26) guided ">$40B" puts H1 CY2026 at roughly $72-76B. Hitting $190B requires ~$115-118B in H2 2026, i.e. ~$58-59B/quarter: an ~85% step-up from the CQ1 actual and ~55% above Microsoft's all-time-high quarter ($37.5B), achieved in one step and sustained. (Global Data Center Hub makes the same structural point but its own arithmetic understates the required run rate at "roughly $50 billion quarterly"; 190 - 30.9 - 40 = 119.1 over two quarters = $59.6B/qtr.) This is the single most important caveat on the number and it is entirely absent from the claim's notes. It is exactly the "reason the number is misleading" a hostile reviewer would lead with: the headline was announced in the same breath as a capex miss.

(3) THE MEMORY EFFECT IS TWO-SIDED, NOT PURELY ADDITIVE. The notes treat component inflation only as a capex inflator. The same DRAM/HBM scarcity that doubled server RAM prices also delays server delivery and pushes capex recognition right; grid interconnection, transmission capacity, and long-lead baseload contracts compound the timing risk. So the $25B is not unambiguously additive to CY2026 dollars.

(4) GRADE-A SOURCING IS NOT SUPPORTED BY THE CITED SOURCES. I verified the $190B does NOT appear in Microsoft's FQ3 FY2026 press release - capex guidance was call-only. Per this repo's own PROCESS.md (A = official filings/disclosures), neither cited source qualifies: CNBC is B, globaldatacenterhub.com is a B/C newsletter. The grade is defensible on substance (official investor call, verbatim quote reproduced widely) but the citation list must include the Microsoft IR webcast/transcript for A to hold. Note also that the cited CNBC URL 403s to automated fetch, so it was corroborated only via search snippet.

(5) DENOMINATOR CAVEAT, LOAD-BEARING FOR THE THESIS. $190B is Microsoft's TOTAL capex, not AI capex and not compute capacity. Microsoft disclosed for FQ2'26 that roughly two-thirds went to short-lived assets (GPUs/CPUs) and one-third to long-lived land/shells with 15+ year lives that belong to no 4-year AI vintage. Layer on $25B of pure price inflation buying zero incremental capacity, and capacity-adding compute capex in CY2026 is nearer $100-125B than $190B. P1's BRIEF explicitly wants a 4-year-amortization payback model, and thesis proposition 4 turns on when US compute supply catches demand - using $190B as either denominator would materially overstate the payback burden AND overstate 2026 capacity growth. Because ~13% of the headline is price rather than volume, dollar capex is a biased proxy for compute supply in exactly the year the thesis cares about.

ADJUSTMENT. Keep corrected_value = 190: the announced plan is a verified fact and the claim's central estimate is right. The claim's downside CI skew (-25/+15) is directionally CORRECT - I initially expected it backwards, since hyperscalers systematically overshot capex guidance through 2024-25 (Microsoft's own FY25 "$80B" landed at ~$88B), but the specific evidence here overrides the reference class: a required 85% H2 ramp off a sequentially declining, consensus-missing quarter argues for genuine downside asymmetry. However the low tail is too shallow. One quarter of data-center or finance-lease delivery slippage moves $15-20B, and $160B only requires H2 to run at ~$43B/qtr - barely above the CQ2 guide, i.e. "capex keeps growing steadily instead of exploding," a very live 10th-percentile scenario. Widen the low bound to 160. Trim the high bound to 203: reaching $205B would need ~$65B/qtr in H2, roughly 2x the CQ1 actual, which sits above the 90th percentile even with memory prices still climbing. Corrected CI: [160, 203].

Finally, a definitional note the data layer should carry: the metric as written ("calendar-2026 plan (announced Apr 29 2026)") is a statement-of-fact whose true uncertainty is near zero (only the rounding in "roughly $190 billion"). The attached CI is really a distribution over REALIZED CY2026 capex. That conflation should be made explicit, or split into two claims - an A-grade statement claim (190, no CI) and a C-grade forecast claim (realized capex, [160, 203]) - because the grade attaches to the former and the CI to the latter.

Analyst convention (and Castellano's "Alphabet's $200 Billion Capex Plan") takes the midpoint. 200 is correct; 205 would be cherry-picking the ceiling.
2. Source quality. The claim's second source (Eastern Herald) is materially unreliable and should be dropped: it reports the guidance as a flat "$205 billion" and states prior guidance was "approximately $75 billion" — $75B was Alphabet's ORIGINAL FY2025 guide, not the prior 2026 guide ($180–190B). That is a ~2.5x error in the source the claim leans on. The CNBC URL cited returns 403 to me, but Bing News confirms it exists with the stated headline. Recommend replacing both with Bloomberg + the SEC 8-K + the earnings-call transcript.
3. Note error (minor, non-load-bearing). "Third raise this year" is wrong. Feb 2026 ($175–185B, given at Q4 2025 earnings) was the INITIAL CY2026 guide, not a raise; April ($180–190B) was raise #1; July ($195–205B) is raise #2. The Feb and April figures in the notes are otherwise corroborated (CNBC 2026-04-29: "ups 2026 capex to as much as $190 billion"; 247wallst: "doubled its 2026 capex to $175 billion").
4. CI calibration. This is the one soft spot. The metric is explicitly "guided," and the guidance range is a known fact ($195–205B), so an 80% CI of 188–210 implies uncertainty that does not exist — 188 lies below anything Alphabet said. The CI is conservative rather than wrong (it fully contains the true range), so it holds up, but 195–205 would be strictly more accurate. Note this CI would be appropriate only if the metric were reinterpreted as ACTUAL CY2026 spend, which brings a real risk the claim should not silently absorb: H1 2026 capex was $80.6B ($35.7B Q1 + $44.9B Q2), so hitting $195–205B requires H2 of $114–124B, i.e. $57–62B/quarter versus $44.9B in Q2 — a 27–38% sequential step-up sustained twice. In 2025 Alphabet's final raise to $91–93B landed at $91.4B, the low end. Anyone reusing this as "Alphabet will spend $200B" should skew low, not use the midpoint.

THESIS RELEVANCE — stronger than the claim states. The capex number is weaker evidence for T2's supply-constraint premise than the direct testimony on the same call: Ashkenazi said "We're still in a supply-constrained environment," management said "capacity remains constrained," and Alphabet disclosed it will EXPAND USE OF THIRD-PARTY CAPACITY in Q3 as a bridge while building internal capacity, accepting "modest near-term margin pressure" to do so. A hyperscaler renting compute from others is a far cleaner supply-constraint signal than a capex line. Also on-thesis: Q2 FCF was negative $5.9B, the first negative quarter since IPO, and Alphabet raised $49.6B of equity + $20.3B of notes in Q2 explicitly for AI capex — inference capacity is now visibly a balance-sheet-funded COGS problem, not zero-marginal-cost software.

CAVEAT for how this claim is used downstream: not all of the $200B is Alphabet's own serving capacity. The 8-K's new segment language states Google Cloud "generates product revenues primarily from the sale of TPU systems," and inventory jumped from $2.4B to $10.0B — some capex/inventory is merchant silicon Alphabet sells to third parties. This cuts both ways for T2 (it is still demand-driven), but the $200B should not be read as $200B of Alphabet-internal inference capacity.

Net: value 200, unit, entity, period, and grade A all confirmed against the CFO's own words and the SEC filing. Fix the notes ("second raise," not third), swap the Eastern Herald source, and optionally tighten CI to 195–205.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY-SOURCE AUDIT. I pulled the actual SEC filings rather than relying on the cited blog. The claim is directionally sound and its 2025 baseline is genuinely good, but the $725B point estimate is built on two unsupportable components and one mislabel, and every independent cross-check lands below it.

WHAT CHECKS OUT. The note's "~$413B actual in 2025" is confirmed. Reconstructing CY2025 from filings: Alphabet $91.4B (17,197+22,446+23,953+27,851, per Q1/Q2 2026 8-K cash-flow columns), Amazon $128.3B net of proceeds (10-K/supplemental TTM table), Meta $72.2B incl. finance-lease principal ($69,691M PP&E + $2,524M FL, FY2025 10-K), Microsoft ~$83.1B cash CY2025 (FY25 Q3 $16,745M + FY25 Q4 $17,079M + FY26 H1 $49,270M). Sum = $373B cash; add Microsoft's finance-lease ROU (~$28B) plus smaller AMZN/GOOGL leases and you get ~$410B. So $413B is right — but only on a finance-lease-inclusive basis. On pure cash capex it is $373B. The claim never states the basis, and that ambiguity is inherited by the $725B.

FLAW 1 — "guided" is false for ~80% of the total. Only Meta publishes a numeric capex guide in a filing: "We anticipate 2026 capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases, to be in the range of $125-145 billion, increased from our prior range of $115-135 billion" (Q1 2026 8-K EX-99.1, 2026-04-29). That is the one verbatim-verifiable number, and its midpoint $135B matches the claim. The other three do not guide: Alphabet's Q1 2026 10-Q says only "In 2026, we expect to significantly increase, relative to 2025, our investment in our technical infrastructure" — no figure; Alphabet's Q2 2026 release (filed today, 2026-07-22) contains zero instances of "expect," "outlook," "guidance," or "anticipate." Amazon's Q1 2026 "Financial Guidance" section gives only Q2 net sales and operating income — no full-year capex line. Microsoft has a June fiscal year and issues no calendar-year capex guide at all, so "MSFT ~$190B (guided)" for CY2026 cannot exist as a guide; it is a consensus estimate.

FLAW 2 — Alphabet at $200B is too high. H1 2026 actual is $80.6B (Q1 $35,674M + Q2 $44,924M). The 2025 H2/H1 ratio was 1.31; applying it gives ~$186B. Reaching $200B needs H2 of $119B, +48% over H1. Not impossible — Alphabet raised $49.6B of equity in June 2026 plus a $40B ATM program explicitly for "capital expenditures to scale AI infrastructure," and Q2 FCF went negative (-$5.9B) — but $200B is the top of the range, not a "new midpoint." Notably the claim's own cited source gives Alphabet $175-185B, so the claim's arithmetic contradicts its own source.

FLAW 3 — the headline source is unreliable and doesn't reproduce its own total. valueaddvc lists AMZN ~$200B, MSFT ~$190B, GOOGL $175-185B, META $115-135B; those sum to $680-710B, not $725B. Its Meta range is stale (superseded 2026-04-29). Its 2025 actuals are materially wrong: Amazon "~$100B" vs actual $128.3B, Microsoft "~$95B" vs actual $83.1B. A B grade is generous for a blog that misses component actuals by 20%+.

FLAW 4 — Epoch is not corroboration. Epoch's $770B is an exponential trend extrapolation ("If this trend continues, they will spend $770 billion in 2026"; 72%/yr fit, 90% CI 66-78%), not a guidance sum, and it covers FIVE companies including Oracle. Oracle's FY2026 10-K shows capex of $55,663M (vs $21,215M FY25, +162%); CY2026 Oracle is plausibly $80-95B. Backing that out implies Big-4 ≈ $683B — below the claim. The CNBC source 403'd and its headline concerns 2027 ($1T), not 2026.

MY BOTTOM-UP (finance-lease-inclusive): AMZN 190/205/222, GOOGL 180/190/205, MSFT 160/175/192, META 125/135/145 → total 655/705/764. Central $705B (+72% y/y, matching Epoch's fitted growth rate). Three independent lines — bottom-up guidance sum (~$705B), Epoch-minus-Oracle (~$683B), and Q1/H1 actuals extrapolation (~$660-700B) — all center below $725B. I therefore shade the point estimate to $705B and tighten slightly to [655, 765]. Roughly $136B of the year (Q1 all four, plus Alphabet's Q2) is already banked, which constrains the low end; component-price inflation (Meta cited "higher component pricing" as its reason for raising) and Alphabet's $89.6B capital raise support the high end.

THESIS CAVEATS. The note's "~2/3 is spent by companies that also sell inference" is wrong in the thesis-favorable direction: MSFT+AMZN+GOOGL is ~$570B of $705B, or 81%. But a larger caveat cuts against the thesis: capex is not merchant inference capacity. Land, shells, power and network are a large share of these dollars; much accelerator spend serves training and internal workloads, and Meta's entire ~$135B is captive (Meta sells no inference). So $725B (or $705B) overstates the compute that could actually collapse the token price umbrella, and the claim should not be used as a 1:1 proxy for "supply catching up."

HEADLINE: the $725B point estimate survives hostile review — it is the exact sum of the four current guides as of today — but the stated CI is mis-specified (too generous on the downside, too tight on the upside), and the primary source cited is the weakest of the available ones. Hence adjust, not confirm.

WHAT I VERIFIED (bottom-up, not from the aggregator blog):
- Amazon: ~$200B for CY2026, guided 5 Feb 2026 alongside Q4'25 results (Reuters/CNBC/Variety headlines, "50% increase"), reaffirmed in July commentary (TradingView 15 Jul 2026, Investing.com 16 Jul 2026). Actual Q1'26 cash capex $44.2B (stockanalysis cash-flow data), consistent with a ~$200B year given the usual back-half ramp. 2025 actual cash capex = 25.0+32.2+35.1+39.5 = $131.8B, so the "+50% to $200B" framing checks out.
- Alphabet: guided "as much as $190B" on 29 Apr 2026 (CNBC), then RAISED TODAY (22 Jul 2026, Q2 print) to $195–205B — CFO quote: "We have adjusted our full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance range to $195 billion to $205 billion." Stock -3–5% after hours. So the claim's note ("GOOGL ~$200B new midpoint") is right, but only as of the same-day after-hours release; before today the correct midpoint was $185B and the Big-4 sum was ~$710B.
- Meta: $125–145B guided 29 Apr 2026 (Yahoo Finance, Fortune, 24/7 Wall St. "Meta Tumbles 8% on $145 Billion CapEx Bombshell"). Midpoint $135B matches the claim.
- Microsoft: "$190B in 2026" (CNBC 29 Apr 2026; The Register: "lifts 2026 AI spend by $25 billion to cover component price rises"). PERIOD IS AMBIGUOUS and this is the single weakest leg of the $725B construct: MSFT reports on a June fiscal year and does not guide calendar years. From the FY26 Q3 press release, 9-month FY26 cash capex was $80.1B ($19.4/$29.9/$30.9B by quarter); adding finance leases (~$11B/qtr; FQ1'26 total-spend-incl-leases was $34.9B) puts 9M FY26 at ~$115–121B, so a fiscal-2026 total of $190B would require a ~$70B June quarter — implausible. $190B therefore most plausibly maps to calendar 2026 (or FY27, which calendarizes to roughly the same ~$180–200B). So the leg survives, but roughly a quarter of the total is a fiscal-year-anchored, finance-lease-inclusive figure pasted into a calendar-year, mostly-cash-capex sum. Mixed basis.
- Arithmetic today: 200 (AMZN) + 200 (GOOGL mid) + 190 (MSFT) + 135 (META mid) = $725B. Exactly the claim. Independent corroboration: Tom's Hardware 30 Apr 2026 ("$725 billion in 2026, up 77%"), Bloomberg 30 Apr 2026 ("Past $700 Billion This Year"), OfficeChai 2 May 2026 ("$715 Billion"), eciks 8 Jun 2026 ("$725B"), TechStock² 20 Jul 2026 and Startup Fortune 22 Jul 2026 (both "$725 billion"). The number is genuinely the market-consensus figure, not one blog's construction.

CONTRADICTING / WEAKENING EVIDENCE FOUND:
1) The cited primary source (valueaddvc, 8 May 2026) is internally inconsistent and factually sloppy: its own table lists Amazon 2025 at ~$100B (actual: $131.8B), Microsoft 2025 at ~$95B, Alphabet 2026 at $175–185B — its own rows sum to ~$695B, not the $725B it headlines. It should be demoted from primary source; the number is right for reasons unrelated to that blog's arithmetic.
2) Epoch AI's $770B is NOT confirmation of $725B: it is a 26 Feb 2026 trend extrapolation ("if this trend continues") for FIVE firms including Oracle on a lease-inclusive basis, off a ~$500B 2025 base. Net of Oracle (~$60–90B) that implies a Big-4 lease-inclusive figure near or below $725B — an apples-to-oranges cross-check, not a corroboration.
3) The claim's "$413B actual in 2025" only works on a mixed basis (MSFT incl. finance leases ~$120B, others cash). On a consistent cash basis 2025 was ~$378B (AMZN 131.8 + MSFT 83.1 + GOOGL ~92 + META ~71), which would make the growth rate ~+92%, not "+75–80%". The growth framing is basis-dependent.
4) Framing: much of the press calls this "$725B on AI," which overstates — Amazon's $200B includes non-AI fulfillment/logistics (~$25–30B). The claim's metric is total capex, so it is fine, but it should not be reused as an AI-capex number. Also the note's "~2/3 is spent by companies that also sell inference" understates: only Meta ($135B, ~19%) is non-cloud, so ~81% sits with sellers of inference — which strengthens, not weakens, the thesis link.
5) Above-range alternatives exist: Morgan Stanley >$800B for 2026 Big Tech AI capex (5 May 2026), MS raised Amazon and Meta capex estimates again 13 Jul 2026, "AI Investment ROI Reckoning: Can $750 Billion in Capex..." (22 Jul 2026), Goldman on 16 Jul 2026 saying hyperscalers keep upping capex into 2027. No source anywhere shows a cut or a downward revision; June's "AI capex fears" selloffs were fear of too much spending, not less.

WHY THE CI IS WRONG:
Downside 660 is not defensible for a metric defined as "guided." Summing the LOW ends of the stated ranges gives ~$700B (AMZN ~195–200, GOOGL 195, META 125, MSFT ~185). To land at 660 all four would have to undershoot their own guides by ~8%, and in this cycle every one of them has raised rather than missed (Alphabet has raised 2026 guidance twice already: Feb, Apr, and now Jul). Upside 780 is too tight: Alphabet added $15B at the midpoint TODAY, and Microsoft, Meta and Amazon all report within the next 8 days with memory/chip cost inflation explicitly cited as a capex driver (Meta was flagged on 17 Jul as heading for a near-doubling of its quarterly capex rate; Meta's own guide top is already $145B). A revised range of $705–790B with a center a touch above the snapshot sum is the honest read.

BOTTOM LINE: keep using ~$725–730B; grade B is fair (arguably B+ on corroboration, held back by the mixed fiscal/calendar and lease-inclusive basis). Swap the primary citation away from valueaddvc. Flag that this figure has a hard expiry date: it will very likely be restated upward in the last week of July 2026.
