verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND AND AUDITABLE. Dell'Oro Group's own press releases (not just the ComSoc/techblog secondary rewrite) give a fully closable arithmetic chain:

(1) Dell'Oro, "Data Center Capex Surged 51 Percent to $455 Billion in 2024": 2024 worldwide DC capex = $455B, +51%; 2025 forecast then was ">30%".
(2) Dell'Oro, Mar 17 2026 (PRNewswire 302715242): "worldwide data center capital expenditures increased 57 percent in 2025"; "We forecast full-year 2026 data center capex to surpass $1 trillion"; growth ">more than 50 percent in 2026"; driver = "well over 10 M high-end accelerators"; Top-4 US cloud +76% in 2025; "Oracle tripled its data center capex."
(3) Dell'Oro 1Q2026 release (June 2026): "The global data center capex outlook was raised to more than $1 trillion for 2026"; Top-4 US cloud +78% Y/Y in 1Q26; 2H26 to accelerate on NVIDIA Rubin ramp; memory/storage price inflation flagged as a major upward capex driver.

Implied point estimate: $455B x 1.57 = ~$714B for 2025; x 1.50-1.55 = $1,071-1,107B for 2026. So the primary source implies ~$1.07-1.11T, NOT $1.05T. The claim's 1050 is at or slightly below the arithmetic floor of the source it cites, and it ignores the June upward revision.

DEFECT 1 (fatal to the CI): ci80_low = 850 is indefensible. To land at $850B, 2026 growth would have to be +19% Y/Y. Dell'Oro's June statement is a RAISED floor of ">$1T" made with 1Q26 actuals in hand (+78% at the Big-4) and explicit 2H26 acceleration guidance. As of the Jun/Jul 2026 vantage point roughly half the year is already banked and the rest is largely contracted (Rubin orders, memory prepurchases, shell deliveries). A 10th percentile 19% below the vendor's stated floor is not honest uncertainty; it is uncertainty imported from an earlier, more ambiguous vintage.

DEFECT 2 (skew): the interval is symmetric (±200 around 1050), but the revision history is one-directional. Dell'Oro guided 2025 at ">30%" and delivered 57%; it guided 2026 at ">50%" in March and raised again in June. Memory/storage cost inflation is an active upward driver the source names explicitly. The honest distribution is right-skewed.

DEFECT 3 (scope label vs. source scope): the metric is labelled "TOTAL data center capital expenditures... all data centers." Dell'Oro's series is the "Data Center IT Capex Quarterly Report," which allocates "data center infrastructure capex for general-purpose and accelerated servers, storage systems, and other auxiliary data center equipment" across the ten largest CSPs plus Rest-of-Cloud, Colocation, Telco and Enterprise. Dell'Oro's own program page describes emphasis on IT equipment, not total capex including real estate. So land, building shell, construction and grid interconnect are largely out of scope. This mislabels the unit, but it makes 1050 CONSERVATIVE, not aggressive: a genuinely all-in "total" would be higher (~$1.2-1.4T).

DEFECT 4 (the bottom-up cross-check is not independent and contains a double-count): the note builds "Big-4 $725B + Oracle $50B." The cited AL Capital page defines $725B as the BIG-5 — "Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle" — with Oracle's ~$50B INSIDE it. That is a $50B double-count. The build also uses Amazon's $200B total capex, which includes non-data-center fulfillment/logistics, while omitting colocation/REIT developers entirely (a $100B+ bucket that Dell'Oro does cover as a segment). Errors partially offset, and the unsourced "other" plug does the work of hitting $1.04T. AL Capital Advisory is also a secondary aggregator of public guidance (it cites McKinsey's $6.7T-by-2030), not a primary source; it should not carry weight alongside Dell'Oro.

WHAT SURVIVES: the direction, the order of magnitude, and every specific fact in the note ("57% in 2025", ">50% in 2026", "surpass $1 trillion", ">10M high-end accelerators") are faithfully quoted from the primary release. The claim is not wrong; it is stale by one revision and its interval is mis-shaped.

CORRECTION: value 1090 (= $714B x ~1.53, mid of the source-implied band, reflecting the June raise). CI80 [1000, 1280]: the low bound sits just below the vendor's raised floor to allow for a memory-price reversal, FX, or a Dell'Oro restatement, and the high bound accommodates the consistent upward-revision pattern plus the definitional upside from the "total" label the claim uses. Grade B is defensible on the Dell'Oro leg alone; drop the AL Capital source or demote it to illustrative.

THESIS IMPACT: none adverse. The correction moves the number up and tightens the downside, which if anything strengthens the "compute supply is scaling enormously, inference COGS is real and capacity-bound" leg. Using the original 850 low would have understated the buildout.

CENTRAL VALUE SURVIVES; THE CI FLOOR DOES NOT.

What I confirmed on the primary source. Dell'Oro's Mar 17, 2026 release contains the verbatim Baron Fung quotes: "The Top 4 US cloud service providers—Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft—increased data center capex by 76 percent in 2025," "We forecast full-year 2026 data center capex to surpass $1 trillion," and a "global data center capex growth outlook to increase by more than 50 percent in 2026." The Jun 10, 2026 update (1Q26 Data Center IT Capex Quarterly) states the outlook was "raised to more than $1 trillion for 2026," with Fung forecasting further acceleration in 2H26 on NVIDIA Rubin ramp and custom-accelerator refresh. I checked Dell'Oro's news index through Jul 2026: no subsequent revision, so the Jun 10 number is current.

Internal arithmetic is consistent, which is the strongest evidence for the value. +50% growth to $1.0T implies 2025 = ~$667B, and 2025's +57% implies 2024 = ~$425B — matching Dell'Oro's known ~$430B 2024 base. So Dell'Oro's own numbers pin 2026 at $1.00-1.07T depending on whether ">50%" means 50%, 55% or 60%. $1,050B sits inside that band.

Bottom-up cross-check also lands there. Accelerators: >10M high-end units at system-level pricing is $400-500B alone; add general-purpose servers, storage (memory-inflated), networking, ~$50B/yr of DCPI equipment (Dell'Oro's Jul 7 release puts 1Q26 DCPI manufacturer revenue at $12B), plus shells/land/construction → $1.0-1.1T. Independent third-party anchor: BNEF (Mar 2026) put just the 14 largest *public* DC operators at ~$750B for 2026, which leaves ample room to $1.05T once China, private neoclouds, sovereigns, telcos, colo and enterprise on-prem are added.

CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE I HUNTED AND WHAT IT'S WORTH:

1. Direct contradiction, but stale. BuilderMuse ("Hyperscaler Data Center Capex 2026") states "Dell'Oro Group pegs total data center capex (hyperscalers plus colocation plus enterprise) at roughly $600 billion for 2026, up about 25% year over year" — a ~40% lower number attributed to the same source. It fails a date check: the same page lists Amazon at $105-120B, Microsoft $80-90B, Alphabet $75-85B, i.e. roughly half of actual 2026 guidance. This is 2025-vintage content, not a live dissent. Discounted.

2. Sloppy secondary coverage. cloudtechdaily reports "Top four U.S. cloud providers expected to spend over $1 trillion combined for the full year," conflating the worldwide total with the Big-4 (~$725B). Evidence that the $1T figure is being garbled downstream, but not evidence against it.

3. Real methodological error in the claim's own notes. The third cited source, AL Capital Advisory, defines its $725B as **Big-FIVE including Oracle** (Amazon $200B, Microsoft ~$190B, Alphabet $180-190B, Meta $125-145B, Oracle ~$50B). The notes' build "Big-4 $725B + Oracle $50B" therefore double-counts Oracle *as cited*. The arithmetic is rescued only because cx-11 independently derives Big-4 = $725B from company guidance (190+200+200+135). The citation should be repaired.

4. Wrong-denominator problem, offsetting. The bottom-up build treats Big-4 *total corporate* capex as data-center capex. Amazon's $200B includes fulfillment/logistics/Kuiper (~$25-40B non-AWS); Meta and Alphabet include offices and non-DC network. That overstates by $40-70B. But the build's "+ other" bucket leaves enterprise on-prem and global colocation/REIT capex ($150B+ combined) essentially unquantified, which more than offsets. Net effect: the build is conservative, not inflated.

5. Definitional drift worth flagging. The Jun 10 figure comes from Dell'Oro's "Data Center IT Capex" report; secondary descriptions of its scope disagree (one says "servers, storage systems, and other auxiliary data center equipment," another says GPUs + storage + power/cooling). Whether shells, land and construction sit inside the $1T is not cleanly established, and that boundary is worth $150-200B. This justifies a wide CI — but it justifies width around a *definition*, not a low outturn.

WHY I'M ADJUSTING THE CI RATHER THAN CONFIRMING. The 850 floor is not supportable under the claim's own stated entity ("all data centers"). Big-4 guidance alone is $725B and is tracking to plan (Amazon Q1 2026 actual $44.2B; Alphabet Q2 2026 $44.9B, +100% YoY). An $850B world total would require everything outside the Big-4 — Oracle (~$60-70B CY2026, with FY2027 gross capex guided to $90-95B), CoreWeave, xAI, China clouds and telcos, global colo, all enterprise on-prem, all sovereign programs — to sum to ~$125-220B. That is not a plausible tail; it is arithmetically excluded. There is no coherent definition that yields $850B: the broad definition gives ~$1.0-1.2T, and an IT-equipment-only definition would give ~$650-700B, which is a different metric, not a CI bound. I move the floor to 950.

I also judge the risk asymmetric to the upside, and note that Dell'Oro's June forecast predates Alphabet's Jul 22 raise to $195-205B (its third raise of the year, from $175-185B in Feb), with Microsoft and Meta yet to report. I keep the central at 1050 rather than raising it, because "surpass $1 trillion" at +50% arithmetically points to ~$1.00-1.07T and I don't want to over-extrapolate one guidance raise.

CAVEAT THAT MATTERS FOR THE LOAD-BEARING USE. Dell'Oro explicitly attributes a large share of 2026 dollar growth to component price inflation, not capacity: Fung says "rising memory and storage pricing substantially increased overall server system costs in the quarter and will likely remain a major capex growth factor this year." Microsoft separately attributes ~$25B of its $190B to memory price inflation rather than added capacity. Since this claim is load-bearing for the thesis that supply is catching up and will collapse the inference price umbrella, the dollar figure overstates the physical compute being added by roughly 10-15%. The $1.05T is right as a capex number and misleading as a capacity proxy. Dell'Oro itself adds the warning that "this heightened level of investment raises the potential for overcapacity in AI infrastructure" — which cuts in favor of the thesis on direction, but on a smaller physical base than $1.05T implies. Grade B is appropriate; I would not raise it, because the primary source gives a threshold ("surpass $1 trillion") rather than a point estimate, and no second forecaster publishes a directly comparable total-worldwide 2026 number.

claims.metric: Total announced multi-year AI infrastructure/compute commitments

sources.title: Tomasz Tunguz: OpenAI's $1 trillion infrastructure spend (vendor-by-vendor)
Yahoo/WSJ: OpenAI lifts planned compute spending to $750 billion through 2030
DCD: Building Stargate — OpenAI's trillion-dollar data center vision

claims.notes: Altman's stated ~$1.4T across ~8 years decomposes to: Broadcom $350B (10GW custom accelerators), Oracle $300B ($60B/yr, 2027-31), Microsoft Azure $250B, Nvidia $100B, AMD $90B, AWS $38B (one report says expanded to $100B/8yr), CoreWeave $22.4B. WSJ (July 22, 2026): planned compute spend through 2030 raised to ~$750B from ~$600B earlier in 2026. Caution: these are commitments/plans, repeatedly restructured (May 2026 reports had Stargate 'build' pledges cut toward renting); treat as intent, not contracted-firm dollars. Against ~$25B revenue run-rate and ~$25B 2026 cash burn, this is Thompson's fixed-cost absorption question (T1/T5) in its starkest form.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND, BUT IT IS A CEO ROUND NUMBER, NOT A FILING. OpenAI is private and files nothing. The origin of "$1.4T" is Sam Altman's X post of 2025-11-06: "We are looking at commitments of about $1.4 trillion over the next 8 years." That is genuinely first-party, so the number is not invented — but it is a verbal, undecomposed, promotional figure with no published schedule, and it is now ~8.5 months stale. The only true primary-document corroboration anywhere in this stack is Oracle's 10-Q RPO disclosure (Sept 2025), which supports the $300B Oracle line and nothing else.

FIVE FIDELITY DEFECTS.

(1) The claim's own decomposition contradicts its headline value. The notes list Broadcom 350 + Oracle 300 + Microsoft 250 + Nvidia 100 + AMD 90 + AWS 38 + CoreWeave 22.4 = $1,150.4B = $1.15T, not $1.4T. That $1.15T is precisely Tunguz's total, verbatim from the cited source: "OpenAI has committed $1.15T in infrastructure spending between 2025 & 2035 across seven major vendors." The claim has stapled Altman's headline number onto Tunguz's decomposition; ~$250B of the $1.4T is unaccounted for by the claim's own arithmetic.

(2) Period is wrong and borrowed from the other source. Altman said "over the next 8 years" → ~2025-2033. The "~2025-2035" window in the claim's period field is Tunguz's, attached to Tunguz's $1.15T. Value and period come from different sources with different spans.

(3) ~44% of the bottom-up dollar total is analyst-estimated, not disclosed. Only Oracle ($300B), Microsoft ($250B), AWS, CoreWeave ($22.4B) and Project Camellia ($20B) have stated dollar values — ~$692B. Broadcom ($350B) and AMD ($90B) were announced as gigawatt commitments (10GW, 6GW) with no disclosed dollar figure; the dollars are third-party imputation. "Announced commitments in dollars" is therefore substantially estimate, which the B grade does not reflect.

(4) Direction error on Nvidia. The $100B is Nvidia investing up to $100B *into* OpenAI, progressively per gigawatt deployed — an inbound capital commitment, not an OpenAI outbound purchase obligation. Counting it as OpenAI compute spend is a category error (the true OpenAI outlay on 10GW of Nvidia systems would be far larger, but that is a different, unannounced number).

(5) The claim is stale in both directions and the notes hedge a fact that is now settled. Since Nov 2025: Feb 20, 2026 — OpenAI reset investor guidance to ~$600B compute spend through 2030 (CNBC: "After previously boasting $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments, OpenAI is now telling investors that it plans to spend $600 billion by 2030"); Feb 27, 2026 — AWS deal expanded from $38B to $100B over 8 years plus a $50B Amazon equity investment (confirmed on openai.com and aboutamazon.com, so the notes' hedge "one report says expanded to $100B/8yr" should be stated as fact); Mar 6, 2026 — Oracle/OpenAI dropped the Abilene TX expansion; May 2026 — Stargate build pledges shifted toward renting; Jul 22, 2026 — raised to ~$750B through 2030.

WHY NOT "REFUTE": the Feb 2026 "cut from $1.4T to $600B" framing that CNBC/Futurism/TechTimes ran is itself apples-to-oranges — it compares an 8-year commitment stack to a 5-year spend plan. Two things vindicate the larger number surviving. First, the Jul 22, 2026 WSJ story (the claim's own source) explicitly refuses to treat $750B as superseding: "It is also separate from the $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments previously discussed by Chief Executive Sam Altman and a $1.15 trillion estimate covering hardware and cloud agreements through 2035." Second, OpenAI added $62B of AWS commitments one week *after* the supposed retrenchment — not the behavior of a company abandoning its stack.

WHY NOT "CONFIRM": the CI floor of 1100 is indefensible. It sits above the entire disclosed-dollar stack (~$692B) and above the company's own current guidance ($750B through 2030), meaning the claim assigns <10% probability to a level OpenAI itself is telling investors. An 80% interval on a metric this contested cannot exclude the company's own number. The stated interval (1100-1650, ±20%) implies far more precision than a verbal CEO figure plus 44% imputed dollars can bear.

CORRECTED FIGURES. Bottom-up as of 2026-07-22 (Broadcom 350e + Oracle 300 + Microsoft 250 + AWS 100 + Nvidia 100 + AMD 90e + CoreWeave 22.4 + Camellia 20) = $1,232B; excluding the mis-signed Nvidia line, $1,132B. Central 1250 sits at that bottom-up total with modest credit for undisclosed deals, and below Altman's un-decomposed round number. Low 800 brackets the disclosed-dollar stack (~$692B) and the company's own through-2030 guidance ($750B) — the world in which gigawatt announcements never convert to the imputed dollars. High 1600 allows Altman's $1.4T plus 2026 additions and further deals through 2033.

THESIS IMPACT: none material. Thompson's fixed-cost-absorption argument works identically at $0.8T or $1.4T against a ~$25B revenue run-rate; the order of magnitude is what is load-bearing. But grade should drop B → C: no filing exists, the headline is a verbal figure, the decomposition doesn't sum to it, and the period is borrowed. Recommend restating the metric as a range across three distinct constructs rather than a point: CEO-stated commitments ($1.4T/8yr, Nov 2025), bottom-up vendor stack ($1.15-1.23T, 2025-2035, ~44% imputed), and company spend guidance ($750B through 2030, Jul 2026).

ADJUST. The $1.4T headline survives as a widely-cited artifact but does not survive hostile review as a best estimate. Four independent lines of contradiction:

(1) THE CLAIM'S OWN PRIMARY SOURCE CONTRADICTS IT. Tunguz's vendor-by-vendor tally (the claim's source #1) sums to $1.09–1.15T for 2025–2035, not $1.4T — below the claim's point estimate and at/below its CI floor of 1100. Tunguz explicitly flags "±30–50% error margins" because "many contracts have undisclosed financial terms" and the year-by-year schedule is author estimate, not published payment terms. The claim cites a source that reports a materially lower number.

(2) LATER CORRECTION — THE COMPANY WALKED IT BACK. On 2026-02-20, CNBC, Reuters and DatacenterDynamics all reported OpenAI resetting planned compute spend to ~$600B by 2030. CNBC: "After previously boasting $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments, OpenAI is now telling investors that it plans to spend $600 billion by 2030." Reuters framed it against "Altman had said last year that OpenAI is committed to spending $1.4 trillion to develop 30 gigawatts." CNBC repeated it 2026-02-27: "OpenAI has been telling investors that it's now targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030." The July 22, 2026 raise to $750B is a partial recovery, still roughly half the headline. The claim's own note concedes restructuring but keeps the pre-reset number as the point estimate.

(3) EXECUTION EVIDENCE CUTS AGAINST THE COMMITMENT FRAME. Stargate reportedly stalled (the-decoder, 2026-02-23); the Abilene, TX expansion was abandoned in March 2026 over financing and what Bloomberg called OpenAI's "often-changing demand forecasting" (unite.ai, 2026-03-07). Mid-2026 trackers cite ~10 GW planned and only ~3.2 GW of contracted power (Georgia Power, 2028–2032) against the ~30 GW that priced the $1.4T. If the GW denominator is a third of what the headline assumed, the dollar headline is doing marketing work.

(4) DEFINITIONAL INFLATION. The $1.4T mixes incompatible categories: Nvidia's $100B line is Nvidia's equity investment INTO OpenAI, not OpenAI purchase spend (a category error either way — the corresponding hardware purchase would be ~$500B, so this single line swings the total by ±$400B); Broadcom's $350B is an estimate on undisclosed terms (only a term sheet was signed as of Dec 2025); AMD's $90B embeds warrants flowing to OpenAI. It also mixes chips-only pricing (~$35B/GW for Broadcom) with full-service cloud pricing (~$67B/GW for Oracle) as if additive. Only ~10% ($140B) was funded at announcement.

OFFSETTING EVIDENCE (why not refute): announced commitments genuinely grew in 2026 — on 2026-02-27 AWS expanded the existing $38B agreement by $100B over eight years alongside Amazon's $50B investment, taking AWS to ~$138B. No vendor deal (Oracle $300B, Microsoft $250B, Broadcom, AMD, CoreWeave) has been reported cancelled outright. And the July 22, 2026 Yahoo/WSJ piece the claim cites explicitly preserves $1.4T as a distinct still-referenced quantity, stating the $750B is "separate from the $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments previously discussed by ... Sam Altman and a $1.15 trillion estimate ... through 2035." Run-rate reconciliation also softens the "57% cut" framing: $750B over 2026–2030 is ~$150B/yr, which annualizes to ~$1.2T over the eight-year window Altman used — close to, but below, $1.4T.

CORRECTED VALUE. Updating Tunguz's tally for the AWS expansion: Broadcom 350 + Oracle 300 + Microsoft 250 + Nvidia 100 + AMD 90 + AWS 138 + CoreWeave 22 = ~$1,250B. CI low 950 reflects the Feb 2026 reset trajectory (~$600B/2030 ≈ $960B on an 8-yr-equivalent basis) and a strict tally that excludes Nvidia's equity line and haircuts Broadcom's undisclosed terms. CI high 1550 reflects Altman's $1.4T headline plus the 2026 AWS expansion. I do not extend to 1650 because that upper bound is only reachable by re-pricing the Nvidia 10 GW deal as ~$500B of hardware, which would be inconsistent with how every other line is counted.

IMPACT ON THE THESIS. The direction of the correction is small enough that Thompson's fixed-cost-absorption point (T1/T5) is unaffected qualitatively — $1.25T against a ~$25B revenue run-rate is the same order-of-magnitude problem as $1.4T. But the more thesis-relevant finding is qualitative and cuts the other way: the Feb-2026 cut, the Abilene cancellation, and "often-changing demand forecasting" show OpenAI actively flexing these obligations up and down with demand. That is evidence these are elastic intent, not rigid fixed costs — which weakens any argument that OpenAI is locked into a fixed-cost overhang it must absorb regardless of demand. Recommend the claim be relabeled from "commitments" to "announced intent" and downgraded from grade B to C given the source-versus-value conflict.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCES: I reached all four originals and verified the exact language.

(1) AWS, anthropic.com/news/anthropic-amazon-compute (Apr 20, 2026): "committing more than $100 billion over the next ten years to AWS technologies"; up to 5GW; ~1GW Trainium2/3 by end-2026; Amazon investing "$5 billion in Anthropic today, with up to an additional $20 billion." (2) Azure, blogs.microsoft.com (Nov 18, 2025): "Anthropic has committed to purchase $30 billion of Azure compute capacity and to contract additional compute capacity up to one gigawatt" — note the 1GW is ADDITIONAL to and unpriced beyond the $30B; no term disclosed. (3) Google, anthropic.com/news/expanding-our-use-of-google-cloud-tpus-and-services (Oct 23, 2025): "up to one million TPUs," "well over a gigawatt of capacity online in 2026," "The expansion is worth tens of billions of dollars"; no term disclosed. (4) Google/Broadcom, anthropic.com/news/google-broadcom-partnership-compute (Apr 6, 2026): multiple GW of next-gen TPU from 2027, NO dollar figure, CFO Krishna Rao calls it Anthropic's "most significant compute commitment to date," and it is explicitly ADDITIVE, not substitutive: "deepens our existing work with Google Cloud—building on the increased TPU capacity we announced last October."

WHAT HOLDS: Every component figure, unit, and date in the claim is faithfully transcribed. Scope discipline is good — the $50B Fluidstack own-build (anthropic.com/news/anthropic-invests-50-billion-in-american-ai-infrastructure) is correctly excluded as capex rather than a purchase commitment, and the investments INTO Anthropic (Amazon $5B+$20B, NVIDIA $10B, Microsoft $5B) are correctly kept out of the compute total rather than circularly added.

WHAT FAILS: the CI80 lower bound. 130 is arithmetically unreachable from the sources. AWS alone is "more than $100 billion" (a floor, not a point) and Azure is a firm "$30 billion" — that is already ≥$130B before any credit for Google, whose October 2025 deal carries its own primary-source dollar disclosure ("worth tens of billions"), i.e. ≥$20B. The honest floor consistent with all four sources is ~$150B. A lower bound of 130 implicitly zeroes out a disclosed figure, which for a load-bearing claim understates the downside case in the wrong direction.

The central of 160 is also mildly conservative in a way the notes acknowledge but under-price: it credits the April 2026 Broadcom tranche at exactly zero. That tranche is unpriced, but it is additive per the source's own wording and is described by Anthropic's CFO as its largest compute commitment to date — which, as of Apr 6, 2026, had to beat the Azure $30B and the Google "tens of billions." Implied rates from the priced deals ($30B/~1GW for Azure; >$100B/5GW for AWS, i.e. ~$20-30B per GW) put "multiple gigawatts" at $40-100B+. Counting it at zero is defensible only under a strict "sum of disclosed dollar figures" reading; the metric label ("Total disclosed multi-year compute commitments") invites that reading, so I keep the central close rather than moving it to ~200, but I nudge it up to reflect that each disclosed figure is a floor.

TWO FIDELITY CAVEATS worth carrying: (a) the stated period "deals span ~2025-2036" is the author's construction — only AWS discloses a term (ten years); Azure and both Google tranches are silent on duration, so the sum is a cumulative total that cannot be annualized from these sources, which matters because the thesis turns on per-year cost burden. (b) All figures rest on unaudited company press releases; I could not find any counterparty SEC filing (Amazon/Microsoft/Alphabet/Broadcom backlog or remaining performance obligation) that breaks out Anthropic, and Broadcom's investor newsroom timed out. Grade B is right; this is not filing-grade evidence, and commitments of this type have historically been restructured. Also note the AWS commitment explicitly covers "training and deploying Claude" — these are inference-serving contracts as much as training ones, so the note's framing of this as training fixed cost being converted to long-term commitments is a slight misread; the contracts actually cut toward Thompson's "marginal costs are back" point rather than away from it.

Net: value survives with a small upward nudge, CI does not — the floor must rise to the arithmetic minimum and the ceiling should be wider given a genuinely unpriced, self-described largest-ever tranche.

VERIFIED COMPONENTS (all confirmed against primary sources; the two priced legs are exact):
- AWS: anthropic.com/news/anthropic-amazon-compute confirms "over $100 billion committed to AWS technologies across 10 years," up to 5GW, Amazon investing $5B now + up to $20B more on top of $8B prior. Reuters (2026-04-20), CNBC and Mercury News independently corroborate the >$100B/10yr figure and the April 20, 2026 date. A-grade.
- Azure: Microsoft blog (2025-11-18) verbatim: "Anthropic has committed to purchase $30 billion of Azure compute capacity and to contract additional compute capacity up to one gigawatt," with NVIDIA up to $10B and Microsoft up to $5B invested. A-grade.
- Google Oct 2025: up to 1M TPUs, >1GW in 2026, deal "worth tens of billions of dollars" (anthropic.com/news/expanding-our-use-of-google-cloud-tpus-and-services; CNBC 2025-10-23). No precise figure ever disclosed.
- Google/Broadcom Apr 6, 2026: confirmed unpriced. Anthropic's page says only "multiple gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity ... starting in 2027." TechCrunch (2026-04-07) and DataCenter Knowledge both report Broadcom's SEC filing implies "roughly 3.5 gigawatts," and quote CFO Krishna Rao calling it "our most significant compute commitment to date."

WHERE THE CLAIM BREAKS DOWN (two problems, pulling in opposite directions):

(1) The label overstates rigor. Strictly *disclosed* dollar commitments as of 2026-04-20 total $130B (AWS $100B + Azure $30B), not $160B. The $30B assigned to Google is the analyst's own triangulation of "tens of billions." The claim's own ci80_low of 130 happens to be exactly the disclosed-only floor, which is a point in its favor, but the metric name "Total disclosed" is inaccurate for the point estimate.

(2) More materially, the central estimate is probably too LOW because it prices Anthropic's self-described largest commitment at roughly zero incremental dollars. The Apr 6, 2026 Google/Broadcom deal is ~3.5GW starting 2027 (Broadcom filing) and Anthropic's CFO calls it "our most significant compute commitment to date" — a statement made when the largest disclosed commitment on the books was the $30B Azure deal, so it implies materially more than $30B. Pricing benchmarks: OpenAI-Oracle implies ~$13B per GW-year; the AWS-Anthropic deal implies ~$4-7B per GW-year (cheaper, custom silicon, strategic investor). 3.5GW over ~2027-2031 is roughly 10-14 GW-years, i.e. $50-110B on those benchmarks, versus the $30B the claim carries for all of Google. Corroborating signal four days after the as-of date: Google committed up to $40B of equity ($10B firm at $350B valuation, up to $30B milestone-contingent — Reuters/WSJ, 2026-04-24), 1.6x Amazon's $25B, which sat against a >$100B purchase commitment. Even a conservative 2x investment-to-commitment ratio implies a Google compute commitment near $80B; Amazon's ~4x ratio implies $100B+.

Net: a defensible central for total announced multi-year cloud compute commitments as of 2026-04-20 is ~$200B (100 AWS + 30 Azure + ~70 Google), not $160B, and the upper tail needs to run past 230 because the largest single leg remains unpriced.

OTHER ADVERSARIAL FINDINGS (noted, not decisive):
- Circular-financing critique is real and widely made (ZeroHedge, FourWeekMBA, ComputeForecast all frame the AWS deal as "Amazon paying itself"): ~$65B of vendor equity (Amazon $25B, Google up to $40B, plus Nvidia/Microsoft $15B) backstops the purchase commitments. This does not change the gross contracted number, but it means the headline is partly marketing framing and the *net* external cash obligation is smaller.
- "Up to" language pervades (up to 5GW, up to 1GW, up to 1M TPUs, up to $20B/$30B). These are ceilings, not floors, so the gross tally has an asymmetric downside if ramps slip.
- Confusion risk with a circulating "$65 billion in hyperscaler commitments" figure — that is equity investment, not compute purchase. Do not conflate.
- Scope/as-of sensitivity is high. The tally excludes the $50B Fluidstack self-build (Nov 2025), which for the thesis's purpose (converting training/inference cost into decade-long contracted obligations) arguably belongs, taking the figure to ~$250B. And the number kept moving after the as-of date: Akamai $1.8B (May 2026), an xAI Colossus arrangement (May 2026), a 20-year TeraWulf Kentucky data center lease (July 2026). Any reader who drops the "as of 2026-04-20" qualifier will understate.
- No evidence found of any later correction, retraction, or downward revision of the $100B or $30B figures.

THESIS IMPACT: unchanged in direction and arguably strengthened. The correction moves the number up, so the load-bearing point (labs converting compute into decade-long contracted commitments rather than treating it as a one-off fixed cost) survives. Grade should stay B, not A, because the single largest component is undisclosed and the estimate spans a wide range.

METHOD CAVEAT: the WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted before I started, so searching was done via WebFetch against lite.duckduckgo.com and direct primary-source fetches. All load-bearing figures above come from anthropic.com, blogs.microsoft.com, Reuters, WSJ, TechCrunch, CNBC or DataCenter Knowledge; low-quality aggregator blogs surfaced in results were not relied on.

PRIMARY SOURCES — both named anchors check out verbatim.

(1) Alphabet Q4 2025 call (abc.xyz event page carries the full transcript). Ashkenazi, answering Michael Nathanson: "Approximately 60% of our investment in 2025, and it's going to be fairly similar in 2026, went towards machines; so, the servers. Alphabet's own 10-K and Q1 2026 10-Q footnote say the opposite: "approximately 60% of technical infrastructure assets were comprised of servers AND NETWORK EQUIPMENT. The remaining balance was comprised of data center land and buildings and related assets." The filing (higher-authority than the verbal call) puts networking INSIDE the 60%, so Alphabet's servers-only share is below 60%, not at it. The claim leans on the CFO's looser verbal framing, which is the version that flatters its definition. The footnote is also a balance-sheet stock ratio, not a capex ratio.

(b) Half the denominator is undisclosed and looks lower. Amazon and Meta are ~50% of big-four capex and never disclose this split. Their filings point lower on a total-capex denominator. Amazon FY2025 10-K: total net PP&E additions $142.4B (AWS $96.5B); gross "Servers and networking equipment" rose $59.3B = 42% of total additions (~61% if you use AWS-only additions as the denominator — Amazon's ~$46B of retail/logistics capex is the dilution). Meta FY2025 10-K: capex $69.7B; "Servers and network assets" +$29.6B (43% of the $69.1B gross PP&E increase) while CIP rose $23.7B (34%). Meta Q1 2026 10-Q: gross PP&E +$22.5B of which servers/network +$7.9B (35%) and CIP +$10.5B (47%) — peak shell-build. Both lines bundle networking into the numerator, so servers-only is lower still. Caveat cutting the other way: CIP/"assets not yet in service" contains undeployed servers (Alphabet's not-yet-in-service jumped $30B in Q1 2026 alone), so placed-in-service ratios understate current server spend; Meta's marginal placed-in-service ratio is ~70%. The honest read is a wide band, not a point.

Capex-weighted CY2025 across the big four (GOOGL $91B @60%, MSFT $118B @54%, AMZN $142B @42%, META $70B @43%) = ~50%. CY2026 shifts up (MSFT ~67%, AWS share of Amazon capex rising) to roughly 54-57%. Blended CY2025–CY2026 on a total-company-capex denominator: ~52-55%. On a data-center-only denominator (excluding Amazon retail), 58-60% holds.

(c) Third source misrepresented. The cited Dell'Oro release is dated Feb 11, 2026 (claim lists "2025") and says "accelerated servers for AI training and domain-specific workloads could account for approximately two-thirds of total data center infrastructure spending by 2030" — not "approaching ~half by 2029" as the note asserts. It is also a global, all-buyer, 2030 forecast, so it is not evidence for a CY2025-26 US-hyperscaler figure at all (direction is upward, so this error does not rescue the low side).

VERDICT. The two disclosed anchors genuinely support ~58-60%, so this is not a refute. But 58 is the top of the defensible band given (i) the claim's own narrow numerator definition, which Alphabet's filing contradicts, and (ii) Amazon's non-datacenter capex sitting in the denominator of every "~$1T hyperscaler capex" tally the thesis uses. Adjust central to 55 and widen the low tail to 45 (the "total big-four capex, servers-only" case) while keeping the high tail near Microsoft's current 67% run-rate. Thesis impact is modest but real: at 55% the "majority sits in 5-6-year assets" claim still holds for CY2026, but for CY2025 on a total-capex basis it is roughly a coin flip, so the load-bearing sentence should be scoped to CY2026 or to data-center capex specifically.

VERIFIED (both cited primary anchors check out verbatim):

1. Alphabet Q4 2025 call, Ashkenazi: "Approximately 60% of our investment in 2025 and it's going to be fairly similar in 2026, went towards machines, so the servers. Then 40% is what you referred to as long duration assets, which is our data centers and networking equipment." (2026 guide $175-185B at that call.) The claim's A-grade characterization of this anchor is accurate.

2. Microsoft FY26 Q1 (Oct 29, 2025), Hood: "Roughly half of our spend was on short-lived assets, primarily GPUs and CPUs..." Total capex $34.9B incl. $11.1B finance leases.

CONTRADICTING / CORRECTING EVIDENCE FOUND — all of it points UPWARD, i.e. the claim is biased low by two specific defects:

(a) STALE MICROSOFT ANCHOR. The claim uses the FQ1'26 ~50% figure as its Microsoft input and only hand-waves at "rising to ~two-thirds... per earnings coverage." Two subsequent quarters are direct CFO disclosure, not coverage: FY26 Q2 — "roughly two thirds of our capex was on short-lived assets, primarily GPUs and CPUs" (capex $37.5B; cash PP&E $29.9B + $6.7B finance leases); FY26 Q3 — "roughly two thirds of our capex was for short-lived assets, primarily GPUs and CPUs" ($31.9B + $4.7B finance leases = $36.6B). Dollar-weighted across FY26 Q1-Q3, Microsoft is at 61.6%, and the two most recent quarters are both ~67%. The claim anchored on the single lowest of three available datapoints.

(b) MISREAD DELL'ORO SOURCE. The claim's note says Dell'Oro "sees accelerated servers alone approaching ~half of all DC capex by 2029." I fetched the cited press release: it actually says "Accelerated servers for AI training and domain-specific workloads could account for approximately two-thirds of total data center infrastructure spending by 2030." The note understates its own source by ~17 points, dragging the synthesis down.

(c) 2026-SPECIFIC UPWARD FORCE. Hood on the FY26 Q3 call: CY2026 capex "roughly $190 billion in capital expenditures which includes approximately $25 billion from the impact of higher component pricing." Memory/HBM cost inflation is pure server content and mechanically inflates the numerator's dollar share in 2026, not the shell/power denominator.

(d) NOTE-LEVEL DEFECT that cuts against the claim's own framing. The note says "the ~40% in shells/power is 15-25-year assets." That is wrong for the networking slice: Ashkenazi explicitly folds "networking equipment" into her 40% "long duration" bucket, but Alphabet depreciates network equipment on the same ~6-year schedule as servers. Defining "short-lived" by depreciation life (the definition the thesis actually needs for T5/T6 payback pressure) puts Alphabet ABOVE 60%, and shrinks the genuinely durable land/shell/power fraction below 40%. Corroborating: Dell'Oro's DCPI (physical infrastructure equipment) ran only ~$12B in 1Q26 worldwide against ~$1T/yr total DC capex, so the non-IT bucket is dominated by construction/land/interconnect, not a large equipment layer.

DOWNWARD FORCES I HUNTED FOR AND WEIGHED (why I do not adjust further, and why the CI stays wide):

- Denominator inconsistency on finance leases. Microsoft's share is computed on a denominator INCLUDING finance leases ($11.1B → $6.7B → $4.7B, falling fast). A material part of the apparent 50%→67% "mix shift" is lease-timing, not real. But this cuts the wrong way for a skeptic: on a cash-PP&E-only basis (Alphabet's convention), Microsoft implies ~73%/82%/77%. So harmonizing conventions raises the number rather than lowering it.
- Amazon dilution — the strongest genuine downward force. Amazon is the single largest CY2026 line ($200B of the $725B four-company total, cx-04/cx-11) and its capex still carries non-AI fulfillment, transportation and Kuiper (plausibly $15-25B/yr). Amazon discloses no server/shell split.
- Meta discloses no split either. Its Q4 2025 call says only that capex "including principal payments on finance leases, were $22.1 billion, driven by investments in data centers, servers, and network infrastructure" (2026 guide $115-135B at that call). Meta's heavy self-build program (own shells, own generation) plausibly skews it more shell-heavy than Alphabet.
- Together AMZN+META are ~46% of the CY2026 aggregate and are undisclosed. That is irreducible.

ARITHMETIC. Capex-weighted, using disclosed shares where they exist and 55%/58% placeholders for Amazon/Meta: CY2026 = 60.1% on $725B; CY2025 = 56.6% on ~$415B; CY2025-26 blend = 58.8%. Restricting to the entities the claim actually names (Alphabet + Microsoft, which is what the sourcing supports) gives 63.4% for CY2026. So 58 is the very bottom of the defensible band and is only reachable by (i) importing Amazon/Meta guesses the claim never sourced and (ii) using the stale Microsoft anchor.

VERDICT: adjust, not refute. The claim's direction and its load-bearing use (majority of the ~$1T wave sits in ~5-6-year assets) survive and in fact strengthen. But the central is systematically low for two identifiable reasons, and the correction matters because the period is weighted toward CY2026 where the number is highest. Move central 58 → 61. Tighten the floor 48 → 52 (no discloser has printed below 50%, and that 50% was on a lease-inflated denominator; a sub-52 blend would require Amazon and Meta both well under 50%, implausible now that both are dominantly AI-infra spenders). Keep the ceiling near 70 rather than narrowing, because Amazon/Meta opacity plus the finance-lease convention alone moves the answer 5-10 points. Grade should stay B, not rise — two of four companies in the natural denominator publish nothing, and the metric label "hyperscaler capex" is doing more work than the sourcing (Alphabet + Microsoft only) can bear. Recommend the metric be relabeled to name the disclosure basis explicitly and the note be corrected on both the Dell'Oro figure and the "40% = 15-25-year assets" characterization.

sources.title: OpenAI's financials have leaked, showing $21 billion in losses against $13 billion in revenue - Fortune
Exclusive: OpenAI Losses Increased Nearly 8X in 2025, With Spending Hitting $34 Billion - Ed Zitron

claims.notes: From audited financial documents obtained by Ed Zitron and independently verified by the Financial Times. Revenue tripled from $3.7B in 2024. Note: recognized revenue is far below the 'annualized run-rate' figures OpenAI quotes publicly (Altman said >$20B ARR exiting 2025). Zitron's separate Microsoft revenue-share documents (20% share) imply lower GAAP-style revenue through Q3 2025, so definitional ambiguity remains; CI reflects the audited number.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE TRACED. The number is faithfully represented; the CI is materially too wide.

1) Primary source located and figure verified exactly. Ed Zitron's "Exclusive: OpenAI Losses Increased Nearly 8X in 2025" reports, from audited financial documents he viewed and that the Financial Times independently verified: FY2025 revenue $13.07B, FY2024 revenue $3.7B, total costs and expenses $34B, cost of revenue $7.5B, R&D $19.18B, S&M $5.73B, G&A $1.57B, net loss attributable $38.53B. Fortune independently reports the same income statement with operating loss $20.92B (FY2025) and $8.78B (FY2024). The claim's value of 13.07, the FY2025 period, the USD-billions unit, and the $3.7B 2024 comparator all match the source verbatim. Internal arithmetic checks out: $34.0B − $13.07B = $20.93B operating loss, matching Fortune's $20.92B to rounding. Zitron's $38.53B net loss vs. Fortune's $20.92B operating loss is not a contradiction — the ~$17.6B gap is below the operating line, almost certainly remeasurement of convertible/preferred instruments from the October 2025 recapitalization.

2) No superior primary source exists. I checked SEC EDGAR directly (company search for OpenAI S-1 filings returned an empty Atom feed; full-text search of S-1s filed 2026-06-01 to 2026-07-22 surfaced only third parties mentioning OpenAI — Gloo, Entrata, QumulusAI, Ambiq, SpaceX). OpenAI's IPO registration is not public as of 2026-07-22, so the leaked audited statements are the best available primary document. There is nothing to check them against in the filing record.

3) The figure survives corroboration from genuinely independent, pre-leak sources — this is the strongest point in the claim's favor and it is not reflected in the CI. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, on the record 2025-09-09: "Revenue this year will grow over 3X. So about $13 billion in revenue from about $4 billion last year." The Information, 2025-09-30: OpenAI generated $4.3B in H1 2025 and was "on track to meet its full-year revenue projection of $13 billion." The Information, 2025-12-19: OpenAI "on track to beat its 2025 revenue goal of $13 billion," with annualized revenue topping $19B by November. Three lines of evidence — the audited statements, the company's own CFO nine months before the leak, and contemporaneous subscription-outlet reporting — converge on the same number. The H1/H2 split is also internally coherent: $4.3B H1 implies $8.77B H2, an average monthly run of ~$1.46B against a ~$1.6-1.7B December exit rate, exactly the ramp shape you would expect. No outlet reports OpenAI disputing the documents.

4) Why "adjust" rather than "confirm": the CI80 of 12.5–13.6 (±~4%, a ±$550M band) is not an honest representation of the source uncertainty — it is inflated by roughly 3-4x. This is an audited income-statement line, verified by the FT, undisputed by the company, and pre-corroborated by the CFO's own public guidance. The uncertainty here is not measurement error; it is a small tail risk on (a) restatement when the S-1 becomes public, (b) the leaked document being a near-final rather than final audit, and (c) entity-scope recasting from the October 2025 nonprofit-to-PBC conversion, which could in principle change the consolidation perimeter mid-year. Those justify roughly ±$150-250M, not ±$550M. I propose 12.90–13.25, slightly asymmetric to the downside to carry the restatement/recast risk. The grade should also move from B to A — this is one of the better-sourced numbers in the set, and marking it B understates it.

5) Hostile checks that did NOT move the number, but that downstream users must not get wrong. (a) Gross vs. net of Microsoft's revenue share: $13.07B is the top-line recognized revenue; OpenAI's $17.2B of payments to Microsoft (including $10.59B booked to R&D, i.e. training compute) sits on the cost side. Anyone computing "revenue OpenAI actually keeps" after the 20% share must not reuse $13.07B as if it were already net. (b) The claim's own note that Zitron's separate Microsoft rev-share documents "imply lower GAAP-style revenue through Q3 2025" is, on inspection, a red herring for this metric — The Information's $4.3B H1 2025 figure and Friar's guidance both reconcile cleanly with $13.07B, so the rev-share back-out is almost certainly capturing only the revenue streams subject to the share, with timing lags. It should not be used to widen this CI. (c) Related-party revenue concentration is real but is a quality-of-revenue issue, not a magnitude issue: SoftBank paid OpenAI $867M and Microsoft paid OpenAI $303M in 2025, together ~9% of the top line. (d) The ARR gap the claim flags is correctly characterized and is the single most important framing point for the thesis: ~$19-20B annualized exiting 2025 versus $13.07B recognized. For any marginal-cost or gross-margin work, $13.07B is the correct denominator; substituting the run-rate figure would inflate apparent margin coverage by ~50%.

6) Thesis relevance, stated plainly: cost of revenue of $7.5B against $13.07B revenue implies ~43% gross margin for FY2025. That is the number that actually bears on Thompson's "marginal costs are back" argument, and it is well-supported by the same primary document. The revenue figure itself is solid enough to build on.

Net: value confirmed at 13.07 unchanged; CI tightened from 12.5–13.6 to 12.90–13.25.

HUNTED FOR CONTRADICTION; NONE SURVIVED. Verdict: confirm $13.07B with the stated CI.

1) Source convergence on the exact figure. Fortune (2026-06-16), Zitron (2026-06-15), Ars Technica, Yahoo Finance, Business Model Analyst and Crypto Briefing all report $13.07B FY2025 revenue vs $3.7B FY2024. All trace to one leaked document set, but the FT independently verified the documents. No OpenAI denial, correction, or retraction found as of 2026-07-22.

2) Internal arithmetic checks out in BOTH years, which is hard to fake. 2025: $34.00B total costs − $13.07B revenue = $20.93B, matching Fortune's independently-stated $20.92B operating loss. 2024: $12.48B − $3.70B = $8.78B, matching Fortune's $8.78B. Revenue is a load-bearing line in a self-consistent income statement, not a stray headline number.

3) PRE-LEAK independent triangulation (the strongest test). The Information/Reuters, 2025-09-30 — nine months before the leak — reported H1 2025 revenue of $4.3B ("16% more than all of last year," i.e., on the same $3.7B 2024 basis) and an OpenAI full-year 2025 target of $12.7–13B. The audited $13.07B lands on that target. A leaked fabrication would not be expected to sit this precisely on a figure OpenAI gave investors months earlier.

4) The ARR objection is a denominator error, not a contradiction. CFO Sarah Friar (Reuters, 2026-01-19) said annualized revenue "surpassed $20 billion" exiting 2025, up from ~$6B exiting 2024. Recognized/exit-ARR ratio: 2024 = 3.7/6 = 0.62; 2025 = 13.07/20 = 0.65. Consistent. Reconstructing from the ARR path (~$6B Jan → ~$10B Jun → ~$13B Aug → >$20B Dec) integrates to ~$4.3B H1 and ~$8.3–8.8B H2, i.e. ~$12.6–13.1B. The claim's own note flagging this is correct and the arithmetic supports $13.07B.

5) THE ONE REAL COUNTER-NUMBER, AND WHY IT FAILS. TechCrunch (2025-11-14) leaked Microsoft revenue-share docs: $493.8M paid in 2024 and $865.8M in Q1–Q3 2025, implying at 20% "at least $2.5B in 2024 and $4.33B in the first three quarters of 2025." Naively annualized this gives ~$5.8B for 2025 and is circulating as such (also in The Decoder). It does not refute the claim, for two reasons TechCrunch states explicitly: (a) it is a floor — "very likely to be more"; (b) the figures are Microsoft's NET revenue share, with Bing and Azure OpenAI Service revenue deducted, and Microsoft does not break those out. The 2024 calibration proves the bias: the same method yields $2.5B against an undisputed $3.7B actual, capturing only ~67%. Grossing up Q1–Q3 2025's $4.33B floor by the same factor gives ~$6.5B for nine months, consistent with $13.07B given a large Q4. The Microsoft method is a floor that understates by roughly a third; it cannot bound the audited figure from above.

RESIDUAL CAVEATS (why I keep the CI at ±~$0.55B rather than tightening to ±$0.15B): (a) single-document provenance — FT verified authenticity, it did not re-audit; (b) no issuer confirmation, and OpenAI's S-1 was submitted CONFIDENTIALLY (May/June 2026), so no official audited figure is public and the full prospectus stays sealed until ~15 days before the roadshow; (c) entity/period scope ambiguity — the Oct 2025 nonprofit-to-PBC recapitalization could imply predecessor/successor periods, and Zitron's piece does not state which entity or whether revenue is gross or net of the Microsoft share; he deliberately declined to editorialize. The $38.53B "net loss attributable" vs $20.92B operating loss spread shows outlets already reading these docs differently, though notably not on the revenue line.

DOWNSTREAM WARNING for the thesis: the load-bearing use is gross margin ($13.07B revenue less $7.5B cost of revenue = ~42.6%). That is a legitimate pairing since both come from the same statement. Do not pair $7.5B cost of revenue against the $20B+ ARR figure, and do not let any co-claim compare $13.07B to competitors' ARR-style numbers.

OpenAI 2025 financials leaked: $38.5B loss ahead of IPO - Yahoo/Quartz

claims.notes: Total costs and expenses $34B: R&D $19.18B (incl. ~$10.6B to Microsoft for Azure compute), S&M $5.73B, cost of revenue $7.5B, G&A $1.57B. Directly supports T1: training/R&D is a giant fixed cost dwarfing revenue ($1.60 spent per $1 of revenue in 2025, improved from $2.37 in 2024). Headline net loss $38.5B includes large one-time non-cash conversion charges.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND — and the claim did not cite it. Both listed sources (Fortune, Yahoo/Quartz) are downstream aggregations of Ed Zitron, "Exclusive: OpenAI Losses Increased Nearly 8X in 2025, With Spending Hitting $34 Billion," wheresyoured.at, published 2026-06-15 (not June 16; that is Fortune's pickup date). Zitron reports working from "audited financial documents viewed by this publication," "independently verified by the Financial Times." No auditor is named and no document title is given — that is the single real weakness in the chain.

VALUE: EXACT. The primary reports "Loss from Operations: $20.92 billion" (2024: $8.78B). The claim's value of 20.92, period (FY2025), unit (USD billions/year), and entity are faithfully represented. This is not a derived or estimated number — it is a transcribed line item.

INTERNAL CONSISTENCY: PASSES. Cost of revenue 7.5 + R&D 19.18 + S&M 5.73 + G&A 1.57 = 33.98 ≈ the reported $34B total; revenue 13.07 − 33.98 = −20.91, matching the reported −20.92 to rounding. An income statement that closes to a penny is strong evidence the leak was transcribed correctly rather than reconstructed. Zitron independently restates "$20.9 billion" as OpenAI's 2025 loss in his 2026-06-30 follow-up, so the figure is stable across his own reporting.

NET LOSS RECONCILES — BUT THE CLAIM'S "~$30B" IS WRONG. The primary gives the full bridge: −$20.92B operating, plus ~$2.12B other income, less a $41.55B fair-value loss on convertible interests and warrant liability (the nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion) = −$60.35B; then $17.87B "attributable to noncontrolling members capital" and $3.95B "attributable to redeemable noncontrolling interests" are stripped out, landing at $38.53B net loss attributable to OpenAI (2024: $5.09B; 38.53/5.09 = 7.6x, consistent with Zitron's "nearly 8X" headline). The claim's metric string says the $38.5B includes "roughly $30B one-time for-profit-conversion charges." That number appears nowhere in the source and is not derivable: the gross conversion charge is $41.55B, the net-of-NCI conversion effect is ~$19.7B, and the operating-to-net gap is $17.58B. "~$30B" is a fabricated intermediate and should be replaced with the sourced $41.55B gross / ~$19.7B net-of-NCI framing.

CI IS THE MATERIAL DEFECT. [19.5, 22.5] is ±7% on an audited, FT-verified, internally-reconciling reported line item. There is no sampling or estimation uncertainty here to represent. The only genuine residual risks are (a) the leaked document not being the final audited version and (b) reclassification when the figure surfaces in OpenAI's S-1. A ±7% band manufactures uncertainty the source does not contain and, if propagated downstream, will wrongly soften a hard number. I tighten to [20.7, 21.1] — roughly ±1%, which honestly encodes "80% chance the eventually-filed figure equals 20.92 or is trivially restated."

NOTES ERROR: "$1.60 spent per $1 of revenue in 2025" is mislabeled. Total spend per dollar of revenue is $2.60 ($34B/$13.07B). The $1.60 is operating LOSS per dollar of revenue (20.92/13.07 = 1.60), and the 2024 comparator $2.37 (8.78/3.70) is likewise a loss ratio, not a spend ratio. The arithmetic is right; the label is wrong and should be corrected before the number is quoted.

THESIS FIT — HOLDS, WITH ONE CAVEAT. The claim is used to support T1 (training/R&D is a giant fixed cost dwarfing revenue). R&D of $19.18B against $13.07B revenue is $1.47 of R&D per revenue dollar, which supports T1 more directly than the operating-loss ratio does. Caveat a hostile reviewer would raise: $10.59B of that R&D line is payments to Microsoft for Azure compute (of $17.2B total to Microsoft across all lines, per the primary), and Azure spend booked in R&D is not cleanly separable into training vs. research-serving inference — so the "pure fixed cost" reading is slightly overstated. The clean marginal-cost line is cost of revenue ($7.5B, of which $6.047B to Microsoft), which is rv-03's territory, so rv-02 is not being misused. Second caveat: stock-based compensation is not broken out in what the primary discloses, so the cash operating loss is unknown and smaller than $20.92B.

GRADE: B is appropriate and should stay. This is a leaked document, not an SEC filing — FT verification and perfect internal reconciliation argue for higher, but until the S-1 lands it is not A-grade. Verdict is "adjust" rather than "confirm" solely because the CI materially misrepresents source precision and the metric string carries an unsourced "~$30B" figure; the load-bearing value itself survives hostile review intact.

POINT ESTIMATE SURVIVES — THE FRAMING AROUND IT DOES NOT.

WHAT HELD. $20.92B operating loss on $13.07B revenue against $34.0B total costs is confirmed independently by Fortune, the FT, Ars Technica, Gizmodo, The Deep Dive, MLQ.ai, and Ed Zitron's line-item extraction of the underlying (reportedly audited) documents. Line items reconcile to the penny: 7.5 COGS + 19.18 R&D + 5.73 S&M + 1.57 G&A = 33.98; 33.98 − 13.07 = 20.93 ≈ 20.92. 2024 checks too (12.48 − 3.70 = 8.78). No correction, retraction, or OpenAI denial found in ~5 weeks of subsequent coverage. So I tightened the CI: 19.5–22.5 implies estimation uncertainty that does not exist for a four-significant-figure reported audited number. Residual risk is pre-S-1 restatement only, hence 20.85–21.0.

FAILURE 1 — THE PARENTHETICAL IN THE METRIC IS ARITHMETICALLY INCOHERENT AND FACTUALLY WRONG. The claim says "net loss $38.5B including roughly $30B one-time for-profit-conversion charges." The actual conversion charge is $41.55B (change in fair value of convertible interests and warrant liability), not ~$30B — the ~$30B is an FT source's loose characterization, not the document figure. And the chain runs: operating loss $20.92B → +$41.55B conversion charge → ~$2.1B other income → total net loss $60.35B → less ~$17.87B attributable to noncontrolling members → $38.53B attributable to OpenAI. The actual non-operating drag inside the $38.5B is $17.61B, not $30B. As written, the claim implies a residual operating loss of 38.5 − 30 = $8.5B, directly contradicting its own headline value of $20.92B. Anyone doing the subtraction gets the wrong answer.

FAILURE 2 — "$1.60 SPENT PER $1 OF REVENUE" IS A MISLABEL, PROPAGATED FROM FORTUNE. $1.60 is operating LOSS per dollar of revenue (20.92/13.07), and $2.37 is the 2024 equivalent (8.78/3.70). Actual spend per dollar of revenue was $2.60 in 2025 (34.0/13.07) and $3.37 in 2024 (12.48/3.70). Fortune wrote "spent $2.37 to generate every $1 in revenue," which is wrong on its face, and the claim inherited the error. This understates the cost intensity by ~60% and should be corrected before it is quoted downstream.

MATERIAL COMPETING FIGURE. The FT quotes "a person apparently familiar with OpenAI's financial situation" saying 2025 losses were "closer to $8 billion once you strip out all of the stuff that should be one-time costs." That $8B cannot be reached from a $20.92B GAAP operating loss by stripping non-operating items alone — it requires stripping roughly $12.4B of operating-line non-cash charges on top, almost certainly stock-based compensation, which the leak does not disclose in any outlet I could find. So there is an unexplained ~$12B wedge between the GAAP figure and the OpenAI-side "true burn" narrative. The GAAP $20.92B stands, but the claim must not be used as a cash-burn number, and the SBC gap is a real hole in the evidence.

FIT TO T1 IS LOOSER THAN THE NOTE ASSERTS. (a) $20.92B blends in $5.73B of S&M — 27.4% of the operating loss — which is customer acquisition, irrelevant to the fixed-vs-marginal cost distinction. CONTRADICTIONS FOUND (why 25 / 23-28 does not survive a hostile read)

1) INTERNAL ARITHMETIC MISMATCH. The claim's own metric string is "~$2B/month," which annualizes to $24B, not $25B. Two of the trackers carrying the March figure state it explicitly as "$2 billion per month… annualized run rate at approximately $24 billion" (axis-intelligence; gradually.ai independently: "$2B/month = approx. $24B annualized"). The $25B figure is separately dated to *February* ("approximately $25 billion in annualized revenue as of February 2026," aibusinessweekly). The claim has fused a February company-stated ARR number with a March monthly-revenue number and taken the higher one. Point estimate should be 24.

2) RECOGNIZED-REVENUE DENOMINATOR CHECK CUTS DOWN, NOT UP. Q1 2026 recognized revenue of $5.7B annualizes to $22.8B as a quarter average; an exit-March monthly of ~$2B gives $24B. Company-stated "ARR" runs ahead of recognized revenue (it annualizes contracted/enterprise commitments), which is exactly the framing risk the claim's own notes flag but then does not price into the estimate.

3) THE UPPER BOUND IS UNSUPPORTABLE. FutureSearch's current 2026 analysis states flatly: "Growth then flattened: the run rate held near $25 billion from February through the spring," reaching ~$25B ARR by May 2026. I could find no credible source placing OpenAI above ~$25-26B at any point Feb–spring 2026 (an explicit search for $26B/$27B/$28B run-rate claims returned zero results). A p90 of $28B for March 2026 implies ~35% annualized sequential growth that demonstrably did not occur. 26 is a generous ceiling.

4) THE NOTE'S CORROBORATION IS MARKETING FRAMING, AND IT INVERTS. The claim says ~$25B is "consistent with OpenAI's own 2026 forecast of $30B." That forecast is now evidence *against*, not for. WSJ (Apr 28, 2026), carried by Reuters and Forbes, reported OpenAI "missed multiple monthly revenue targets earlier this year after losing ground to Anthropic in coding and enterprise markets," and missed its 1B ChatGPT WAU goal (plateau ~900M). OpenAI's spokesman called the WSJ piece "clickbait" and said the business is "firing on all cylinders" — the company-stated framing the claim leans on is precisely the disputed side. Arithmetically: with Q1 recognized at $5.7B and the run-rate flat near $25B through spring, Q2 lands ~$6.2B, leaving ~$18.1B needed across H2 to hit $30B recognized — implausible. FY2026 recognized revenue is tracking ~$24-27B, not $30B. The $30B should be dropped as corroboration.

5) CITED SOURCE DOES NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM. The claim cites https://futuresearch.ai/openai-revenue-forecast/ dated 2026-06. That URL currently serves an older analysis anchored to March 2025 (~$8B ARR, "$12.7B in revenue in 2025," 2024 revenue $3.7B) and contains no 2026 run-rate figure and no mention of missed targets. The live 2026 analysis lives at /openai-financial-forecast/. As cited, source #2 is a dead reference. Grade should stay B at best; the surviving 2026 evidence chain is one paywalled Information report plus SEO statistics aggregators that all appear to trace to it.

6) PERIOD STALENESS. The claim is dated "as of March 2026" but is being used to test a July 20, 2026 thesis. It happens to remain roughly current only because growth flattened — that is luck, not construction. The honest framing is "run-rate plateaued near $24-25B from February through at least May 2026."

RELEVANCE TO THE THESIS (flag for the parent agent)
The correction is small for margin arithmetic (a $24B vs $25B numerator barely moves implied inference gross margin against mc-11/mc-12). But the *reason* for the correction is load-bearing for T2/T5. A revenue run-rate that plateaus for four-plus months while flagship prices rose ~4x (px-04) and realized cost-per-task rose ~55% (px-05) is evidence of demand resistance at umbrella prices, not of demand outstripping supply without limit. It also complicates T2's "demand concentrated on OpenAI and Anthropic gives *both* pricing power": the WSJ reporting attributes OpenAI's miss specifically to share loss to Anthropic in coding and enterprise, i.e., intra-duopoly competition already biting before any supply catch-up. Thompson's stated uncertainty about demand elasticity is the right place to route this.

WHAT SURVIVES. The $10.9B figure itself is real and multiply reported: WSJ (May 20, 2026) and CNBC the same day both carried it, sourced to figures Anthropic shared with prospective Series H investors — Q1 2026 actual $4.8B, Q2 2026 projected $10.9B (~127-130% QoQ), with ~$559M operating profit. Summing implied monthly run-rates for Apr/May/Jun gives ~$10.4-10.8B for the quarter, i.e. the $10.9B is internally coherent rather than a stray number. So a flat refute is not warranted.

WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE — four material problems, in descending severity.

(1) PERIOD/PROVENANCE IS WRONG IN THE CLAIM. The claim says "reported June-July 2026." It was reported May 20-21, 2026 — roughly six weeks BEFORE the quarter closed — and it came out of an active fundraise at a $965B valuation, the single most upward-biased context a private company ever discloses in. As of today (July 22, 2026, three weeks post-close) I could find no actual or audited Q2 figure; Anthropic filed a confidential S-1 on June 1 and remains private. The claim is mid-quarter fundraising-deck guidance, not "guidance reported after the quarter."

(2) THE OPERATING-PROFIT CLAUSE IS MISLEADING AS WRITTEN, AND IT IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF. WSJ's own reporting states the $559M "includes model training costs but excludes stock-based compensation." At Anthropic's valuation, quarterly SBC almost certainly exceeds $559M, so on a GAAP basis the company is very likely still loss-making in Q2. WSJ also reported the company "might not remain profitable for the full year" given planned compute/training spend. Zitron (May 21) adds that the profitable quarter is exactly the quarter in which Anthropic pays SpaceX a reduced ramp fee against a $1.25B/month (~$15B/yr) steady state — i.e., the margin is transiently subsidized by a contract structure, not by durable unit economics. Calling this a "first-ever quarterly operating profit" without the non-GAAP/transient qualifiers overstates the evidence for T2 (pricing durably above cost).

(3) GROSS-VS-NET ACCOUNTING — the classic wrong-denominator problem. Anthropic books cloud-reseller revenue (AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex, Microsoft) on a GROSS basis, counting total end-customer spend as revenue and partner payouts as expense; OpenAI reports NET (deducting ~20% to Microsoft). Forbes (Mar 25, 2026) quotes Khosla's Ethan Choi saying Anthropic "would be materially lower in rev" on OpenAI's basis; BofA estimated up to $6.4B of 2026 cloud revenue-share (vs $1.9B in 2025). FutureSearch flags a forced gross-to-net restatement (20-40% haircut to headline) as the biggest tail risk at IPO, though it puts the probability in single digits. Note this cuts the revenue line but NOT the operating-profit line (gross-up inflates cost of revenue equally) — so it damages any margin-percentage or revenue-comparability use of the number, which is exactly how a thesis about price-vs-marginal-cost would want to use it.

(4) REVENUE-QUALITY / FRONT-LOADING. Zitron documents enterprise prepayment of tokens ("$50 million intended to be spread over 12 months that it takes in as revenue") and 10-30% discounted credit packs, plus irreconcilable prior ARR disclosures (Feb $14B, Mar $19B ARR vs a March 9 court filing where the CFO said revenues "exceeding $5 billion to date"). A 130% single-quarter jump is anomalous enough that some of it plausibly reflects recognition timing rather than run-rate consumption.

WHY ADJUST RATHER THAN CONFIRM. The point value 10.9 holds for the as-reported gross basis, so I keep it. But the original 80% CI of 8.5-12.5 is both too wide and wrongly symmetric: three independent corroborations plus the ARR triangulation make anything above ~11.7 essentially unsupported (nothing suggests upside to a self-published fundraise projection), while the downside carries real, identified mass (net-basis presentation, front-loading, projection-vs-actual). I tighten to a downward-skewed 9.5-11.7. I would also downgrade the grade from B toward B-/C for load-bearing use, and restate the metric as: "Anthropic Q2 2026 revenue of ~$10.9B (gross basis, company projection shared with Series H investors, May 20 2026; no actual/audited figure published as of July 22 2026), with a projected ~$559M NON-GAAP operating profit that excludes stock-based compensation and benefits from a temporarily discounted SpaceX compute ramp; company does not claim profitability persists."

IMPLICATION FOR THE THESIS. Used carefully, this is still meaningful support for T2/T5-T6: even a non-GAAP, SBC-excluding operating profit that INCLUDES training costs implies inference is being priced well above serving cost under scarcity. But it is much weaker than a clean "the leading lab turned profitable" datapoint, and it cannot support any claim about durable margin structure — the transient compute discount and the company's own disclaimer point the other way.

claims.notes: Cuts both ways for the thesis: positive gross margin on tokens supports T2's price umbrella, while the 10-point downward revision from unexpected inference cost overruns is direct evidence for T1 (inference is real, volatile COGS). ARR per megawatt reportedly rising from $16M to ~$60M in under a year shows the operational-efficiency lever T5/T6 predict labs will compete on. Value/CI refer to the 2025 projection.

verification.reasoning:
CORE NUMBER CONFIRMED, CI TOO WIDE, METRIC STRING PARTLY REFUTED.

(1) The 2025 figure is faithfully represented and well-triangulated. Primary is The Information (Sri Muppidi, Jan 22, 2026), paywalled, but three independent renderings agree: Anthropic lowered its FY2025 gross margin projection to ~40%, from a >50% target (a 10-point cut), after inference costs on Google/Amazon cloud came in ~23% above plan. Investing.com (Jan 22, 2026) gives 40%/50%/23% explicitly. BigGo (Feb 25, 2026) gives "only 40% in 2025, still 10 percentage points below its previously set target" plus 2025 inference COGS growing >3x to $2.7B. Zitron independently echoes the 23% overrun. Decisive check: $2.7B inference COGS against the separately-reported $4.5B FY2025 revenue reconciles to exactly 40% gross margin. Value, unit (percent gross margin), and period (FY2025 projection, reported Jan 2026) are all faithful.

(2) CI is under-confident. Given four consistent renderings plus arithmetic closure with independently-reported revenue and COGS, 33-47 is wider than the evidence warrants. Residual uncertainty is only rounding of "roughly 40%" (±2) and definitional variation in what Anthropic books into COGS (free-tier serving, reserved-capacity underutilization) (±2). Tighten to 36-44.

(3) The 2026 half of the metric string is materially wrong and must be corrected. "SemiAnalysis estimates blended margin mid-60s%, API >80%" is NOT what SemiAnalysis says. On targeted re-read of the May 1, 2026 piece, a blended mid-60s margin and an API margin >80% are both explicitly ABSENT. What SemiAnalysis actually states is that gross margins ON INFERENCE INFRASTRUCTURE rose "from 38% to over 70%" as ARR went $9B to $44B — a narrower quantity that excludes free-tier serving, cloud markups, and unutilized reserved capacity. The corpus's own sibling claim mc-09 states this correctly at 70%; rv-13 garbles one real number into two numbers that do not exist. The notes' "ARR per megawatt rising from $16M to ~$60M" is likewise not present in SemiAnalysis or any source I could reach — treat as unverified.

(4) "2026 reporting shows sharp improvement" overstates and partly inverts the record. The Yahoo/PitchBook source (Harrison Rolfes, June 10, 2026) is correctly quoted on $0.71 (Q1 2026) and $0.56 (Q2 2026) compute spend per revenue dollar, but $0.71 implies ~29% margin — WORSE than the 40% FY2025 projection, not better. Only the PROJECTED Q2 $0.56 (implying ~44%) exceeds 2025. The "44%" is the author's own 1-minus-0.56 derivation, not a company disclosure. Further, compute spend per revenue dollar is not gross margin: it includes training compute, which the thesis itself classifies as fixed R&D rather than COGS, so 1-minus-x understates true gross margin. Honest framing is "deteriorated in Q1 2026, projected to recover to ~44% in Q2," not "sharp improvement to mid-60s."

(5) Thesis impact is asymmetric. The T1 leg (inference is real, volatile COGS that scales with usage) is STRENGTHENED — a 23% cost overrun and a 10-point margin miss on a projection made near year-end is clean, direct evidence. The T5/T6 leg (operational-efficiency lever) is WEAKER than the claim advertises, because the mid-60s/>80% figures supporting it are not real and Q1 2026 shows deterioration before recovery.

(6) Housekeeping: rv-13 and mc-10 are the same underlying fact from the same Information reporting (mc-10's source is dated 2025 but is the same Sri Muppidi Jan 2026 story under an alternate headline). Both sit in the corpus; weighting them as independent evidence would double-count.

Verdict is adjust rather than confirm because, although value/unit/period survive, the claim as written would not survive a hostile reviewer: the SemiAnalysis attribution is checkable and false, and the CI is under-confident. Value stays 40.

HEADLINE NUMBER SURVIVES HOSTILE REVIEW. I hunted for alternative estimates, later corrections, and denominator games. On the stated scope (FY2025 projected gross margin), value=40 is exactly and consistently reported by every source I could reach, and I found no competing estimate and no subsequent correction.

Corroboration (all tracing to one Information report, but rendered identically across outlets):
- Investing.com (2026-01-22): Anthropic "now projects roughly a 40% gross profit margin in 2025," 10pp below prior internal estimate; cloud infra costs "climbed about 23% more than anticipated." Exact match to the claim's 50%->40% and ~23% overrun.
- BigGo Finance (2026-02-25): Anthropic 2024 actual -94%, 2025 projected 40%, 2025 target 50%; Anthropic 2025 inference cost ~$2.7B (>3x YoY). Also gives the OpenAI comparator (2024 40%, 2025 33%, vs 46% forecast) consistent with sibling claims mc-11/rv-03.
- The Information's own article snippet: "projected it would generate a 40% gross profit margin ... in 2025, ... 10 percentage points lower than its earlier optimistic expectations."
- Trajectory anchors bracket it cleanly: SemiAnalysis puts blended GM at -94% (2024) and mid-60s (Q2 2026). 40% for FY2025 sits on that line.

Timing detail that STRENGTHENS the number: The Information says Anthropic projected this "last month" relative to a 2026-01-22 article, i.e. a December 2025 projection carrying ~11 months of actuals. This is closer to an estimate than a forecast, which is why I did not widen the CI despite it being single-primary-sourced.

WHY I STILL LEFT THE CI AT 33-47 RATHER THAN TIGHTENING. The Information's exact wording is a 40% margin "from selling AI to businesses and application developers" - arguably a segment margin, not company blended. That matters: backing out SemiAnalysis's Q2 2026 figures (API GM >80% on ~75-85% of revenue, blended mid-60s) implies the residual ~20% of revenue carries a near-zero or negative gross margin. If a similar low-margin drag existed in 2025, true blended FY2025 GM could sit several points below 40. That live downside keeps the 33 floor honest. Countervailing: consumer subs are only ~5% of revenue, and secondaries explicitly place the 40% in the same blended series as 2024's -94%. Net: 33-47 is right; I would not tighten and would not shift the point estimate.

MATERIAL PROBLEMS FOUND - IN THE METRIC STRING AND SOURCE LIST, NOT THE VALUE. The parent should fix these even though the verdict is confirm:

1. WRONG SOURCE FOR THE 2026 FIGURES. "SemiAnalysis estimates blended margin mid-60s%, API >80%" and the "ARR per megawatt $16M -> ~$60M" note do NOT come from either cited source, nor from the May 2026 SemiAnalysis piece cited in sibling claim mc-09 (that piece says something different: "gross margins on their inference infrastructure have increased from 38% to over 70%" - an inference-infrastructure margin, not blended). They come from a SemiAnalysis piece absent from the source list: "Anthropic 3Q26 Profit Over $1B: The Anthropic IPO Financials Sneak Peak" (2026-07-07). The substance checks out against that piece and its aggregator summaries; the attribution does not. Add the source.

2. THE $0.71 -> $0.56 SERIES IS A BAD GROSS-MARGIN PROXY AND SHOULD BE DEMOTED. The Yahoo source (Harrison Rolfes, 2026-06-10 - an opinion/valuation piece, not primary reporting) derives "roughly 44%" as simply 1 - 0.56. Arithmetic check: 1 - 0.71 implies a 29% margin for Q1 2026, which would be a DETERIORATION versus FY2025's 40% and sits ~35pts below SemiAnalysis's mid-60s blended for the adjacent quarter. The two 2026 series bundled into this one claim contradict each other unless "compute spend per revenue dollar" includes training compute and/or reserved-capacity commitments that never enter COGS - which is almost certainly the case. So the claim's "2026 reporting shows sharp improvement" is doing work on a metric that is not 1 minus gross margin. Compounding it: the $0.56 is explicitly a PROJECTION, not an actual - and this is a company whose last published projection had to be cut 10 points because costs came in 23% over plan. Recommend dropping the Yahoo derivation or flagging it as cash-compute-to-revenue, not COGS.

3. DUPLICATE CLAIM / DOUBLE-COUNTING RISK. rv-13 (value 40, CI 33-47) and mc-10 "Anthropic company-wide gross margin, 2025 projection" (value 40, CI 34-46) are the same underlying fact from the same primary reporting, both currently in the claim set. Only one should carry weight in thesis scoring.

4. STALENESS ON A LOAD-BEARING CLAIM. As of today (2026-07-22) the operative number is not 40%. SemiAnalysis's July 2026 estimate is mid-60s blended with API >80%, alongside ~$1B GAAP EBIT expected in Q3 2026. Any downstream synthesis that reads "Anthropic gross margin = 40%" understates present economics by roughly 25 points.

THESIS IMPLICATION (direction of the error matters). Corrected for staleness, this evidence is stronger for T2/T6 and weaker for the pessimistic reading of T1 than the claim as written suggests. API gross margin >80% is direct evidence of the scarcity price umbrella; ARR per megawatt going $16M -> $60M in nine months is exactly the operational-efficiency lever T5/T6 predict; and SemiAnalysis explicitly books training/R&D below the gross-profit line, which is the T1 fixed-vs-marginal split stated as accounting fact. The genuine T1 support here is narrower than the note implies: it is the volatility (a 23% cost overrun forcing a 10-point revision), not the level.
