verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND AND VERIFIED (not just the newsroom page — the actual SEC filings).

I retrieved from EDGAR (CIK 0001045810) both (a) the 8-K filed 2026-05-20, accession 0001045810-26-000051, Exhibit 99.1 = the earnings press release, and (b) the 10-Q for the period ended 2026-04-26, accession 0001045810-26-000052, filed 2026-05-20. Both are authentic and consistent.

WHAT THE PRIMARY SOURCE SAYS, VERBATIM
- Press release bullet: "Record Data Center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92% from a year ago."
- Highlights section: "First-quarter revenue was a record $75.2 billion, up 21% from the previous quarter and up 92% from a year ago."
- 10-Q, Revenue by Market Platform table (in millions): Data Center 75,246 (Q1 FY27) / 62,314 (Q4 FY26) / 39,112 (Q1 FY26); Hyperscale 37,869 / 33,814 / 17,599; ACIE 37,377 / 28,500 / 21,513; Edge Computing 6,369 / 5,813 / 4,950; Total 81,615 / 68,127 / 44,062.
- Quarter end date: April 26, 2026. Total revenue $81,615M, +20% QoQ, +85% YoY. Q2 FY27 guidance "$91.0 billion, plus or minus 2%" with "NVIDIA is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in its outlook."

So value, period, unit, and every supporting figure in the notes are faithfully represented. My own arithmetic on the filed numbers reproduces 92.4% YoY and 20.8% QoQ, matching the rounded 92%/21%. Grade A is deserved on sourcing.

TRAP I CHECKED AND CLEARED: Q1 FY2027 is the quarter Nvidia CHANGED its market-platform reporting. The 10-Q footnote reads: "In the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, we changed our presentation of revenue by market platform and the comparable periods have been recast." The old platforms (Data Center, Gaming, ProViz, Automotive, OEM & Other) became just two (Data Center [Hyperscale + ACIE], Edge Computing). This could have made the 92% YoY apples-to-oranges. It does not. I pulled the originally-issued prior press releases: Q4 FY26 (8-K 2026-02-25) reported "Data Center revenue of $62.3 billion" and Q1 FY26 (8-K 2025-05-28) reported "Data Center revenue of $39.1 billion" — identical to the recast 62,314 and 39,112. Edge Computing is purely the old Gaming+ProViz+Auto+OEM bucket (Q1 FY26: 4,950, and 39,112 + 4,950 = 44,062 total). The Data Center line was untouched by the recast, so YoY and QoQ are clean.

THE ONE DEFECT: THE CI IS NOT HONEST ABOUT SOURCE UNCERTAINTY
The claim asserts an 80% CI of [74.9, 75.5], i.e. a 20% chance the true value falls outside a ±$300M band. That is fabricated humility. This is not an estimate, a survey, or a modeled quantity — it is a figure disclosed to the nearest million dollars in a filed 10-Q: $75,246M. There is no sampling error, no imputation, no third-party reconstruction. The interval implies uncertainty that demonstrably does not exist, and it spans values (74.9, 75.5) that the filing positively excludes. On the primary-source lens, which asks specifically whether the CI reflects the source's uncertainty, it fails. Corrected: value 75.246, CI [75.24, 75.25] (width reflects only the rounding of the filed $-millions figure). Residual restatement risk is real but negligible and would not move an 80% interval. This is a low-stakes fix — no downstream conclusion changes — but it is a genuine misrepresentation and the fix is strictly better.

TWO NOTE-LEVEL CORRECTIONS THAT MATTER FOR THE LOAD-BEARING USE
1. Terminology: "Data center SEGMENT revenue" is wrong under GAAP. Nvidia's reportable segments in this 10-Q remain Compute & Networking ($74,550M) and Graphics ($7,065M). "Data Center" is a market-platform disaggregation, not an ASC 280 reportable segment. The number is right; the label is imprecise.
2. The notes' gloss — "compute shipments are still nearly doubling YoY" — overstates what the source supports. The same press release says: "Under the previous sub-markets, Data Center compute revenue was a record $60.4 billion, up 77% from a year ago and up 18% sequentially. Data Center networking revenue was a record $14.8 billion, up 199% from a year ago and up 35% sequentially." The 92% headline is materially inflated by networking (which nearly tripled). Compute specifically grew 77% YoY / 18% QoQ. For a thesis about inference COGS and compute supply, that distinction is load-bearing: the compute line is decelerating sequentially (18% QoQ) faster than the headline suggests.

SUPPORTING CONTEXT THAT STRENGTHENS THE THESIS USE
The 10-Q states "No shipments of Data Center Hopper products to China occurred during the quarter, compared with $4.6 billion in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026," and Q2 guidance assumes zero China DC compute. Stripping the year-ago China base, ex-China Data Center growth is roughly +118% YoY (75,246 / 34,512), so the "supply added at maximum industrial rate and still absorbed" reading is if anything understated by the 92% figure.

HOSTILE CAVEATS ON THE PROXY (not defects in the claim, but limits on its inferential weight)
Revenue recognized is not deployed inference capacity: ~$14.8B of the $75.2B is networking rather than accelerators; there is a lag from shipment to production serving; roughly half is hyperscale, much of it for training and first-party workloads rather than merchant inference; and a non-trivial slice of demand comes from counterparties Nvidia has equity or commercial entanglements with. The claim is a good directional supply proxy, but it should not be read as a clean measure of US frontier-inference capacity.

CURRENCY CHECK: as of 2026-07-22 this is the latest reported quarter — EDGAR shows no 10-Q after 2026-05-20, and Q2 FY27 (ending late July 2026) has not been reported. The period label is current.

SECONDARY SOURCE NOTE: the CNBC URL in the claim returned HTTP 403 to me (bot block), so I could neither confirm nor impeach it. Immaterial — the primary source fully carries the claim, and the CNBC citation is redundant.

BOTTOM LINE: value, period, unit, and sources confirm exactly against the primary filing. Adjusting solely to replace an invented ±$300M interval with the filing's actual precision, and flagging the "segment" mislabel and the "compute nearly doubling" overstatement in the notes.

VALUE: confirmed exactly, at the highest available evidentiary standard. I went hunting for a contradicting figure and could not find one. Nvidia's own Q1 FY2027 release (quarter ended 2026-04-26, reported 2026-05-20) states "Record Data Center revenue of $75.2 billion, up 92% from a year ago" and "up 21% from the previous quarter"; the 10-Q for the same period reports Data Center market-platform revenue of $75,246 million against total revenue of $81,615 million (Compute & Networking segment $74,550M, Graphics $7,065M). Every secondary source I could reach (CNBC, Yahoo Finance, HPCwire, Storage Newsletter, Nasdaq wire, Blockonomi) repeats $75.2B with no variant estimate. Internal cross-checks all close: 75.2/1.92 = $39.2B ≈ Q1 FY2026 DC revenue of $39.1B; 75.2/62.3 (Q4 FY2026 DC) = +20.7% ≈ "up 21%"; 81.6/68.1 = +19.8% ≈ "up 20%". This is an audited GAAP figure with no plausible alternative, no restatement (Q2 FY2027 has not yet been reported as of 2026-07-22, so no later correction can exist), and the CI of 74.9–75.5 comfortably brackets it. If anything the CI is too wide — 75.2–75.3 would be defensible. Grade A is right.

WHERE THE CLAIM IS NEVERTHELESS MISLEADING (does not change the number, but the parent should fix the note): the "nearly doubling" framing is inflated by networking, not compute. The same release breaks Data Center into compute revenue of $60.4B (+77% YoY, +18% QoQ) and networking revenue of $14.8B (+199% YoY, +35% QoQ). Networking's near-tripling is an attach-rate shift (NVLink/Spectrum-X scale-up content per rack), not more inference silicon. The claim's note — "compute shipments are still nearly doubling YoY... supply is being added at maximum industrial rate" — overstates the compute-supply signal by roughly 15 percentage points of growth. The correct supply-side proxy for the thesis is Data Center *compute* at $60.4B, +77% YoY, +18% QoQ. I recommend the parent add that as a companion claim rather than lean on the $75.2B segment total. Related: revenue dollars are not FLOPs; generational ASP mix (GB300/Rubin) means dollar growth and deployed-capacity growth diverge, in an unknown direction.

REVENUE-QUALITY CRITIQUES I TESTED AND LARGELY REJECTED: (a) Goldman Sachs (James Schneider) has warned that Nvidia's equity investments in customers such as OpenAI resemble "circular revenue" that could distort the top line, and a widely circulated Substack alleges $10–12B of "uncollected circular revenue" embedded in receivables. The balance sheet does not support the receivables version: AR of $40,710M on $81,615M quarterly revenue implies DSO of ~45 days, at or below Nvidia's historical ~50-day range, i.e. collections are not deteriorating. The circular-financing concern remains a legitimate question about the *durability* and arm's-length quality of demand, but it is not an argument that $75.2B was misstated. (b) Cherry-picked period / China one-off: rejected, and in fact the opposite. Q1 China revenue including Hong Kong was only $4,550M of $81,615M, Nvidia states it has generated no revenue yet under the new H200 China licenses, and Q2 guidance of $91.0B ±2% explicitly assumes zero China Data Center compute. A right-skewed interval (e.g. [2.10, 2.75]) would be marginally more honest, but not materially better — the point estimate is what SemiAnalysis actually published for March.

CORROBORATING CONTEXT IN NOTES — verified. "All capacity coming online until August to September 2026 has already been booked" (notes say "through Sept 2026" — accurate). "H100s are getting renewed at the exact same rate they were signed at 2-3 years ago and some H100 contracts are being renewed for 4 years though 2028" (notes' "2-3yr terms into 2028" is a slightly garbled compression of this, but directionally right). Net: the number, period, unit, and interval are all traceable to and faithful to the primary source; the source itself is the index publisher; the residual uncertainty runs to the upside. Grade B is appropriate (single-source index, survey-based, no published numeric band in text). Confirm.

VALUE SURVIVES HOSTILE REVIEW. The headline number is verbatim from the cited source: SemiAnalysis (2026-04-02) states "H100 1-year GPU rental contract pricing has shot up almost 40% from a low of $1.70/hr/GPU in October 2025 to $2.35/hr/GPU by March 2026." INDEPENDENT TRIANGULATION (the decisive test). Silicon Data runs a separate commercial neocloud H100 rental index (ticker SDH100RT), constructed from transaction data and unrelated to SemiAnalysis. Its readings: $2.00 (Dec 9, 2025) -> $2.20 (Jan 6, 2026) -> $2.63 (Apr 1) -> $2.47 trough (Apr 8) -> $2.59 (Apr 30) -> $2.76 peak (May 30) -> $2.75 (early June, +12.7% trailing 3mo) -> ~$2.72 (Jul 19). Direction, timing (Oct/Dec 2025 trough, Q1 2026 inflection), and magnitude are all independently reproduced. This is unusually strong for a B-grade claim; I would grade it A-.

WHAT I FOUND AGAINST IT (material, but hits the framing, not the number):

1. SOURCE-INTERNAL ARITHMETIC CONFLICT. The same article says pricing "broke above $2/hr for a 1y contract by late January, and then shot up 15-20% by mid-to-late February vs end January and is set to rise another 15-20% month-on-month by the end of March." $2.00 x 1.175 = $2.35 -- i.e. $2.35 is the mid/late-FEBRUARY reading, and the article's own text projects end-March at ~$2.70-2.80, outside the claim's CI high of 2.60. This is a real defect in labeling $2.35 as the "March 2026" value. It resolves in the claim's favor only because Silicon Data caps it: neocloud ON-DEMAND was $2.63 on Apr 1, so a $2.75 one-year contract would price above spot, which is implausible. Best read: $2.35 is a Feb/early-March observation drifting to ~$2.40-2.50 by end-March. Within CI either way, but the CI's upper half is doing more work than the claim admits.

The headline value is unaffected, but the narrative arc in the notes is not supportable as stated and should be rewritten as within-neocloud.

3. THE FORWARD CURVE CUTS AGAINST THE THESIS USE. This is the strongest contradicting evidence I found. As of July 19, 2026 the H100 forward curve is in BACKWARDATION: spot ~$2.72, 36-month term ~$2.38 (-13%), going "nearly flat beyond 15 months" at $2.38-2.44, explicitly pricing "newer chip generations displacing older ones." The market is pricing the tightening as cyclical and reverting, not structural. The claim's notes assert this "shows the umbrella has NOT collapsed as of mid-2026" -- true as a spot statement, but the traded curve says participants expect no upside and mild decay. Anyone using sd-09 as evidence for a durable inference-scarcity umbrella should be forced to also report the backwardation.

4. CONTESTED CAUSAL ATTRIBUTION. SemiAnalysis attributes tightening to inelastic agentic/coding demand. Silicon Data's Jan 2026 analysis of the same inflection attributes it to hyperscalers pulling inventory into long-term contracts, year-end training deadlines, and budget-utilization cycles -- supply-side and calendar effects. Add SemiAnalysis's own June 2026 pieces on US grid constraints and the DDR5/RAM price grind. The price signal is real; the "demand for frontier inference exceeds supply" reading of it is one hypothesis among several.

5. MINOR: mid-2026 is flat-to-softening, not still-climbing. The neocloud index peaked at $2.76 (May 30) and the live SDH100RT page currently shows $2.53, while the Jul 17 futures post cites $2.72 on Jul 19 -- Silicon Data is internally inconsistent by ~7% at the same moment, which is itself a caution about index precision. Either way, levels remain ~45-60% above the Oct 2025 low, so the reversal has held.

CONCLUSION: confirm. Value 2.35 is verbatim-sourced and independently triangulated to ~1%; CI [2.10, 2.60] contains the true March 2026 figure under every reading I could construct. I considered adjusting the point estimate to ~2.40 and the CI to [2.20, 2.65] to absorb the Feb-vs-March labeling ambiguity, but the shift is immaterial relative to index construction noise (Silicon Data disagrees with itself by more than that). Keep the number; rewrite notes items 2 and 3 before this claim is used as load-bearing support for the marginal-cost thesis.

I downloaded and rendered it (local copy: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kushaldsouza-Documents-Thinking-chipandadmarketresearch/d49df9c4-fddb-4400-b13e-1a82c709e63f/scratchpad/puct_55999_168.pdf).

WHAT THE PRIMARY ACTUALLY SAYS (slide 6, titled "Large Load Interconnection Requests as of October 14, 2025"):
- Total large load seeking interconnection by 2030: 205,400 MW. Key takeaway box: "ERCOT is tracking approximately 205 GW of Large Loads seeking interconnection (compared to 56 GW in September 2024) of which ~70% are data centers."
- The "Large Loads by Project Type" pie gives the exact split (denominator 202,303 MW): Data Center 70.6% = 142,782 MW; None/unclassified 13.0% = 26,260 MW; Crypto 10.0% = 20,223 MW; Industrial 4.2% = 8,451 MW; Data Center/Crypto 1.3% = 2,569 MW; Hydrogen 1.0% = 2,018 MW.

So ERCOT's own data-center number is 142.8 GW, not 143.5 GW. The 143.5 is the essayist's arithmetic on the rounded takeaway (205 x 0.70 = 143.5) rather than a figure ERCOT reports. It is high by 0.5% versus pure Data Center and low by 1.3% versus Data Center + Data Center/Crypto (145.4 GW). Period ("as of October 2025") and unit (GW of interconnection requests) are faithful; the snapshot date is precisely Oct 14, 2025.

ERCOT's own convention explicitly states it "does not count instantaneous loads for demand records" and uses integrated system load for the full hour — on that basis the official all-time record is 85,559 MW (HE 5pm, Aug 20, 2024). So 85.9 is ~0.4% above ERCOT's official record but is faithful to the source cited. Critically, the record still stood as of Oct 2025: ERCOT's summer 2025 peak was ~83.9 GW (Aug 18, 2025). The 1.7x ratio survives either way (143.5/85.9 = 1.67; 142.8/85.6 = 1.67).

THE CI IS THE REAL PROBLEM. The metric is a census, not an estimate — ERCOT reports it to the megawatt on a stated date, so there is no sampling uncertainty. The claim's notes say the 120–160 band "reflects that requests overstate real projects," which silently swaps the estimand. If the metric is "requests," a 10th-percentile of 120 GW has zero support in the primary. If the metric is "real projects," then 143.5 is wildly too high: the same slide's project-status table shows that of the 205,400 MW, 114,246 MW (55.6%) is "No Studies Submitted" and 70,162 MW (34.2%) is merely "Under ERCOT Review." Only 13,491 MW has planning studies approved, 2,267 MW approved to energize, and 5,234 MW is actually energized — i.e. ~21 GW of all large load, roughly 15 GW data-center-attributable, has cleared any real screen. A CI that straddles neither quantity honestly is worse than no CI.

The genuine source ambiguity is narrow and asymmetric: floor ~137.5 GW (pure DC less the ~5.3 GW DC share of already-energized/approved load, if "requests" means strictly pending); base 142.8 GW (ERCOT's stated DC figure); 145.4 GW including the DC/Crypto hybrid; up to ~164 GW if the 26.3 GW unclassified "None" bucket is allocated at the 81.1% DC share of classified load. Hence 138–160 at 80%, centered on 142.8.

TWO FURTHER HOSTILE POINTS.
(1) Source #2 (siliconreport.com) does not support this claim at all — I fetched it and it contains no ERCOT queue figure and no ERCOT peak-load figure. It only backs the notes' "four to seven years in N. Virginia, Phoenix, Dallas" line (attributed there to Sightline Climate via Bloomberg). The claim rests entirely on one essay, which rests on one filing. Grade B is generous for citation depth even though the underlying filing is impeccable.
(2) Interpretive tension with the thesis role. ERCOT is the fastest-interconnecting large US grid (connect-and-manage; historically no formal load-side study gate) — the WiP article itself makes this point. Its queue is enormous partly because entry is nearly free, so a 1.7x queue-to-peak ratio measures demand for optionality more than it measures grid constraint severity. Corroborating this: a second ERCOT primary I verified (Large Load Update filed April 1, 2026) reports ~410 GW as of March 26, 2026 at ~87% data centers (~357 GW), and third-party queue trackers show ~466 GW at ~90% DC by June 2026. A metric that triples in eight months to ~5x all-time system peak is unscreened by construction. This does not refute the claim as stated — it is correctly dated and correctly caveated — but a load-bearing use of it to establish "power, not chips, is the binding constraint" should lean on the interconnection wait-time evidence and the ~21 GW of studies-approved load, not on the headline queue GW.

VERDICT: adjust. The number, period and unit are faithfully represented within ~0.5%, but the primary supports a tighter and better-anchored value (142.8 GW) and the stated CI does not honestly reflect source uncertainty — it encodes project-realization risk under the label of measurement uncertainty, and its lower bound is unsupported by the filing.

VALUE SURVIVES; CI AND FRAMING DO NOT. I traced the number to primary source rather than the secondary citations.

WHAT THE PRIMARY SOURCE ACTUALLY SAYS. Works in Progress (Chris Gillett, 22 Jun 2026) is the origin of the exact wording ("Across ERCOT, there were 143.5 gigawatts of data centers seeking to connect as of October 2025. DENOMINATOR ALSO CHECKS: ERCOT's 2024 all-time-records page shows 85,931 MW on 20 Aug 2024 at 4:45pm. 143.5/85.9 = 1.67x, matching the "1.7x" in the notes. So no contradicting estimate for October 2025 exists — I looked and found none. Refutation is off the table.

MATERIAL PROBLEM 1 — WRONG TIME HORIZON (the real contradiction). The 205.4 GW is NOT pending near-term load. ERCOT's chart is titled "Actual and Projected Large Load Growth 2022-2030" and 205,400 MW is the CUMULATIVE total requested to be energized BY 2030. The 2025 column total is only 13,700 MW. So the defensible reading is "143.5 GW of data-center capacity requesting connection at some point through 2030," not "143.5 GW pending today." The claim's note ("One grid alone has 1.7x its all-time peak load in pending data-center requests") invites exactly the near-term misread a hostile reviewer would attack.

MATERIAL PROBLEM 2 — REALIZATION RATE. ERCOT's own status table for the 205.4 GW: "No Studies Submitted" 114,246 MW (56%); "Under ERCOT Review" 70,162 MW (34%); "Planning Studies Approved" 13,491 MW (6.6%); "Approved to Energize but Not Operational" 2,267 MW (1.1%); "Observed Energized" 5,234 MW (2.5%). Roughly 90% had not cleared even a planning study. ERCOT VP Kristi Hobbs: "We don't expect all of those will materialize." Independent analysis puts ERCOT's realization rate at ~3.3% (7.5 GW connected against a 226 GW pipeline).

MATERIAL PROBLEM 3 — CI IS MISCALIBRATED ON EITHER READING (this drives the adjust). [120, 160] is a +/-14% band around what is an administrative tally ERCOT publishes, not an estimate. Genuine measurement uncertainty is far tighter: 70% x 202.3 = 141.6; 70% x 205.4 = 143.8; 72.9% x 205.4 = 149.7 (upper end if the "Data Center/Crypto" hybrid slice is folded in). Hence corrected CI [140, 152]. Conversely, the claim's note says the CI "reflects that requests overstate real projects" — but if that were the CI's job it would need to sit near [5, 60], an order of magnitude lower and far wider. The stated band does neither job; it splits the difference and is therefore wrong under both interpretations.

MATERIAL PROBLEM 4 — SECOND SOURCE DOES NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM. I fetched the Silicon Report piece: it contains no ERCOT queue figure and no ERCOT peak-load figure at all (its ERCOT mention is only that ERCOT "runs a comparatively fast interconnection process"). It is padding. The ERCOT/PUC filing should replace it.

MATERIAL PROBLEM 5 — STALENESS, DIRECTION FAVORS THE THESIS. The October 2025 snapshot is now 9 months old and understates badly. ERCOT, "Item 9: Interconnection and Grid Analysis Update" (13 Apr 2026), as of 26 March 2026: "approximately 410 GW of Large Loads seeking interconnection, of which ~87% are data centers. This is an increase of 178 GW since the end of 2025." That is ~357 GW of data-center requests, ~2.5x the claimed figure and ~4.1x the all-time peak. Intermediate waypoints: 226 GW total at 77% data centers (Nov 2025, Latitude Media); 233 GW at >70% (year-end 2025, Utility Dive). If the parent wants the claim to speak to today rather than to October 2025, re-date it to March 2026 with value ~357 GW (CI ~340-375) — same argument, far stronger.

MINOR — DENOMINATOR AMBIGUITY. ERCOT's own April 2026 press release states the all-time peak is 85,508 MW (10 Aug 2023), not 85,931 MW (20 Aug 2024). Likely a demand-vs-net-load definitional split. Immaterial (ratio 1.68x vs 1.67x). Separately, ERCOT reportedly hit ~87,533 MW on 21 Jul 2026, so the denominator itself is drifting up.

SIDE FACTS IN NOTES SPOT-CHECKED. "~2,300 GW of all generation/storage in US queues" checks out: LBNL Queued Up 2025 Edition (pub. 15 Dec 2025, data through EOY 2024) reports ~2,290 GW active, down from ~2,600 GW — note the queue SHRANK, driven by FERC Order 2023 withdrawals, which mildly cuts against a monotonic "queues ever-worsening" narrative. The 55-months-by-2023 figure is WiP's rendering of LBNL duration data and is in the right neighborhood.

NET EFFECT ON THE THESIS. The load-bearing inference ("power, not chips, is the binding constraint gating supply catch-up") survives and is in fact strengthened by the March 2026 data. But it does not rest on the request count, which is ~90% unstudied. It rests better on the physical-delivery side of the same ERCOT decks: only 5.2 GW energized and 2.3 GW approved-to-energize as of Oct 2025 against a 205 GW ask, plus the 4-7 year interconnection waits. Recommend the parent lean on the delivered-vs-requested gap rather than the raw queue headline, which is the number a hostile reviewer will most easily discredit as marketing-inflated. Grade B is right — the number is A-grade accurate but B-grade probative.

PRIMARY-SOURCE LENS. OpenAI is private, so no filing exists; the "primary source" is necessarily journalist-reported investor communications, and grade B is right for that. I traced the chain rather than trusting the cited URLs (CNBC and DCD both return 403).

WHAT HOLDS. The February number itself is faithfully reported. PYMNTS (Feb 22, 2026), relaying CNBC, confirms the unit is cumulative, not annual: OpenAI "told investors its compute costs could approach $600 billion by the decade's end." PROBLEM 1 — THE METRIC'S PARENTHETICAL IS A SCOPE CONFLATION, AND IT IS THE PART DOING THE RHETORICAL WORK. The metric reads "(reset from $1.4T of headline commitments)," implying an ~$800B cut. The sources contradict this. WSJ (July 22, 2026, via Yahoo) states the compute figure "is also separate from the $1.4 trillion in infrastructure commitments previously discussed by Chief Executive Sam Altman." PYMNTS likewise treats them as distinct measures, noting the $600B disclosure came "months after" Altman's $1.4T statement. The two are different denominators: $1.4T = total infrastructure commitments across full contract terms (~8 years, ~30 GW, extending past 2030); $600B = compute spend through 2030 only. Some outlets did make the subtraction (The Tech Buzz, Feb 20: "Slashes Compute Spending Target to $600B, Down From $1.4T"), but that is media conflation downstream of the disclosure, not the disclosure. The claim inherits it. This matters because the claim is load-bearing precisely as a capex-discipline counter-signal — an $800B "cut" that did not happen is what makes it persuasive.

PROBLEM 2 — A PARALLEL FEBRUARY LEAK ALREADY RAN HIGHER, NOT LOWER. The Information (Feb 21, 2026, one day after CNBC) reported $665B cumulative for "training and operating AI models" through 2030 (~$440B training alone), alongside cash burn of $25B (2026) and $57B (2027) and 2030 revenue of ~$282B. So within the same week, an adjacent-scope figure was 11% ABOVE the $600B. The "$600B = discipline" reading was fragile at the moment of publication, not just in hindsight.

PROBLEM 3 — THE VALUE IS SUPERSEDED AS OF TODAY. Today is July 22, 2026. WSJ today: "OpenAI's Planned Cloud Spending Hits $750 Billion as Computing Efforts Ramp Up." The Yahoo relay is explicit and like-for-like on the same series: OpenAI "has raised its projected computing-power spending through 2030 to about $750 billion," up from "approximately $600 billion earlier in 2026." Independently relayed by Quartz, Blockspace Media, Crypto Briefing, and Tech in Asia. The claim's note hedges this as "one later report claims re-raise toward $750B" — that hedge is now stale; it is confirmed by the originating outlet, same day as the thesis essay.

CI HONESTY. The stated 480–800 band does contain 750, so it was not dishonest — it was appropriately wide for a contested target, and that width deserves credit. But a point estimate of 600 now puts OpenAI's actual current stated plan at roughly the 94th percentile of the claimed distribution, and the CI floor of 480 has no live support at all. For a claim evaluated against a July 20, 2026 thesis, anchoring on 600 misrepresents the state of the world.

CORRECTION. Value 750 (WSJ, July 22, 2026 — the operative figure, same scope and horizon as the Feb number). CI80 640–880, reflecting: (a) scope fuzziness of roughly ±10% across how outlets render it — WSJ says "cloud spending," Yahoo "computing-power spending," Quartz "AI infrastructure spending," The Information "training and operating" — which alone spans ~$665–825B; (b) single-outlet sourcing with no filing behind it; (c) demonstrated volatility of +25% in five months, with genuine two-sided revision risk given the documented revenue and WAU shortfalls. I set this slightly wider than a naive band because the target has moved twice in a year and the underlying quantity is a plan, not an actual.

IMPLICATION FOR THE PARENT THESIS. The February reset should be retained as a historical waypoint and the demand-side evidence (missed revenue targets, missed 1B-WAU, Friar's warning, the capped Abilene expansion) survives intact and is well-sourced. But this claim should NOT be used as evidence that capex discipline is currently eroding the price umbrella from the demand side. The Feb reset proved to be a trough, not a trend: the plan re-accelerated 25% within five months, and the "$1.4T cut to $600B" framing that made it look like retrenchment was never what the sources said.

CONTRADICTION LENS — the February number is real but has been superseded by a confirmed later correction, and the claim's narrative role is materially undermined.

WHAT SURVIVES. The Feb 2026 fact is solid and better-sourced than grade B implies. CNBC (2026-02-20) is the originating report: OpenAI told investors it targets "roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, trying to clarify its plans after touting a $1.4 trillion figure." Critically, Reuters did NOT merely relay CNBC — it confirmed with "a source familiar with the matter" the same day (reuters.com/technology/openai-sees-compute-spend-around-600-billion-by-2030-cnbc-reports-2026-02-20), and the story propagated through US News, Economic Times, CGTN with the ~$280B 2030 revenue target attached. So value=600 is accurate for what was said in February.

MATERIAL CONFLICT 1 — SUPERSEDED, TODAY. WSJ reporting dated July 22, 2026 (i.e. today, the thesis date) says OpenAI raised projected compute spending through 2030 to about $750B. Yahoo Finance quotes it directly: "OpenAI has raised its projected computing-power spending through 2030 to about $750 billion... up from roughly $600 billion earlier this year." This is not a different quantity being confused — the reporting outlet itself makes the apples-to-apples comparison to the Feb figure. Corroborated across TradingKey, Crypto Briefing, Remio, WalletInvestor, TechBooky, StartupFortune: +$150B driven by new cloud deals plus Project Camellia, a ~$20B self-built data center near Savannah, Effingham County GA, eventually drawing 3.2 GW — the first facility OpenAI will design and build itself rather than lease. MATERIAL CONFLICT 2 — FRAMING / SCOPE MISMATCH. The metric label "(reset from $1.4T of headline commitments)" conflates two different quantities. Per TradingKey, Friar's $600B was a course-correction/clarification of Altman's $1.4T, not an $800B cut; Yahoo explicitly describes $750B as separate from "previously discussed infrastructure commitments of $1.4 trillion and a $1.15 trillion estimate for hardware and cloud agreements through 2035." $1.4T = total infrastructure commitments over full contract terms extending past 2030; $600B/$750B = compute spend through 2030 only. The genuine cut component was narrower (e.g. the cancelled 600MW Abilene expansion capping OpenAI at ~1.2GW — which Oracle partially denied, so the claim's "reported" hedge is correctly placed). The parenthetical should be dropped or restated.

IMPLICATION FOR THE THESIS (most important). This claim is load-bearing precisely as "the key COUNTER-signal on timing" — evidence that the pricing umbrella erodes via demand disappointment and capex discipline, not only supply arrival. That reading is now substantially weakened: the Feb reset was a trough, not a trend. Within five months the plan re-accelerated +25% and OpenAI added vertical integration into self-build and power. The demand-side evidence survives intact and remains a legitimate counter-signal (missed 1B-WAU, missed early-2026 monthly revenue targets, Friar's private warning, Abilene cancellation, ~$25B ARR against these numbers) — but the headline capex-discipline number does not. The parent should keep the demand-disappointment evidence and stop using $600B as a capex-restraint datapoint.

Grade B remains right: journalist-reported private-company investor communications, no filings.

Not a refute — the underlying February fact is correct and well-sourced. Adjust, because a confirmed later correction moves the number 25% and reverses the claim's directional meaning for the thesis.

claims.metric: Median 'frontier lifespan' of AI chip designs (release to last frontier model trained on them)

sources.title: Leading AI chip designs are used for around four years in frontier training - Epoch AI

claims.notes: Median 2.7 years including pre-V100 chips; Epoch's headline says leading designs serve ~4 years in frontier training. Reconciles the debate: premium (frontier-training) life is 2.7-4 years — close to Burry's 2-3 — while physical life far exceeds it (MTBF >100k hours vs ~35k hours of heavy economic use), so accounting life depends on the value of cascaded inference workloads. Directly relevant to T6: payback depends on what older chips earn serving inference near marginal cost.

verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE LOCATED AND VERIFIED. Epoch AI data insight "Leading AI chip designs are used for around four years in frontier training" (Luke Emberson, Ben Snodin, David Owen), published 5 March 2025 at https://epoch.ai/data-insights/gpu-frontier-lifespan. Confirmed against Epoch's data-insights index: no newer insight on chip lifespan/depreciation exists, and the page carries no update notation or changelog.

WHAT SURVIVES. The value 2.7 is not fabricated. Epoch writes verbatim: "Including chips older than the NVIDIA V100 shortens the median lifespan from release to final use for frontier training to 2.7 years." Unit (years) is right. The metric definition in the claim ("release to last frontier model trained on them") faithfully matches Epoch's construction (chip release date to publication date of the last top-10-by-training-compute model using that design). The note's conceptual framing — frontier-training life != physical life != accounting life — is sound and is the part that actually carries the thesis.

DEFECT 1: WRONG CUT, AND IT CUTS ONE WAY. Epoch reports three medians off the same dataset: 2.1 years (all 9 V100+ designs, no idle filter), 2.7 years (all 12 designs pooled across eras), and 3.9 years (the 5 V100+ designs that pass the 7-month idle filter). The claim selects 2.7. But 2.7 is the pooled-all-eras sensitivity figure that adds 7 pre-V100 designs (Kepler/Maxwell era, median 2.6, one as short as 0.6 years) whose frontier lives were compressed by the 2012-2016 compute scale-up. Epoch's own headline — the sentence it leads with, and the title the claim cites — is 3.9 years for LEADING designs. The claim's own metric line says "leading," and its cited source title says "around four years." Reporting 2.7 under a source titled "around four years" is the single strongest hostile objection here, and it is directionally loaded: it pulls the estimate toward Burry's 2-3 years, which is precisely the debate the note says the claim adjudicates.

DEFECT 2: THE CI IS INVENTED AND IMPOSSIBLE. Epoch publishes no interval of any kind. The stated 2.4-3.1 (+/-0.35) has no source basis and cannot be reconstructed. The sample is 12 chip DESIGNS (not deployments, unweighted, K20 counts equal to A100) spanning 0.6 to 6.5 years. A distribution-free interval on a median of n=12 runs [X(4), X(9)] for ~85% coverage and [X(5), X(8)] for only ~61%; an 80% interval sits between them. Given the subgroup structure (7 values in [0.6, 3.7] with median 2.6; 5 values in [2.3, 4.5] with median 3.9), X(4) lands near 2.0-2.3 and X(9) near 3.9-4.0. An honest 80% band on the pooled figure is roughly [2.1, 3.9] — more than four times wider than claimed. Worse, the claimed band [2.4, 3.1] excludes both of Epoch's other two published medians (2.1 and 3.9), which is disqualifying: an interval that cannot contain the source's own alternative estimates of the same quantity is not representing source uncertainty, it is suppressing it.

DEFECT 3: SURVIVORSHIP / RIGHT-CENSORING, UNFLAGGED. The 7-month idle filter drops every design still in frontier use — i.e. it selects on the outcome, systematically excluding designs whose eventual frontier life is longest while they are young. The economically relevant chips for the thesis (H100, H200, GB200, TPU v5e/v5p/v6) are excluded by construction. Epoch's own contrast (2.1 with censored designs included vs 3.9 with them filtered) shows the estimate is dominated by this choice, not by sampling noise.

DEFECT 4: PERIOD OVERSTATED. "Data insight current as of 2025-2026" is misleading. The insight is March 2025 with data ending around late 2024; it has never been updated and carries zero 2026 information. Source date in the claim ("2025") should be 2025-03-05.

FURTHER SOURCE-ACKNOWLEDGED LIMITS the claim omits: chip data missing for 24 of 88 frontier models (9 posing relevant uncertainty); endpoints defined by model PUBLICATION date rather than training completion, which Epoch notes inflates measured lifespans by an unknown lag.

CORRECTION. Anchor on the source's headline figure for leading designs, 3.9 years, with an 80% band of 2.5-4.5. The band is set to span Epoch's own methodological cuts on the low side (2.1 pooled-censored, 2.7 all-designs, 2.3 modern minimum) and the observed modern maximum on the high side (4.5), acknowledging that censoring means true modern-design lifespans may exceed 4.5. If the metric is genuinely intended as the all-eras pooled figure rather than "leading" designs, then 2.7 stands as the point estimate but the CI must widen to approximately [2.1, 3.9]; either way the published 2.4-3.1 band must go.

THESIS IMPACT — this matters, it is not pedantry. At 2.7 years the note reads "close to Burry's 2-3," implying aggressive depreciation and short payback. At 3.9-4 years, frontier-training life is materially longer and sits much closer to hyperscaler 5-6 year accounting lives, which weakens the "depreciation is understated" reading and strengthens the thesis's actual claim — that inference COGS, not premature chip obsolescence, is the binding economic constraint. The load-bearing inference (payback depends on what cascaded chips earn serving inference near marginal cost) survives under either number, but the sign of the depreciation-gap argument flips. Grade B is too generous for a claim whose interval excludes two of the source's three published estimates; C is appropriate until the CI is corrected.

MATERIAL CONFLICT FOUND — the claim selects the wrong statistic from its own source, and its CI excludes the source's headline value.

WHAT THE SOURCE ACTUALLY SAYS. Epoch's "Leading AI chip designs are used for around four years in frontier training" (Luke Emberson, Ben Snodin, David Owen; published 5 Mar 2025) opens with: "The median time from the release of leading AI chips to the publication date of the last frontier model trained using them is 3.9 years." That sentence is a definitional match for the claim's stated metric ("release to last frontier model trained on them"). The claim instead reports 2.7 — a secondary pooled figure — while citing a source whose title says ~4 years. The claim is internally self-contradictory on its face.

(1) WRONG DENOMINATOR. Epoch identifies 149 frontier models trained on 14 unique chip designs, but reports lifespans for only 12: 5 designs V100-or-newer (median 3.9 yrs, range 2.3–4.5) and 7 pre-V100 designs (median 2.6 yrs, range 0.6–3.7). Pooling all 12 gives 2.7. So the claim's headline number is an artifact of a sample that is 58% obsolete 2012–2016-era parts, from a period when frontier compute doubled roughly every 6 months, total frontier training spend was in the low millions, and much "frontier" work ran on consumer/HPC silicon. Epoch itself de-emphasizes these, focusing on modern designs because of "their relevance to current industrial-scale training practices." For a thesis about the payback economics of chips bought in 2025–2026, pre-V100 designs are not the reference class. This is a textbook wrong-denominator error.

(2) CENSORING BIASES DOWNWARD, NOT UPWARD. Epoch: "We exclude any AI chip design that has been used to train a frontier model published within the last 7 months, because these chip designs may still be used in future frontier training runs" (threshold = 95th percentile interval between successive frontier runs). That exclusion is why 14 designs yield only 12 lifespans — the two dropped are the newest and longest-running. Epoch also states it must "assume that AI chip designs such as NVIDIA A100 or Google TPU v4 will not be used to train a frontier AI model in future." Both are right-truncations that shorten measured lifespans. The claim's implicit defense — Epoch's "weak upper bound" language — does not apply: that caveat concerns release→*training completion* (publication lags training by weeks/months), whereas the claim's metric is explicitly release→*publication of last frontier model*, for which the censoring bias runs the other way. Net: 3.9 is more likely an underestimate than an overestimate for modern designs.

(3) FABRICATED AND INDEFENSIBLE CI. Epoch publishes no confidence interval. The claim's 2.4–3.1 asserts 80% confidence that the true value lies below 3.9 — the number its own cited source leads with. Even taking the pooled sample at face value, n=12 with a clearly bimodal distribution (old cluster ~2.6, modern cluster ~3.9) cannot support an interval that narrow; a bootstrap median CI on 12 bimodal points would be far wider and would straddle both modes.

(4) STALE PERIOD LABEL. The claim says "current as of 2025-2026." The insight is dated 5 March 2025 with data through roughly late 2024. Epoch's genuinely recent hardware work (Global AI Computing Capacity is Doubling Every 7 Months, 9 Jan 2026) contains no lifespan estimate and explicitly assumes retirement is immaterial: "We do not account for depreciation, but its effects are negligible since compute quantities are growing far faster than they depreciate" — mild corroboration that deployed chips are not being retired on a ~2.7-year cadence.

(5) MISLEADING FOR THE THESIS. The notes use 2.7 to bracket Burry's 2–3 year figure ("premium life is 2.7–4 years — close to Burry's 2-3"). Correcting to 3.9 breaks that alignment and pushes the opposite way: frontier-training life alone is ~4 years for modern accelerators, and this metric is a strict LOWER bound on revenue-generating life because it stops counting the moment a chip leaves frontier *training*, ignoring the cascaded inference tail that hyperscalers monetize. Hyperscaler accounting lives of 5–6 years for the same silicon are consistent with 3.9 years of frontier training plus a multi-year inference tail; they are hard to reconcile with 2.7. Using the shortest available version of an already-narrow metric compounds the understatement in the direction that flatters the short-life narrative.

WHY ADJUST RATHER THAN REFUTE. The 2.7 figure is genuinely printed in the source, so this is misselection rather than fabrication — but the correct value for the metric as the claim defines it, for the reference class the thesis requires, is 3.9 years.

CORRECTED CI DERIVATION. Point estimate 3.9 (Epoch's modern-chip median, n=5, observed range 2.3–4.5). Sampling uncertainty on a median with n=5 is wide — a bootstrap spans roughly the 2nd-to-4th order statistics, about 3.0–4.3. Adjusting upward for the two structural truncations (H100-class exclusion; the assumed retirement of A100/TPU v4 from frontier training, which by 2026 looks optimistic) and downward slightly for publication lag, I set an 80% interval of 3.2–4.5. This brackets Epoch's own "around four years" headline and excludes 2.7, which belongs to a different reference class.

GRADE. B is too generous for the 2.7 version; it should be C, since the stated value contradicts the title of its sole source. The corrected 3.9 merits roughly B/B- — single source, n=5, known right-censoring, and a metric that measures only frontier-training life rather than the total economic life the thesis actually needs.

The 72% figure is only reachable by comparing a hyperscaler-tier peak (~$8-9.34) to a marketplace/neocloud-tier trough (~$1.92-2.20). Silicon Data's own May 2026 post is literally titled "Same Chip, Two Tiers, Two Regimes" and reports the hyperscaler tier trading at a ~3x premium to neocloud. A large part of the "72% price decline" is buyers substituting tiers, not a like-for-like price falling.

COVERAGE ARTIFACT. Silicon Data's methodology post ("Building a Robust GPU Index," Mar 2026) states verified data spans "Sep 1, 2024 onward." Their own table shows Marketplace coverage starting June 2024 and Neocloud July 2024 — before that the series is hyperscaler-only by construction. So the 2023/early-2024 "peak" cannot be compared to a 2026 blended/neocloud level without measuring index coverage expansion as price movement.

THE NOTES' TROUGH AND REBOUND ARE NOT CORROBORATED. The claim's "1-yr reserved bottoming ~$1.70 (Oct 2025) then rebounding ~40% to ~$2.35 (Mar 2026)" comes from the Value Add VC blend, not the index. The primary index shows: Aug 2025 $2.22-2.26; Sep 2025 low $2.13, close ~$2.16 (Silicon Data flagged $2.13-2.15 as the floor); Dec 9, 2025 $2.00; Jan 6, 2026 $2.20 (+10% over four weeks); neocloud $2.63 on Apr 1, $2.47 trough Apr 8, $2.75 on May 31, and +12.7% over the trailing three months to early June 2026. So the trough is ~$2.00 in Dec 2025, not $1.70 in Oct 2025, and the measured rebound is ~+10-13%, not ~40% — the claim overstates the rebound by roughly 3x and mixes 1-yr reserved (trough) with on-demand (peak).

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. The metric says "peak-to-trough ... through 2026-03," but the notes place the trough in Oct 2025 with a rebound thereafter. 2026-03 is a post-rebound endpoint, not a trough.

WHAT SURVIVES. A large decline in the price a marginal buyer pays for an H100-hour is real and well documented; Silicon Data's own prose makes the mixed-tier comparison ("early 2024 ~$8.00/hr" vs "$2.00"), which yields ~75%. The absolute maximum defensible with primary data is $9.39 (max hyperscaler H2 2024) to $1.92 (min marketplace H2 2025) = 79.6% — max-to-min across tiers, which is why I cap the CI at 77 rather than 82. The claimed 82 high requires the uncorroborated $1.70.

CI VERDICT. The claim's note says "CI wide because 'the' H100 price spans tiers," but the interval 60-82 excludes the entire like-for-like within-tier range (20-40%) that the tier ambiguity generates. That is the fatal flaw: the acknowledged uncertainty is not reflected in the interval. A corrected 80% CI must straddle both readings. I set 60 [30, 77]: central pulled down from 72 to reflect ~25-40% weight on the strict within-tier reading, low bound at 30 to cover hyperscaler-only and marketplace-only like-for-like, high bound at 77 to cover the aggressive mixed-tier reading without the unsupported $1.70.

NOTE FOR THE THESIS (T5): the tier-separated data is actually stronger evidence than the 72% headline. Silicon Data shows a two-regime market as of mid-2026: an administered hyperscaler tier flat at ~$7.5/hr with 3.8% annualized volatility (pricing far above marginal cost, unmoved by neocloud supply entry), and a competitive neocloud/marketplace tier at ~$2.5-2.8 with 18.4% annualized volatility that fell toward marginal cost and has been firming since Dec 2025. The "prices fell toward marginal cost as supply arrived, then firmed when demand caught up" story holds cleanly for the neocloud tier — but the magnitude of the fall in that tier is ~25-40%, not 72%. Recommend the essay cite the two-tier structure and the ~10-13% measured 2026 firming rather than the 72% composite, which will not survive a hostile reviewer.

CONTRADICTION FOUND — the 72% is a denominator switch, and it is visible inside the claim's own primary source.

1. Silicon Data's per-tier table (the claim's source #1) shows the "collapse" is a composition artifact, not a price series. Re-extracting the tier breakdown: Aug–Dec 2023 and Jan–May 2024 contain ONLY a hyperscaler tier (~$7.7, then $7.37–8.24 / median $7.92). The Marketplace tier first appears June 2024 at $2.50–3.19 (median $2.58) and the Neocloud tier July 2024 at $2.74–3.01 (median $2.99) — i.e. both cheap tiers enter the index INSIDE the claim's own stated peak window ("2023-H2 2024 peak"), already fully formed and already ~3x below hyperscaler list. The 72% therefore requires taking the numerator from the only tier tracked in 2023 (hyperscaler) and the denominator from a tier that entered coverage in mid-2024.

2. No single tier declines anywhere near 60–82%. Like-for-like arithmetic (Silicon Data tiers + SDH100RT live + GetDeploying Jul 2026): Hyperscaler $9.34 (H2-24 peak) → $6.26 (H2-25) = −33%; → $6.88–6.98 (Jul-26) = −26%; vs the 2023 level $7.76 → $6.93 = −11%. Marketplace $2.58 (Jun-24 debut) → $1.92–2.00 (late-25 trough) = −24%; → $2.35 (Mar-26) = −9%; → $1.89 (cheapest Jul-26) = −27%. Neocloud $2.99 (Jul-24 debut) → $2.53 (SDH100RT, Jul-26) = −15%; → $2.00 (Dec-9-25 low) = −33%. The maximum defensible same-tier decline is 33% — the entire claimed CI (60–82) excludes every like-for-like construction. The prior contradiction pass noted the tier-mixing objection but dismissed it; it did not have the tier-entry dates, which is what converts the objection from a caveat into a defect. The cheap tier's absence from 2023 data is a statement about index coverage, not about the market: Lambda, RunPod, Vast.ai, CoreWeave and others were renting H100s in 2023, and a tier that appears "tightly clustered at $2.50–3.19" on its first observation did not spring into existence that month.

3. The three cited sources disagree by ~2x on the same tier and period, so "multiple trackers" is not corroboration. Introl (source #2) puts Dec-2025 hyperscaler on-demand at $3.25–3.50 (AWS P5, GCP A3-High, Azure ND); Silicon Data puts the hyperscaler tier at $6.20–6.64 for Jul–Dec 2025, and GetDeploying reads $6.88–6.98 in Jul 2026. Both cannot be right. Worse, Introl and Value Add VC both derive their figures from Silicon Data, so the evidence base is effectively one index provider plus two SEO restatements — thinner than grade B implies. And the sources' own published numbers are lower than 72: Introl states 64%, Value Add VC states 64–75%.

4. Endpoint is internally inconsistent and cuts against the framing. The metric says "peak-to-trough" but the period runs "through 2026-03," after a documented rebound. SDH100RT is $2.53 today (Jul 2026), +27% off the $2.00 Dec-2025 low; 1-yr reserved rebounded ~40% from $1.70 (Oct-25) to $2.35 (Mar-26). Anchoring on early 2026 is peak-to-partial-recovery, not peak-to-trough — the two readings differ by ~10pp and the claim uses whichever is convenient.

5. Marketing framing and wrong deflator. Silicon Data's prose ("plummeted from around $8/hr in early 2024 to $1.50–3.00 by late 2025" ≈ −72%) contradicts the structure of its own tier table, and the company sells GPU price indices and derivatives — volatility is the product. Separately, H100 is a 2022-architecture part competing in 2026 against H200/B200/GB200/MI355X; a falling rental rate on a legacy SKU is substantially vintage depreciation, which inflates the measured decline relative to the thesis-relevant quantity (price per unit of frontier-quality intelligence).

WHY ADJUST RATHER THAN REFUTE: the direction and a large magnitude survive. The blended price a typical buyer actually pays for an H100-hour did fall a lot (~65–70%) because hyperscaler list came down ~26–33% AND demand migrated to a cheap tier — a real effect, and the ~300-neocloud supply-entry mechanism the thesis needs is genuine. But whether the "peak" price is $8 (hyperscaler list, the only 2023 observation) or ~$2.60 (what a price-sensitive buyer could already pay at the H2-2024 peak) is unresolved and hinges on 2023 low-tier capacity availability, which I could not verify (archive.org fetch blocked, search budget exhausted). That irreducible ambiguity belongs in the CI, and the current CI puts zero mass on the same-tier reading.

CORRECTION: value 60 (down from 72), CI 28–78 (from 60–82). The upper bound retains the published consensus (64–80%, cross-tier/blended); the lower bound admits the like-for-like readings (15–33%) the current CI wrongly excludes. Grade should drop B → C: single effective source, 2x internal disagreement, undisclosed denominator switch. For thesis use, the honest framing is "the blended market-clearing price of an H100-hour fell roughly 60–70% as supply entered, then firmed ~27% off the Dec-2025 low," not "H100 rental prices fell 72%."

claims.notes: SemiAnalysis: an H100 placed in service ~2023 'may have already recouped its investment' (~2 yr payback at $4-8/hr scarcity pricing); an H100 deployed at late-2025 prices has NEGATIVE project NPV on 1-3-month and 1-year terms; a B200 on a 3-yr contract at high-$2/low-$3 per hour reaches positive IRR only near end of year 3. verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCES LOCATED AND READ IN FULL.

1) Source #2 is the real primary source, and I recovered it verbatim. The X post (402-blocked to normal fetch) is a long-form note tweet; I pulled the full text via the fxtwitter API and confirmed the snowflake/created_at as 2025-09-03T02:08:11Z. Every mechanism sentence in the claim's notes is verbatim-faithful: "an H100 put into service two years ago may have already recouped its investment"; "an H100 placed into service today would have a significantly negative project net present value (NPV) in both scenarios: selling into the 1-3 month term market and with a one-year fixed contract"; "a B200 rented on a three year term contract in the high $2 or low $3 range will reach a positive project IRR around the end of the third year of the contract." The parenthetical in the metric and the qualitative mechanism therefore CONFIRM cleanly.

2) I also recovered the chart attached to that post (pbs.twimg.com/media/Gz4xo80bAAIXrgi.jpg) — an actual table from SemiAnalysis's AI Cloud TCO model: "AI Neocloud Comparative 5-Year Project IRR with 3y Fixed Initial Term," H100/B200/GB200 "Neocloud Giants," Total Cost per Unit per Hour $1.62 / $2.26 / $2.62, an 11-row H100 IRR grid from $4.00/hr (130.3%) down to $1.50/hr (-7.3%), with footnotes fixing yr4/yr5 H100 rents at $0.70 and $0.50. This is a genuine primary disclosure and materially obviates the claim's "paywalled model" caveat.

3) THE NUMBER IS NOT FAITHFUL. Neither source ever states a payback period. The only quantitative anchor is "put into service two years ago may have already recouped its investment," said in Sept 2025 — i.e. payback ≤ ~2.0 years for a 2023-vintage unit, with "may" placing it right at that boundary. The claim's value of 2.5 years is ABOVE the source's own ceiling. The claim's own notes even say "~2 yr payback," so the value field contradicts its own annotation.

4) INDEPENDENT RECONSTRUCTION from SemiAnalysis's own parameters. I least-squares-fit the 11-row H100 IRR grid for (capex per annual hour, opex): opex = $0.72/GPU-hr, capex/annual-hour = $2.82 (per-row implied values cluster $2.7-3.1 across the mid-grid; the fit is not exact, so their model carries additional structure — taxes, ramp, or terminal value). That implies ~$23-25k/GPU capex for a late-2025 deployment. A 2023 buyer paid far more: Source #1's public text (fetched; Part 2 economics genuinely paywalled, and it contains NO payback/IRR/NPV figure) gives ~$318k per 8-GPU compute server reference architecture = ~$39.8k/GPU, or ~$283k = ~$35.4k/GPU optimized, excluding storage, as of Oct 2024 — with 2023 higher still. Running payback = capex/((price - $0.72)*hours) at $40-50k/GPU and 80-93% utilization on a declining 2023-onward rent path yields 1.4-2.3 years (central ~1.7-1.9). On a fixed 3-yr 2023 contract at $4.00/hr with $45k capex and 85% util, 1.84 years. Nothing in the defensible parameter space lands at 2.5 unless you assume a poorly-run small operator at ~70% utilization with $50k capex — which is the opposite of the operator SemiAnalysis is describing ("There is a great way to run a Neocloud business... Time to market is essential").

5) THE CI IS NOT HONEST AT THE TOP. ci80_high = 4.0 years would require the 2023-vintage H100 to be less than two-thirds paid back by Sept 2025 — a flat contradiction of the claim's own primary source. A 4-year payback only appears in my grid at $50k capex, 80% util, and $2.50/hr rents, i.e. late-2025 pricing applied retroactively to the scarcity era. The upper tail is unsupportable and should be truncated at ~2.5.

CORRECTION: value 1.9 years (reconciling my reconstruction's ~1.7-1.9 center with the source's hedged ~2.0 ceiling), ci80 [1.3, 2.5]. Low bound admits sustained high-scarcity rents ($6+/hr) at high utilization (0.9-1.1 yr at the extreme, so 1.3 is a fair 10th percentile); high bound admits $50k capex, 80% util, and faster price decay while stopping where the source's own sentence stops.

CAVEATS ON MY OWN WORK: the session's web-search budget was exhausted before I started, so I could not re-verify third-party 2023-24 H100 rental trackers this session; the price path I used ($4.50/$3.50/$2.75) is from prior knowledge, not freshly sourced, which is a reason to keep the CI as wide as I have. Also flagged: Source #1 is mis-cited — it supports capex only, not payback, and the "$4-8/hr scarcity pricing" in the notes appears in neither cited source.

DIRECTION OF ERROR AND THESIS IMPACT: the correction moves payback DOWN, which strengthens rather than threatens the thesis mechanism. A ~1.9-year scarcity-era payback against explicitly negative NPV for a late-2025 H100 deployment is a sharper contrast than 2.5 years, and the recovered $1.62/hr "total cost per unit per hour" reconciles with the fitted capex only under roughly 3-year depreciation — itself an independent datapoint that economic life is running well short of hyperscaler 5-6 year book lives. Grade B remains appropriate, arguably generous for the specific payback figure since the source never numbers it.

ADJUST on two independent grounds: the point value is higher than its own primary source supports, and the parenthetical half of the metric ("negative NPV for new H100 deployments by late 2025") has since been falsified by SemiAnalysis itself.

(1) PRIMARY SOURCE RETRIEVED VERBATIM. x.com blocked WebFetch (HTTP 402), but the tweet was recovered in full through the fxtwitter and vxtwitter API mirrors (posted 2025-09-03 02:08 UTC). Exact text: "an H100 put into service two years ago may have already recouped its investment, but today, buyers will only sign one-year term contracts at most... Our analysis shows that an H100 placed into service today would have a significantly negative project net present value (NPV) in both scenarios: selling into the 1-3 month term market and with a one-year fixed contract... a B200 rented on a three year term contract in the high $2 or low $3 range will reach a positive project IRR around the end of the third year." The B200/negative-NPV notes are faithful. But "put into service two years ago may have ALREADY recouped" logically caps payback at ~2 years for that vintage — a 2.5-year payback would make the sentence false. The claimed 2.5 is not derivable from the source; ~2.0 is.

(2) THE CLAIM'S STATED RATIONALE IS ARITHMETICALLY INCOHERENT. The notes justify 2.5 as "~2 yr payback at $4-8/hr scarcity pricing." Those are contradictory: $4-8/hr does not produce a 2-2.5 year payback. Reconstructing SemiAnalysis's own published cost model (SemiAnalysis, "GPU Cloud Economics Explained," 2023-12-04, public section): GPU server capital cost $7,025/month and hosting $1,871/month per 8-GPU node, giving an all-in $1.525/GPU-hr — and implying $33-44k capex/GPU depending on debt tenor ($38.6k at 5yr/13%, cross-checked against the Oct-2024 Playbook's $283-318k per 8-GPU server BoM), with hosting ~$2.8k/GPU/yr. At $4/hr and 90% utilization payback is 1.2-1.6 years; at $8/hr it is 0.6-0.8 years. The $4-8/hr band is the on-demand/spot tier, not what a fleet actually earned. SemiAnalysis's own scarcity-era statement was: "even the most favorable GPU cloud deals are around $2 an hour per H100, and we have even seen desperate folks get fleeced for more than $3 an hour." At $2.50-3.50/hr contract pricing the model yields payback of 1.4-2.7 years, centering ~2.0-2.3. Corroborated independently by SemiAnalysis (2026-04-02): "H100s are getting renewed at the exact same rate they were signed at 2-3 years ago" — i.e. 2023-24 contracts were struck near today's ~$2.35-2.85/hr, not $4-8.

(3) THE "NEGATIVE NPV BY LATE 2025" HALF IS NOW REFUTED BY THE SAME SOURCE. SemiAnalysis, "The Great GPU Shortage" (2026-04-02, public text): "H100 1-year GPU rental contract pricing has shot up almost 40% from a low of $1.70/hr/GPU in October 2025 to $2.35/hr/GPU by March 2026. On-Demand GPU rental capacity is sold out across all GPU types"; "all capacity coming online until August to September 2026 has already been booked"; "some H100 contracts are being renewed for 4 years though 2028"; and explicitly: "Before late 2025, the prevailing expectation across the ecosystem was that Hopper rental prices would drop considerably as Blackwell deployments ramped... Instead, the opposite happened in late 2025." The Sept-2025 negative-NPV call rested on a forecast — "the rollout of GB300 NVL72... will put significant pressure on H100 prices" by Sept 2026 — that did not materialize. An H100 placed in service at the Oct-2025 trough is renewing into a shortage at 40%+ higher rates, so it is very unlikely to have realized a significantly negative NPV. This matters for the thesis: the datapoint was recruited to show "the scarcity umbrella collapsed and pushed payback beyond depreciation lives," but the umbrella re-formed within six months. The honest mechanism is two-sided timing risk (SemiAnalysis's Sept-2025 call was itself a casualty of it), not a one-way collapse.

(4) SOURCING WEAKNESS. Source #1 (Oct-2024 "AI Neocloud Playbook") is paywalled at exactly the economics section — I pulled its full public text and it contains no payback, IRR, NPV, utilization or rental-rate figure, only BoM ($318k reference / $283k optimized per compute server). So the tweet is the sole public evidence, and it points to ~2 years.

CORRECTED CI. The upper bound of 4 years is not defensible for the 2023/early-2024 vintage: reaching 4 years requires ~$1.7/hr gross, below the $2/hr floor SemiAnalysis reported for that era, or utilization well under 70%. Cap at 3.0 (the $2.00/hr, high-capex, 90%-utilization corner). Low bound 1.4 (a $3.50/hr deal on $35k capex); going below that would require the on-demand-tier pricing that fleets did not actually realize on committed capacity. Note also that the vendor-marketing pole (Nvidia's "$1 of GPU capex returns ~$5 of rental revenue over 4 years," which SemiAnalysis derides as "Jensen Math") points to a shorter payback still — recalled, not verifiable in this session, so not relied on. Net: value 2.0, CI80 1.4-3.0; keep grade B but strip or heavily qualify the "negative NPV by late 2025" parenthetical, since as an ex-post statement it is wrong and as an ex-ante model output it was a forecast the author has since walked back. Caveat: the session's web-search budget was exhausted, so this verification is built on primary SemiAnalysis text retrieved directly (sitemap/archive API + article HTML) plus arithmetic on their published figures, rather than a broad third-party critique sweep.

claims.notes: Lineage: $200B question (Sep 2023) -> $600B (Jun 2024) -> ~$3T needed against ~$1.5T of 2026 infrastructure spend. verification.reasoning:
PRIMARY SOURCE FOUND — and it is not either source the claim cites. The $3T figure originates in David Cahn's own Substack post "AI's $1.5T Question" (dcahn.substack.com/p/ais-15t-question, July 8, 2026), which TechCrunch's Tim Fernholz wrote up the next day. Three material problems:

(1) THE NUMBER IS THE WRONG ONE. Cahn's post says verbatim: "Most forecasts have 2026 hyperscaler data center CapEx in the $750B ballpark," and the heuristic is to take that "and multiply it by two (reflecting the margin requirement)" — "Doubling that yields the same $1.5T." Hence the title, "AI's $1.5T question," and "July 2026: AI's $1.5T question." The $3T appears only as a *cumulative* figure across all vintages: "These numbers are cumulative — if you wanted to know the total required revenue for today's AI buildout (cumulatively) since ChatGPT, you'd add up the numbers and arrive at roughly $3T of lifetime required revenue thus far." So $3T = 2023+2024+2025+2026 capex vintages summed, not the revenue required to justify 2026 spending. The claim's metric ("required to justify 2026 AI infrastructure spending") maps to $1.5T in the primary source. The claim's CI [2, 4] does not even contain the correct value — a hard CI failure, not just a point-estimate miss.

(2) THE CAPEX BASE IN THE CLAIM'S NOTE IS ITSELF THE ANSWER, DOUBLE-COUNTED. The note says "~$3T needed against ~$1.5T of 2026 infrastructure spend." That comes from TechCrunch: "Cahn's got a new number on AI infrastructure spending for 2026: $1.5 trillion. All told, he calculates that the AI industry will have to earn $3 trillion..." But in Cahn's post $1.5T IS the required revenue and $750B is the capex. TechCrunch appears to have promoted the output to the input and re-applied the 2x, or fused the cumulative $3T with the 2026 vintage. The claim inherits that error verbatim.

(3) UNIT/PERIOD IS MISSTATED. Cahn is explicit: "This analysis arrives at the lifetime end-customer revenue requirement for a single year of CapEx." It is lifetime revenue against one vintage of capex, not "USD trillions per year." (Defensibly, $1.5T/yr is still the right steady-state annual number IF capex holds at ~$750B/yr and assets have uniform lives — L simultaneous vintages each needing 2C over L years = 2C per year — so I am keeping "per year" units at the corrected value, but the claim should flag that this is a steady-state reinterpretation, not Cahn's stated framing.)

SOURCING HYGIENE: The cited Sequoia essay "AI in 2026: A Tale of Two AIs" (Dec 3, 2025) contains NO required-revenue calculation at all. It only says end revenue is "on the order of tens of billions per year" against investment "on the order of trillions over the coming five years," and that coding and ChatGPT will each "approach or cross double digit billions of revenue this year." The claim's period field ("Calculated for 2026 (essay Dec 2025; restated via TechCrunch Jul 2026)") therefore asserts a provenance that does not exist — the calculation is seven months later and on a different masthead. Methodology lineage does check out: the June 2024 "$600B Question" states the same rule verbatim — "take Nvidia's run-rate revenue forecast and multiply it by 2x to reflect the total cost of AI data centers (GPUs are half of the total cost of ownership)... multiply by 2x again, to reflect a 50% gross margin for the end-user of the GPU." Note the 2x-TCO leg only applies when starting from chip revenue; starting from total data center capex, only the margin 2x applies. The claim's metric string ("~2x TCO x ~2x for margin") implies 4x on the 2026 capex base, which would give $3T from $750B — that may be the arithmetic that made $3T feel self-consistent, but it double-counts non-chip capex.

Grade B is too generous for a load-bearing number sourced through a secondary write-up that a primary check contradicts by 2x; I would drop to C even after correction, because the corrected value still depends on an unobservable margin assumption and a forecast capex base.

CORRECTED: $1.5T. CI: capex base uncertainty (2026 hyperscaler DC capex forecasts plausibly $600–900B against Cahn's "$750B ballpark," and he warns "the required revenue per GW of CapEx has sharply increased due to these bottleneck dynamics and rising costs of construction") times margin-multiple uncertainty (1.6x–2.5x for a blended hyperscaler + AI-product-company margin) gives roughly 1.0–2.2; I set an 80% CI of 1.1–2.1.

THESIS IMPACT: The demand-elasticity burden this claim places on T5/T6 is half what was assumed for the 2026 vintage. If the argument elsewhere compares required revenue to current AI revenue (TechCrunch cites Anthropic "thought to have hit $60 billion in ARR" and OpenAI "$13 billion" in 2025 / "$20 billion ARR" in Nov 2025), the gap is ~$1.5T lifetime against 2026 capex, not $3T/yr. Any downstream sentence of the form "AI must generate $3T a year" should be rewritten as either "$1.5T of lifetime revenue against 2026's ~$750B of capex" or "~$3T cumulatively across the entire post-ChatGPT buildout."

CONTRADICTION FOUND, DECISIVE, IN THE PRIMARY SOURCE. The $3T figure is a media garble of Cahn's own arithmetic, and it is off by 2x for the metric as stated.

1) What Cahn actually wrote. The real primary source is not the Dec 2025 Sequoia essay (which I fetched: it contains NO required-revenue arithmetic — only "The end revenue from AI remains limited (on the order of tens of billions per year)" vs "data center and energy investments (on the order of trillions over the coming five years)"). It is Cahn's Substack post "AI's $1.5T Question" (dcahn.substack.com, Jul 8, 2026), which is the post the cited TechCrunch article is reporting on. Verbatim: "Take Nvidia's projected Q4 run-rate data center revenue x 2 (to reflect total data center CapEx, including non-chip expenses) x 2 (to reflect a 50% margin across the hyperscaler and the AI product company)." Cross-check in the same post: "Most forecasts have 2026 hyperscaler data center CapEx in the $750B ballpark. Doubling that yields the same $1.5T."

2) The claim inverts the two numbers. Under Cahn's own math, 2026 AI infrastructure spend is ~$750B (not $1.5T), and the required revenue for that vintage is $1.5T (not $3T). The claim's own metric string is internally incoherent on its face: "~2x TCO x ~2x margin" applied to "~$1.5T of 2026 infrastructure spend" would give $6T, not $3T — the tell that $1.5T had already absorbed both multiples. The title lineage confirms it: in Cahn's series the headline number is always the REQUIRED REVENUE ($200B question 2023, $600B question 2024, $1.5T question 2026), never the capex.

3) What $3T actually is. Verbatim from the post: "if you wanted to know the total required revenue for today's AI buildout (cumulatively) since ChatGPT, you'd add up the numbers and arrive at roughly $3T of lifetime required revenue thus far" ($200B + $600B + ~$840B + $1.5T). So $3T is CUMULATIVE across four capex vintages, 2023–2026 — a different denominator entirely. TechCrunch ("Cahn's got a new number on AI infrastructure spending for 2026: $1.5 trillion... the AI industry will have to earn $3 trillion to justify all those chips") conflated the two, and the claim inherited that error plus a misattribution to the Dec 2025 essay.

4) Unit problem, second-order. Cahn also explicitly reframes the output as lifetime, not annual: "This analysis arrives at the lifetime end-customer revenue requirement for a single year of CapEx." That is a material walk-back from the 2024 "$600B Question" framing (which read as an annual gap) and it defuses the standard wrong-denominator critique. $1.5T of lifetime revenue against ~5-6 year hardware life is ~$250-300B/yr of incremental revenue attributable to the 2026 vintage. The claim's "per year" unit only survives under a steady-state reading (five overlapping vintages each at ~$300B/yr, with capex held at ~$750B/yr, sums back to ~$1.5T/yr) — which is coincidentally coherent, but only at 1.5, never at 3.

5) Rival estimates land near 1.5-2.0, not 3. Bain's 2025 Global Technology Report (~$2T of combined annual AI revenue needed by 2030, ~$800B shortfall) is a cash-funding rather than payback-with-margin construction, and it puts an ~$2T requirement four years LATER than the claim's $3T-for-2026 — an independent sanity check that 3 is too high for 2026. (I could not re-fetch the Bain page directly this session — 404 — so I am not listing it as a verified extra source.) Morgan Stanley's $1.5T financing gap on $2.9T of capex through 2028 is likewise a different metric and does not support $3T/yr in 2026.

6) No later correction found. Google News surfaces only the TechCrunch piece (Jul 9, 2026) and a CryptoRank syndication of it; no correction, and no third-party critique of the $1.5T post yet (two weeks old). The prior contradiction-lens pass that confirmed 3 relied on TechCrunch's wording without reading Cahn's post; reading the post breaks it.

CORRECTION: value 1.5 USD trillions (Cahn's stated requirement for 2026-vintage capex), CI80 [1.2, 2.0]. Bounds reflect the two live input uncertainties — 2026 hyperscaler/DC capex forecast dispersion (~$600-850B) and the 50% margin assumption (40-60% → 1.67x-2.5x) — with upside skew from Cahn's own caveat that his number is "probably an underestimate" given rising memory costs, inference-specific silicon, and that "the required revenue per GW of CapEx has sharply increased." The upper bound also spans Bain's $2T. Grade should stay B (heuristic-dependent, not an observable) and the notes should be rewritten: source is the Jul 8 2026 Substack, not the Dec 2025 essay; $3T is cumulative-since-ChatGPT; the figure is lifetime-per-vintage, not a strict annual run-rate. The thesis-relevant point (T5/T6 demand elasticity required for payback) is unharmed in direction — a $1.5T requirement against AI end revenue in the tens of billions is still an enormous gap — but the load-bearing magnitude is halved, which matters if the parent essay quotes "$3 trillion a year" as the hurdle.
